items.title: FAA Identifies Patches for Last Week's Flight-Grounding Router Issue. But Was Staffing an Issue?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
CNN published an exclusive report Tuesdayon what caused last week's nationwide ground stop for flights in the U.S.. A source familiar with the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation says they've recreated the issue in a lab "and believe they found the culprit."

Investigators have focused on determining why a new router at a remote Arkansas radio site overwhelmed the nation's air traffic control system with a massive amount of data, triggering gaps in radar and radio communications. They found an overlooked router setting affected how it interfaced with other decades-old routers that the FAA is decommissioning, the source said. Investigators believe software updates are needed and that those patches will prevent a repeat of the system failure... 

This month's ground stop not only focused attention on upgrades being made to the aging system, which have been paused as the agency investigated the incident, but also raised questions about FAA oversight of private companies charged with maintaining the network... On the day of the network meltdown, L3Harris was undertaking a maintenance job that involved switching the system from a decades-old router to a new one. In the past, this kind of work typically involved at least six FAA employees. Under the Trump administration, it's now often coordinated by one employee: an FAA liaison. And there are only four people in the country with that title, according to sources familiar with the process. 

The liaison's job involves coordinating and scheduling these upgrades — not approving them, sources said... The Trump administration's effort to move maintenance work along faster also eliminated a layer of FAA review that was critical to assessing risk [according to a source familiar with the process]. Previously, local technical operations managers, site technicians and others would determine when the work could be done with the least impact on air traffic and to game out worst-case scenarios. The union contends that process did not happen before L3Harris arrived at the El Dorado, Arkansas, site on November 13... [David Spero, president of the union], contends the FAA has given private companies "too much authority and generally unfettered access." 

CNN also points out a 2009 incident where 129 of America's air traffic facilities experienced an outage of FAA telecommunications "that delayed thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide. 

"The cause: A technician with Harris Corp., which later merged with L3 Technologies to form L3Harris, incorrectly configured an FAA telecommunications router at the Los Angeles Center..."

items.title: The Birds Are Listening: Scientists Used Seabirds to Track Hidden Ships
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
, our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week.

In what sounds like an avian riff on , scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders in order to listen in on their interactions with fishing vessels across the world’s oceans, according to a study published on Wednesday in .

The approach exposed a large number of so-called “unseen” vessels that did not have their location trackers switched on. Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship’s location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons—such as evading pirates—or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. 

The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming “bycatch” when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.

Unseen vessel activity “is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal,” said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a “powerful tool for improving risk assessment” by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map. 

Rutter and his colleagues were inspired to combine these approaches by attaching audio recorders to three seabird species—the northern gannet, Balearic shearwater, and Westland petrel—which all frequently interact with fishing vessels. The team tracked the movements of the birds with GPS, and then analyzed whether the audio overlapped with AIS data at the same time and location during recorded interactions.

The recordings showed that about 32 percent of the audio captured by seven gannets in the North Atlantic were from ships with their trackers off, while 12 percent of the audio captured by four shearwaters in the Mediterranean Sea were from unseen vessels. The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off.

Rutter noted that the shearwaters were likely often interacting with smaller Mediterranean fishing boats that are not legally required to keep trackers on. However, the gannets encountered larger commercial vessels that are obligated to keep trackers active. While the researchers made a very conservative estimate that these birds visited unseen vessels for about one-third of the total duration of their daily encounters (or, about 22 minutes out of 68 minutes), it may well exceed half of that time.

“The fact that we found at least one third, and probably more than one half, of the audio detections being unseen was pretty surprising,” Rutter said. “This is not the same thing as saying that half of vessels are unseen; it's half of the time that gannets go to vessels, those vessels are unseen.”

“There are multiple reasons this could be,” he continued. “It could be illegal disabling, but at the same time, it could be poor satellite reception. There are lots of reasons that AIS can be off, and we want to emphasize that illegal fishing is a possibility, but that is not actually what we're showing. It's showing that there's a lot we're not seeing.”

Seabirds are attracted to fishing vessels to feed on discarded catch, but many perish during these encounters after becoming tangled in lines or caught on baited hooks. Rutter and his colleagues hope that their study could help to prevent these deadly incidents, while also providing a new tool for monitoring unseen vessel activity. 

While this approach could enable real-time vessel detection, the team urged “caution in the use of animals as a fisheries surveillance tool, lest fishers come to mistrust scientists and/or marine animals themselves,” according to the study.

Though environmental and commercial interests are often at odds, there is plenty of collaboration between fisheries and conservation scientists with the goal of sustainable and healthy long-term fish stock. Fisheries that adhere to regulations also have an interest in working with researchers to combat illegal activity by competitors.

In addition, these audio recordings offer a new way to eavesdrop on wild seabird behavior. For example, the petrel’s recordings captured distinct landing and takeoff sequences previously observed in albatrosses, opening a new avenue of research into the flight patterns of this species. The recordings also highlight how human activity has upended food webs, as seabirds have become dependent on fishing vessel waste as a major source of food. 

“One of the advantages of this is that we can understand in a more unbiased way how much [seabirds] actually interact with vessels—every day, multiple times a day for all the species we looked at actually, which is crazy if you think about it,” Rutter said. 

“They're going out every day and just visiting boats all the time, and that shows the impact that we have on them as humans is really changing their feeding ecology,” he concluded.

items.content:
The Associated Press reports:


A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks. But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company's lawyer said was a "profound rejection" of the government's narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying. Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners. 

The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds. In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case in Brooklyn federal court involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September... 

Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in "economic bullying" and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.

items.title: The New Robber Barons Aren’t Ready For The Fight
items.author: Anil Dash
items.content:
Ten years ago, I began writing a series about how we could move toward humane tech. Over the next year, I tried to get the people who build technology to look honestly at what the industry was becoming, while there was still time to change it. As you may be aware, that didn’t quite succeed.

Every once in a while, I’ll see people passing around links to some of those pieces, specifically to call out a couple of predictions that I made with the genuine hope that I would turn out to be wrong.

In a time of rising inequality, those who profit greatly while massively disrupting the stability of ordinary people tend to not be seen very kindly. The oil and steel barons of the past were seen as high tech innovators and valuable job creators for a while, until their excesses and abuses earned them a serious backlash.

That post was framed around a simple warning: unless people in tech became more self-critical, the industry’s leaders would come to be seen as the new robber barons. And then about six months later, in “How do we reform tech?”, I tried to say what was at stake if we didn’t:

The single biggest threat to the long-term health and growth of the tech sector is the backlash that could be caused by tech’s worst abuses and excesses.

At the time, plenty of people in the industry read those as the worries of a pessimist. That was also the era when tech’s most powerful voices (the investors who would have you believe that writing checks matters more than writing code) began a systematic campaign to undermine all criticism. They began to position journalists as their enemies, and said that anyone who was critical of tech leaders having absolute, unaccountable power over the economy and society was an enemy of progress, someone who hated innovation. It did not matter if, as was often the case, those of us who were being critical were actually creating innovations than the financiers who were pushing this big lie about tech criticism.

It may be hard to remember now, but a decade ago, tech was still treated as the unalloyed good guys. Founders and CEOs were the job creators and the inventors of the future, and politicians of every stripe were happy to be photographed next to tech’s biggest names. Media stories were framed around how parents would want their kids to be “the next Zuckerberg”.

As you may be aware, that is not the world we live in now.

We’ve arrived at the reckoning I was describing, and it’s worse than we’d have imagined. Tech’s most powerful voices have embraced authoritarianism wholesale, enthusiastically adopted an openly corrupt form of cronyism as central to their business models, and aggressively gone to war against their own workers (and labor in general) as part of a campaign to ensure that they’re never held accountable for any of the harms or wrongs that they cause. The result? A political environment where the largest tech companies and their founders are seen, accurately, as completely unregulated and unaccountable powers that inflict their will upon people across the world without consent or consideration.

The part I most wish I had gotten wrong is the last bit of the first quote. I said the robber barons of the past got their backlash “until their excesses and abuses earned them” one. I was hoping that the industry would choose to reform itself it got to that point. That was the entire point of all the writing and public speaking I did in that era.

But unfortunately, I failed. We weren’t able to stop the abuses. And now, the tech tycoons who’ve led us here are about to find out just how angry the world is at their abuses, their excesses, and their obvious attempts to show the rest of society that they are above the law and any moral or ethical rules.

Things are not going to go the way that they think.

Just how bad it gets is going to depend on how quickly they understand just how poorly they’ve read the room. As I keep pointing out, hundreds of thousands of tech workers have lost their jobs; when I wrote about it at the beginning of the year, it was half a million — now it’s closer to a million.

None of those ordinary tech workers lost their jobs because they were having inappropriate relationships with a subordinate, or because they had bribed the President of the United States with tens of millions of dollars, or because they had a sexual relationship with a foreign asset that compromised national security. But they can see that someone can get away with of those harms, and still have a job paying unimaginable riches, even while decent people are struggling to get by. They will not miss the lesson that’s being taught.

I don’t take any pleasure in having called this one. If anything, it makes the case for the rest of what I wrote back then stronger, not weaker. The reforms I was asking for in 2016 are no more radical now, and they are far more urgent. And the people inside the industry who still care about doing right by the world have a much stronger argument to push for change than they did a decade ago, because the alternative is being lumped in with the tycoons who are feverishly working to become the most hated people in the world.

If you’ve been waiting for a sign that it’s time to speak up, you’re out of excuses. The backlash that’s coming is going to be extreme. And I know that because all we have to do is look at the time there was a class of robber barons who abused their power to this degree. Those tycoons probably controlled of the economy, and had less of an obvious impact on people’s day-to-day lives, and yet the reason they ended up funding all those libraries and museums we see today is because they spent enough years dodging bombing attacks and assassination attempts that they finally realized something had to change. I would love to see today’s tycoons invest in the public sphere in order to rehabilitate their image, but they’ve already shown that their preference is to double down on shamelessly acting like they’re untouchable.

Perhaps they really are above any accountability. We will certainly find out.

Everyone is going to have to pick a side on today’s robber barons. I think they’re in such an isolated and extreme cultural and media bubble that they genuinely don’t understand how wildly unpopular they are. But for ordinary tech workers, and the people affected by the decisions that these tycoons make, now is the time to make clear which side you’re on. The lessons of the past are clear: you will not want to side with the people who are willing to shamelessly abuse others and assume that the chickens will never come home to roost.

items.title: Those Five Tons of Bomb-Making Chemicals in Iowa Will Be Detonated Wednesday Morning
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
The detonation is back on. Nearly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives will be detonated Wednesday morning at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, reports the Iowa Capital Dispatch (part of the nonprofit States Newsroom network 

"The scheduled time follows numerous delays over the past week from the Army, a lawsuit, intervention from the president, and widespread public concern of the health and environmental effects associated with detonating a lead-based explosive."

Lead deposition maps released by the Army Tuesday morning show lead released by the detonation could be dispersed in the air as far as 100 miles southwest of Middletown and cross into Missouri. An additional map shows there is a potential for lead surface dust to settle as far as 50 miles southwest of the detonation site. The Army has recommended, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency is supporting, the evacuation of Iowans in Middletown and the immediate area — a 5-mile cone to the southwest of the detonation site — during the detonation period. Soldiers, environmental teams and other federal officials are in the area helping to sample soils and alert residents of the detonation plans... 

A slew of federal officials from the Army, the EPA, Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, Department of Agriculture and more gathered at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant Tuesday for a press conference and shared new information with the public about the response... Speaking at the press conference Tuesday, Sean Kaufman with HHS said the highest risk is for pregnant individuals, children, or people with chronic illnesses who live or plan to be in the areas the Army forecasts will be impacted. "You definitely want to be out of that area," Kaufman said of the at-risk groups. "I would evacuate that area that's signaled in the model... " As many as 100 Iowa National Guard soldiers will be available to aid local, state and federal agencies in their public safety plans [according to a news release from the governor]. They will also help provide guidance and assistance to around 150 households with a temporary evacuation... 

At the news conference, acting Secretary of the Army Hon. Adam Telle emphasized that the government's priority was the "health and safety of the citizens of this region." Telle said those involved have sought advice from "every expert" in and outside of the federal government and have considered all viable options and data before reaching the conclusion to proceed with detonation.
"There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, is far preferable to an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said. Some of those mitigations include: sand around the structure holding the barrels; two walls of four, 16,000-gallon water tanks; a plan to "flood" the exterior of the storage area with aqueous foam to help absorb particulate matter from the blast; and modeling to forecast impacted areas based on weather conditions.

items.title: Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You'll Be the Main Character.
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Longtime Slashdot reader schwit1 shares a report from 404 Media: Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized "shows" starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.
 
Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don't end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called "creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user," describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called "My Channel," which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make "the user as the protagonist for the whole video." The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.
 
"You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist," a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. "The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The and parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred."

items.title: I Listened to ‘Sandstorm’ Through a Sex Toy
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
You don’t really realize how much downtime there is in the song “Sandstorm” by Darude until you’re waiting for the bass to drop while it’s playing inside your vagina. 

In August 2025, I got an email with the subject line “‘Airpods for your @ss’ raises nearly half a million in Kickstarter campaign.” I get a lot of zany pitches for products that don’t exist yet, and a lot of pitches for products that do exist but perhaps should not. This one was for a device called the , a sex toy that turns music into vibration patterns. But the pitch didn’t include the phrase “sex toy” at all. Instead, it’s called an “internal music player.” 

I asked for a unit to review, expecting this to be purely conceptual. But they had one, and offered to send it. “The prototype functions very similarly to the final product but we do want to stress it’s a garage built prototype,” the rep for Groove Thing told me. I thought for a moment about putting something “garage built” and connected to a wall outlet into an orifice and passed. While , I decided to wait until the version they planned to send to customers in the fall was ready. 

The production-ready Groove Thing arrived at my doorstep last month in an intimidatingly large box. The configuration consists of a fairly hefty speaker that’s meant to sit on your nightstand, an AC power cable, and a “resonator base,” which connects to the speaker with a pinned cord. It also came with three attachment shapes: vaginal, anal, and external (a vac-u-lock adapter is available separately for attaching your own dildos to the base). The attachment shapes are made of hard plastic, not the soft, flexible silicone I’m used to in a sex toy. They lock onto the resonator with a twist. 

Opening the box and feeling the hard, inflexible plastic raised my skepticism that this thing would be comfortable. Most sex toys are covered in silky silicone that offers a little flexibility and give. But as I’m told over and over by the pamphlets that come in the box, Groove Thing “isn’t a vibrator.” Groove Thing inventor Michael Weiss-Malik, who co-founded it with Elizabeth Dell, told me it’s hard plastic for a reason, and is the result of testing feedback from the around 180 people they handed a prototype before putting it on the market.

“We started with off-the-shelf silicone dongs, and they were already producing an interesting experience for people,” Weiss-Malik told me on a call. “But we experimented with different types of materials, and what we found was that the silicone transmitted way fewer ranges of frequencies than hard plastic, and the hard plastic produces much higher fidelity.” 

The mechanism that vibrates the base to the beat of the music is also different from most other sex toys on the market today, Weiss-Malik said. But he declined to share what actually runs the toy, beyond mysteriously stating it’s not “a motor.” Weiss-Malik is a former NASA engineer, where he worked on the software that helped map Mars. He’s also worked at Google, where he worked on Earth mapping software, and previously worked leadership roles at Uber and Cruise, the self-driving car company General Motors later acquired and ultimately shut down after a serious accident. But he’s been involved in the sex positive community in the San Francisco bay area “for going on 20 years,” he told me, and is the type of guy to pop into a sex shop anytime he passes one when traveling. All of this taken together makes a lot of sense to me, given that he’s the kind of guy to spend a summer between jobs tinkering in his garage, designing a device that could put music up your ass. 

“Groove Thing doesn't use a motor. We don't say what is in there, but it's not a motor,” he said. “It uses a different set of physics that's more similar to audio equipment, and as a result, it can actually reproduce a full sound form, not just an on-off. You know, a sound-responsive vibrator is mostly just an on-off switch that's connecting to the beat.” Other vibrating sex toys work in that way: An eccentric rotating mass motor spins, turning pre-programmed patterns into vibration. Handheld sex toy makers have to work around several factors, including the limits of these motors, the tendency of soft silicone to dampen vibration, and the shapes they need to compact them into to fit in a device that doesn’t wear out customers’ wrists. Groove Thing seems to get around some of these problems by skipping the typical rotating motor, shaping the attachments in such a way that you can insert them and then go mostly hands-free when lying down, and choosing a plastic that feels kind of awkward at first.

The combination means different instruments and ranges come through as different levels of vibration. “A piano or bass guitar feels different than a drum kit. It almost feels like having a third ear,” Weiss-Malik said. “There's a level of fidelity there, where you have a whole new dimension to the sound that you're hearing. It works particularly well in bass, but it works all the way up to the mid frequencies.” Groove Thing replicates frequencies you can’t hear with your ears, he said — kind of like being at a concert and standing close enough to the stack that you feel it in your chest. As someone who recently almost lost their eyebrows and gained tinnitus at a Mogwai show, I get it, and I think for most people this comparison is what will make the Groove Thing click for them.  

”Some of what you're feeling is subsonic; it's down below 20 hertz, and we actually reproduce that as well,” Weiss-Malik said. “So you actually experience parts of your music that you never even noticed were there before, or that your ears can't hear, and that at the very least, home stereo equipment has a very hard time reproducing. So you're getting an experience that hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of speakers are normally required for you to get that out of the recording.” This was my experience with “Sandstorm.” You wouldn’t believe how much not-music is going on in that song, but also, how the moments that seem like they should be intense rumbly bass-drops are actually at a higher register. 

The creators of Groove Thing want you to be able to play whatever you want, which you can from your phone via Bluetooth or the optional aux jack, but they also really, really want you to try their intro playlist, I assume to prevent people like myself from putting “Crab Rave” on the stereo and then writing it off as a bust. is eclectic, beginning with “Beads on the Wind: The Human Experience Remix” and “Aya,” which I would place in a repeat-Burning-Man-attendee genre (no judgement here), but continues into “Blinding Lights” by The Weeknd and, to my pleasant surprise, an underrated track from Taylor Swift’s album, “I Think He Knows.” An with more songs features mostly EDM but also throws “Piece of Me” by Britney Spears in there. 

This entire test run of this not-vibrator made me, an admittedly tone deaf and musically unsophisticated person (see the previous lines), realize how much is happening in music that I’m never picking up with my own two ears. The “third ear” analogy is pretty spot-on: To enjoy the Groove Thing with an open mind, you have to let go of the typical expectations of other sex tech. Climax isn’t the point. The point is to use your junk to go on a musical journey, which is something that will resonate strongly for some, and miss others. 

“You know, people don’t go to a concert just to hear the finale and go home. Groove Thing isn’t a tool like most vibrators are,” Weiss-Malik told me. “It's more like a concert experience. You get to bask in pleasure for a period of time. In our early beta tester groups, most people who had unlimited usage of it used it for over an hour in their first session. Most of the second time users in that beta group also used it for over an hour in their second session.” 

The entire sex tech market has been trending away from the literal, anatomical, and climax-centered for years, with more toys coming in abstracted colors, shapes, and features that focus on pleasure and experience over getting your own personal money shot. I see Groove Thing as a logical step in that evolution.

Groove Thing is shipping out orders as of this month, and retails at $369 for the single unit and more for add-ons and additional units for partnered play.

items.title: Trump FCC (AT&T) Says California Can’t Enforce Its Broadband Protection And 911 Reliability Laws
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
As the federal U.S. government has given up on consumer protection and corporate oversight, states have filled the void with various degrees of success. That’s been particularly apparent in areas like telecom, where the corruption-fueled death of federal privacy and net neutrality protections have been replicated in a handful of states like California, which passed their own state-level laws.

This year, the Trump administration told California that it can’t enforce any of its own consumer protection laws if it wants to receive $1.4 billion Congress already earmarked for broadband expansion under the 2021 infrastructure bill. It’s extortion on behalf of regional telecom giants eager to see less and less oversight of their predatory business practices in uncompetitive markets.

Now the Trump FCC is again directly backing AT&T, and demanding that California can’t enforce its own Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules. These COLR rules mandate that state residents have reliable access to voice calls, 911, deaf and disabled assistance services, customer service support, protection from unwanted charges, and flexible billing options.

A new order by Brendan Carr’s FCC grants AT&T’s request to pre-empt all state consumer protection rules. It’s a giant hand out to unpopular telecom monopolies, misleadingly framed by Carr as a “modernization” of “outdated regulation” (that just so happens to ensure people don’t die as a result of not being able to reach 911):

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago. But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

That all rules and regulations shitty telecom monopolies say are “outdated” and must be “modernized to protect innovation” is an industry lie that captured regulators have been parroting for most of my adult life. As is any claim that U.S. telecom is remotely “competitive.”

AT&T lobbyists have worked tirelessly to eliminate such requirements in 20 of its 21 state service territories, falsely claiming the regulations stifled the company’s ability to install next-generation fiber. In reality, AT&T has long been criticized for cheaping out on fiber investments, and is primarily interested in eliminating already dwindling oversight on both the state and federal levels.

In countless communities where AT&T cheaped out on fiber investments and upgrades (despite spending untold billions on doomed media mergers), they’ll insist that 5G wireless is “good enough.” But 5G still doesn’t uniformly reach many parts of the state, and as AT&T has hung up on aging DSL lines, many communities are being left without access to essential online services, or life-saving 911 support.

While most states and the federal government have basically abandoned telecom and broadband consumer protection, California remains an outlier. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has been doing some amazing work on trying to ensure that broadband is both reliable and affordable, something lumbering monopolies simply refuse to accept.

While California’s efforts are mischaracterized as “extreme” by industry and our captured regulators, these kind of bare-minimum quality control standards are commonplace in most developed countries. Increasingly, the U.S. struggles to insist it’s a developed country, with corruption hollowing out already shaky regulatory autonomy and corporate oversight.

Telecom monopolies have had an intimate ally in the Trump administration, which has repeatedly declared that government effort to ensure your shitty local cable or phone company isn’t ripping you off is “woke.” With so much else going on, the efforts have been a broad success (for AT&T, Comcast, Charter, and Verizon), with little meaningful attention from a consolidated U.S. corporate press.

items.title: Is Nvidia's Legal Trouble Over - Or Just Beginning?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
America's Justice Department "is still investigating Nvidia," reports the New York Post, adding that Monday President Trump posted on Truth Social that Nvidia should also "continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security." 

But President Trump also told The New York Post Monday in an exclusive interview "that he's willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should 'tell the truth' to Congress when he testifies next week...

Huang doesn't need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday and appears before a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, Trump added... 

The president said that Nvidia's success was essential to the US retaining an edge in artificial intelligence — and that he's even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed over 10% of its value last year. "I thought about it. I said, 'You know, maybe I should do it,' but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late," Trump said. 

Earlier a source familiar with Jensen Huang's comeback "told the New York Post that President Trump and Vice President Vance 'became convinced that Jensen was a singular figure protecting Open Source models and preventing the closed-source model companies from becoming too powerful.'" 

And CBS News reports that Nvidia's Jensen Huang "still has security clearance, sources say." (Although revoking Huang's clearance "was discussed..."

It is not uncommon for executives at tech companies that do classified federal work to have security clearances... [U.S. Attorney General Todd] Blanche said the government relies on a "collective consensus" among federal agencies to assess national security risks and determine whether somebody is able to access sensitive government information. 

An Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment on Huang's clearance. 
Asked whether the Justice Department investigated Jensen Huang before Mr. Trump assured Nvidia's board that he had not engaged in wrongdoing, Blanche said he would have informed the president if the department had evidence Huang had committed a crime. "To the extent that that Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this ... that's something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true," Blanche said. Pressed on how the department could rule out potential criminal liability while export-control investigations remained ongoing, Blanche said he could not predict whether future investigations might produce different findings. 
"I can't predict the future," Blanche said.
 

Jensen Huang is still testifying before the U.S. Congress next week, reports The Hill:


The Republican chairs of three different House committees stressed the need to address concerns regarding national security despite Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.. "The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chair John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) wrote in a joint statement obtained by NewsNation... 
"We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary's AI capabilities," it continued.

 

U.S. Senators are also promising to grill Nvidia's Jensen Huang, reports Politico, and to pass new legislation regulating future chip exports:

"The controversy with Nvidia ... is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," Senate Intelligence Chair Tom Cotton posted Monday. "Congress has much to investigate," he said, "and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other." Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter is also expected to testify Dec. 2, and one House Democratic aide said lawmakers are already "considering" asking other Nvidia board members to provide information.... 

Sen. Kevin Cramer, a member of Senate Banking, predicted that between Democrats outraged by Trump's backing of Huang and GOP wariness toward China, an export control measure would pass by a margin large enough "to overcome a veto." Even if Huang ends up not participating in the hearings, or if Republicans back away under pressure from Trump, Democrats like incoming Banking Chair Elizabeth Warren could turbocharge their investigation plans using their new subpoena powers next year. "Chairman Elizabeth Warren and a number of Banking Committee Republicans ... are going to put the screws to these people like they've never had the screws put to them before," Cramer said in an interview. 
Jensen Huang's scandal revealed that American export-control policy "remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy," according to Foreign Affairs (the magazine published by the nonprofit Council on Foreign Relations think tank). 
While the magazine applauded a recent tightening of restrictions, it suggests more action from Congress since the current administration's "lax enforcement of past controls — and internal divisions over the new ones — raise serious questions about its willingness to follow through."
As a starting point, Congress should pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would give the administration clear legal authority for controlling remote access to data centers powered by U.S. compute. While implementation will require close congressional oversight, getting the right legal structure in place is an important first step. Next, it should work with industry and technical experts to fund and fast-track "on-chip" technologies — basically, features that can verify a chip's location and counter smuggling and diversion. Beyond sorting out the technical feasibilities, Congress will need to work with industry to understand the implications of on-chip security mechanisms for global competitiveness and the potential surveillance risks should China develop similar controls since it produces much of the world's legacy chips. Along with these technical fixes, Congress should seize on the Megaspeed scandal to strengthen oversight. The AI Overwatch Act, which may be included in the annual defense bill, would codify existing export controls on advanced chips into law, preventing the current or a future administration from reversing them. It would also empower Congress to review and block advanced chips sales to U.S. adversaries. 

Congress can go even further by establishing a new investigative committee or inspector general to strengthen oversight of sensitive chip export-control policies. [Another suggestion the article makes? "[C]ondition advanced chip sales on the buyer's ability to protect them from diversion and guard against misuse by malign actors looking to skirt safety and security rules."] Together, these actions would go a long way toward combating the circumvention that let firms such as Megaspeed thrive... Congress has a role in ensuring that the president faithfully executes the laws and is supported by the right resources, oversight, and strategic priorities. The United States' AI lead may hinge on whether it meets the moment.

items.title: Amazon Drone Crashes On Garage After Delivering Shampoo, Draws FAA Probe
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has opened an investigation into an Amazon Prime Air delivery drone that struck a fiber-optic cable and crashed onto a residential garage in Michigan after delivering shampoo. The drone lost a propeller and became entangled in power lines, prompting Amazon and local utility workers to coordinate its removal. Amazon offered to help repair the damaged roof and gave the homeowner a $100 gift card. Ars Technica reports: Amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case -- so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.
 
The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as "UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff." That notice was posted on November 23. The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe, according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents. 
Amazon said the Michigan crash was the first involving its drone delivery operations near Detroit, but federal regulators are already investigating several incidents in Arizona and Texas involving collisions with a construction crane, an internet cable, and an apartment building.
 
An Amazon spokesperson said Prime Air drones make nearly 6,000 flights per day and have delivered "hundreds of thousands of packages this year."

items.title: Experts: It Will Take Years & A New President To Regain Our Measles Elimination Status
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
I’ve been writing about the ongoing measles outbreak in America since March of 2025, and first began predicting we would lose our measles elimination status in April of 2025. While America did recently lose that status, I’m no Nostradamus. I simply watched how the case counts continued to rise at increasing rates and then watched what the federal government did about it, which was mostly fuck-all. It didn’t require any clairvoyance to see where this was heading.

But now that we’ve lost our elimination status… how do we get it back? The answer is obvious: vaccinations. It was a massive vaccination campaign that gained us elimination status in 2,000, after all. But even if we all accept that as the right answer, what’s it going to take to get it done? According to at least one expert, the answer is several years and a new president.

The PBS post above goes into great detail about how the measles came back and the history of how we eliminated it previously. Then it talks about how to regain that status.

[Professor William] Moss said that, while it’s impossible to predict when or if the U.S. will regain the status, he would expect it to take around five years and a different presidential administration. He said the Trump administration’s undermining of vaccines counteracts the efforts needed to regain measles elimination status.

“I don’t see them completely turning around and giving the messaging and support that we would need to regain elimination status in the next two years,” he said. “It would take a new administration and a real focus on clear messaging about the value of vaccines and the measles vaccine in particular.”

Take a moment to realize how damning and pathetic that statement is. How do we re-eliminate a deadly disease for which we have the tools at hand? Well, obviously we need to wait until the idiot leader that’s in charge is gone, of course. A more clear demonstration for the need to get rid of RFK Jr. from HHS I couldn’t come up with oh my own.

But the reason a new administration is necessary to do the work on this is because the cure for our measles outbreaks is vaccination. Specifically childhood vaccination, which the current president and Kennedy won’t advocate for because your children should have the freedom to die with angry rashes on their skin.

Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO’s Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization, said the U.S. and other countries that lost their elimination status are expected to present corrective plans outlining the strategies they will take to regain that status.

To do that, the U.S. needs to increase its vaccine coverage, identify cases quickly, track people who have been in contact with infected patients and respond rapidly to outbreaks, Gordon said.

Roess said requiring vaccines for children entering schools is key to protecting communities from measles.

“The key is to make this required with very few exemptions,” she said.

I can’t see any of that being done under the Trump administration, even if he launched Kennedy, which I also don’t expect to happen. That means the next two years could get very dark from a measles and health perspective, which I expect might elongate the timeline further for getting our elimination status back.

This is all so needless, it’s infuriating.

items.title: US Spy Agencies Suffer Breach of Some Unclassified Information
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to U.S. officials and other people familiar with the matter. The intrusions affected an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, the people familiar with the issues said. It was not clear specifically what information was compromised, but classified material was not jeopardized, the people said. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, according to two of the people.
 
Open-source intelligence can include vast troves of commercially available data sets, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. Much of it is publicly available, but it can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data. Spy agencies can also use the data alongside other sources of intelligence to inform analytical judgments. It is not uncommon for federal agencies to suffer cybersecurity breaches, but several have recently detected intrusions into some of their systems, prompting heightened concern among current and former U.S. intelligence officials. When asked about the recent hack of the FBI crime database, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said breaches occurred frequently and that there was no cause for alarm. "Cyberprobing, cyberincidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time."
 
"And what we're hearing about the F.B.I., and what I've talked to them about is, they have an incident. They're dealing with it in the ordinary course."

items.title: Spotted On The D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan For Smithsonian Overhaul
items.author: Andy Kroll
items.content:
Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s departure as head of the Smithsonian, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

As recounted by ProPublica in September, the American history museum has faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in 2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-reckoning.

By the time of Trump’s return to office in 2025, there was no shortage of fodder for the new administration to seize on. The July report noted a recent exhibit on Ben Franklin that speculated about whether he had used enslaved members of his household as subjects of his experiments with electric shocks. And it chastised the museum for having trained staff using the “Museums as a Site for Social Action Toolkit,” a 200-plus-page tract on how to “truly transform the museum space,” which it says is linked “with white supremacy, hetero-patriarchy, abuse of labor, colonization, imperialist theft of art and artifacts, destruction or absencing of alternative ways of interpreting or representing art and artifacts, structural racism and other oppressions.”

The White House report emphasized that the museum should not whitewash blights on the nation’s history such as slavery and Jim Crow, but argued that it was failing to give visitors any sense of how it developed into the country that it is. “It should tell the whole story of a nation,” the report stated, “including the good and the bad, so Museum visitors can understand the development that led our nation to where it is today.”

The report was released with symbolic fanfare on the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding. The administration’s announcement of its next move on this front may have less pop, given its soft rollout on the Orange Line.

items.title: Hackers Compromise Check Point Servers In 22 Organizations
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Hackers have compromised 24 Check Point Security management servers across 22 organizations in 17 countries in a suspected cyberespionage campaign, according to threat intelligence firm GreyNoise. BleepingComputer reports: The researchers track the activity as GT13 and confirmed it was ongoing between October 17 and November 2, when their visibility ended. However, given the threat actor's persistent access to Check Point devices, they believe the campaign remains active. GreyNoise says the 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries, and show no clear evidence of specific targeting. They include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors. The attacks were launched from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes.
 
A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments. While GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached, it observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232 during the post-compromise stages. The vulnerability is an authentication bypass in Check Point SmartConsole that allows attackers to obtain an application login token and authenticate with administrator privileges. Check Point warned about the flaw in July, marking it as an actively exploited zero-day. The researchers also observed attempts to exploit CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF).

items.title: The Global War On VPNs Draws Closer
items.author: Glyn Moody
items.content:
Back in March, Walled Culture noted that companies were increasing their attacks on VPNs, in part because of claims that the latter were being widely used for the circumvention of copyright law. Unfortunately, since then the trend discussed there has continued, with a notable uptick in recent months. For example, the LaLiga professional association football league in Spain, which has appeared a number of times on this blog, has called for major VPNs to be placed on the European Union’s “Counterfeit and Piracy Watch List”. TorrentFreak explains:

The 14-page submission targets a wide range of sites and services, including traditional piracy threats, but the VPN section is new. The league notes that it doesn’t take offense with the technology itself, but with how these providers are marketed by others through their affiliate programs.

That may be so, but putting VPN providers on “counterfeit and piracy watch lists” is a slippery slope. Once the precedent is established, it will be easy for others to claim that the marketing of a VPN provider is somehow promoting copyright infringement. And once VPNs are officially associated with breaking the law in this way, it will be natural to attack them more vigorously.

That is what is beginning to happen in the US, with a number of legislative proposals that would impact VPNs. For example, the absurdly named “Shielding Children’s Retinas from Egregious Exposure on the Net Act” or the “SCREEN Act”. The EFF explains that the main aim of the bill is to require online services to verify users’ ages before they can access any sexually explicit content. But VPNs are explicitly targeted:

The bill requires covered websites to verify users’ ages based on their IP addresses unless the service can determine that the user is outside the United States, and specifically requires age verification on traffic coming from known VPN addresses. In practice, this discourages the use of VPNs and proxy servers, which millions of people rely on for legitimate purposes such as protecting personal privacy, securing public Wi-Fi connections, safeguarding journalists and activists, and preventing data tracking.

Under the ACPA, any broadband provider, DNS resolver, or VPN with 100,000 or more monthly users or subscribers in the United States can be named in a blocking order. Smaller services are exempt, as well as root nameservers and top-level domain registries.

Interestingly, a “competing” site-blocking proposal is notable for not including VPNs in its scope:

The DEFEND IP Act explicitly excludes services that exclusively provide VPN connections or similar encrypted routing, as well as DNS services that only work through encrypted protocols, such as DoH.

That’s welcome, but it’s not yet clear which of those differing approaches, if any, will become law. Meanwhile, it is only too clear that VPNs are already under attack. This has prompted some pushback from the Internet Infrastructure Coalition:

The i2Coalition (Internet Infrastructure Coalition) ensures that those who build the infrastructure of the Internet have a voice in public policy. We are the leading voice for web hosting companies, data centers, domain registrars and registries, cloud infrastructure providers, managed services providers, and related tech. We protect innovation and the continued growth of the Internet’s infrastructure, which are essential to the global economy.

It has a site called VPNs at Risk, and a new report of the same name, which it says is “A comprehensive, content-neutral look at the technical and human impact of proposals affecting Virtual Private Networks.” It is a good introduction to the entire field, providing an approachable explanation of the technology that lies behind VPNs, as well as a useful survey of VPN regulations around the world, including those in India, United Kingdom, Pakistan, France, Iran, and Russia. It points out that there is a need for a broader conversation, since the questions raised by VPNs are not unique to that field:

Similar debates increasingly surround encryption, cloud computing, hosting, domain name systems, artificial intelligence, digital identity, and other technologies that provide general-purpose capabilities upon which many different users and services depend.

The rapid development and adoption of artificial intelligence make this broader conversation more urgent. As more consequential activities depend on connected systems, strong encryption, secure networking, and trustworthy Internet infrastructure become increasingly important. Policies that weaken these foundations can create vulnerabilities that extend well beyond their immediate targets. Addressing emerging risks should strengthen the infrastructure on which people and organizations depend, rather than compromise the tools that protect it.

an EU-wide system of anti-piracy injunctions – requiring providers to block access to websites and servers containing copyright-infringing content. Such a system risks turning providers of virtual private networks (VPNs) into watchdogs that have to filter traffic, undermining their core privacy-protecting function.

The DisCo article makes an important point:

In practice, pirates can quickly circumvent such measures, meaning that injunctions harm users’ privacy without delivering lasting results. Yet the blocking system remains under consideration for the Commission’s Copyright Package, due in the second quarter of 2027.

It’s time for EU policy- and decision-makers to commit unequivocally to preserving strong privacy protections and encryption, to focus anti-piracy enforcement on services that host illegal content and also have the ability to remove it, and to maintain a predictable regulatory environment for trusted VPN providers.

That certainly makes sense, but sense has never been much in evidence in the copyright world, which is driven by emotion and lobbying. Instead, we can probably expect increasingly strident calls for VPNs to be “reined in” in order to protect copyright – and the children, of course…

items.title: Microsoft Declares 'Code Red' After Historic Outage
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" initiative to overhaul its engineering and crisis response practices following a 24-hour outage on November 12-13 that disrupted governments, financial firms and airlines worldwide, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, said M365 Core President Jason Henderson. "Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team," Henderson added. From the report: Amanda Silver, Microsoft's corporate vice president overseeing M365 Core and Work IQ, the company's workplace intelligence platform for AI agents, said in a separate memo on Monday that engineers had to work through a "fog of war" as the outage unfolded. Despite deploying top engineering personnel, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to maintain a cohesive picture of hypotheses and decisions because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems, Silver said.
 
[...] As part of the Code Red, a high-priority mobilization reserved for critical crises, Silver outlined five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft set a target of achieving worldwide resolution within an hour during future incidents and plans to deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said he would hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering group responsible for underlying Microsoft 365 services, to track actions stemming from the outage, along with weekly reviews. The company spokesperson said Microsoft is committed not only to resolving issues when they occur, but to doing everything possible to prevent future disruptions.
 
"Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson said, adding that he had conducted an extensive review of the broader organizational and structural issues that allowed the failures to occur. In another memo earlier this month reviewed by Reuters, Henderson said "urgent patches to our M365 Core services" took too long to deploy worldwide. "In a separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here yet," he wrote.

items.title: Students Detained At Gunpoint After AI Says Their Bag Of Chips Is A Gun File Federal Lawsuit
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
We covered the originating story almost exactly a year ago. That makes sense, because if you want to sue someone for rights violations, you almost always need to file that lawsuit prior to its 365-day expiration.

A year ago, there was a bit of an AI arms race between two companies who claimed adding their AI-enhanced cameras (or simply applying their algorithms to existing cameras) would be a game-changer when it came to school shootings. But neither of the companies got it right.

Evolv was generating tons of false positives in schools in which it had been deployed. Rather than make security easier for schools, schools were finding themselves forced to engage in far more in-person searches of inbound students, thanks to the tech deciding nearly student be carrying a gun.

“Today was probably the least safe day,” one principal observed the day scanners were deployed at her school, because the machines were triggering false alarms and requiring manual searches on “almost every child as they walked through” monopolizing the attention of safety officers who would otherwise be monitoring the halls and other entrances.

When asked about this, Evolv blamed the messenger. First, it claimed discussion of these failures “endangered” both students and educators. It also pulled publicly-available documentation of its tech from its website following this exposure of its failure, again pretending that anyone questioning the tech (or simply seeking more info) similarly “endangered” kids and teachers.

Omnilert is another major player in this space. Unlike Evolv’s apparently faulty body scanners that require students to walk through them before being searched by unpaid (at least by Evolv) human backstops, Omnilert uses AI to detect guns via analysis of camera images.

Omnilert soon proved itself to be equally incapable/infamous. Its public profile was raised after the tech to detect a gun carried by a student who killed one student and injured another before (self)-tapping out by turning the (undetected) gun on himself.

Adding insult to an un-prevented school shooting, Omnilert dug deeper, declaring a bag of Doritos carried by a student to be a gun. Multiple students were held at gunpoint during this investigation prompted by a rather egregious false positive. The Baltimore, Maryland students were accosted at gunpoint by a number of officers who were all carrying (and aiming) guns no human would mistake for a bag of Doritos. The students were handcuffed and held at gunpoint until further investigation revealed the MacGuffin was actually just a bag of Doritos.

Omnilert apologized, but did so in a way meant to shift blame from itself and its tech and to everyone else who was expected to act (perhaps violently!) every time its software cranked out a false positive.

Omnilert, the company that operates the AI gun detection system, expressed regret over the incident and emphasized that its system is designed to identify a possible threat and elevate it to human review.

“While the object was later determined not to be a firearm, the process functioned as intended: to prioritize safety and awareness through rapid human verification,” the company added.

That is some wild shit right there. When I think “human review,” I tend to think of employees of the tech provider doing some further inspection and providing a second opinion if things don’t seem to add up. “Human review” of potential false positives should be nothing more than scrambling a bunch of cops to the area, while feeding them no more information than the computer equivalent of “BRO SAW A GUN.” That’s the sort of thing that gets people killed.

Fortunately, these students managed to survive this encounter — one that was backstopped by “human review” that apparently involved not a single employee of Omnilert, but plenty of public servants who had real guns of their own. Once again, the private sector is perfectly happy to profit from its faulty tech. And it’s certainly not going to spend any money of its own on “human review,” not when it can outsource it to public employees and let the public pay (literally and otherwise) for any damage resulting from false positives.

Four current and former students at a Maryland high school have filed a lawsuit a year after armed police detained them, prompted by an AI alert that mistook a bag of Doritos for a gun, in an incident that left them “fearing for their lives”.

The plaintiffs sued Omnilert, the company behind the AI gun-detection system, Baltimore county police, the board of education, individual officers and the school principal, alleging unlawful detention and search because of technological and human errors.

The lawsuit itself contains a number of alarming details, including the sad fact that the officers distrusted Omnilert’s alerts, but still felt compelled to respond to them anyway.

The encounter was terrifying and life-threatening. With armed police encircling them for no apparent reason, each student feared for his life and the lives of his friends.

The officers’ search of the students turned up nothing. Only after the search did one of the officers reveal why they had been dispatched: “it’s the Omnilert.”

The officers on the scene knew OGD [Omnilert Gun Detect] was unreliable. One told the students that “AI is not the best.” Another muttered “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts.” Yet officers relied on the Alert to initiate this painful encounter with the students.

Worse, a “human review” did take place. Two school administrators who received the alert canceled it within two minutes of receiving it, having determined it showed nothing more than a student holding a bag of chips. Another “alert” was automatically generated by Omnilert, informing other school administrators (along with the police officers) that the “alert” had been canceled.

That should have been the end of it, but the principal of the school, Kate Smith, decided well after the original notification (and cancellation) that cops needed to go out and accost the chip-eating students.

But Defendant Catherine “Kate” SMITH, principal of Kenwood High School, never acknowledged the Alert’s cancelation or took any steps to verify whether the Alert remained active.

Instead, more than ten minutes after the Alert was canceled, Defendant SMITH viewed the text message containing the OGD Alert, opened the website linked in the text message, took a screenshot of the video footage of Taki holding the chip bag from that website, and sent the screenshot to School Resource Officer (“SRO”) John Douglas on his personal cell phone. SRO Douglas then forwarded the screenshot to BCoPD, prompting an armed police response.

A ten-minute delay in response is its own form of negligence, especially when Omnilert is expecting school administrators to backstop its AI. The principal obviously felt the (apparently innocuous) footage demanded a police response, but couldn’t be bothered to care until well after other, far more responsive school administrators had already responded to the alert.

Then, because the alert had been canceled, she was forced to screenshot the footage and manually send it to the school’s SRO to provoke an (extremely belated) police response to her message.

Finally, a few hours later, she decided to do a bit of lol’ing about the students she subjected a situation that easily could have turned deadly (for the students).

If you can’t see or read the embed, it’s a text message sent to other school administrators by Principal Kate Smith that reads:

Yep, that’s a principal laughing because the guns-out interaction she had personally provoked found nothing more than some students in possession of a bag of chips — a message punctuated by the “crying laughing emoji” which indicates (if you’re somehow not familiar) that the whole incident made the principal laugh so hard she produced tears of joy.

The footage captured by the school’s cameras clearly shows Taki holding (and eating from) a bag of chips. While you could grab a couple of frames here and there that might show some partially obscured metallic glints that could conceivably be to be a gun, the principal had access to the footage and could have seen the same thing we all can see here:

But instead of watching this, she chose to send images deprived of their context to the school resource officer, apparently in the sincere hope of provoking a police response. This decision seems at best to be deliberately negligent. At worst, it looks dangerously malicious. And when the cops showed up and miraculously managed to defuse the situation on their own, she laughed about it.

Vibes-wise, I think only the principal and school resource officer should be held personally accountable for this outcome. The law says otherwise, which means every defendant is fair game until a judge says otherwise. But what’s clearly demonstrated here — all rights aside — is that Principal Smith can’t be trusted to run a school, not if she’s carelessly (or callously) willing to endanger her own students.

items.title: Mayo Clinic To Give Appointment Workers 5 Paid Minutes a Day To Boot Up Computers
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Mayo Clinic has agreed to pay more than $906,000 in back wages to employees who schedule patient appointments. An investigation by Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison found that employees were performing unpaid work before and after their shifts, including time spent booting up computers and finishing patient calls. Under the settlement (PDF), Mayo will stop rounding employees' work hours and give them five paid minutes at the start of each shift to boot up their computers. CBS News reports: In a statement, Mayo Clinic said it reached the agreement to resolve concerns about "certain timekeeping practices" involving a group of the specialists. The clinic said it doesn't agree with the attorney general's position but decided that a resolution in which money went to its staff, rather than to defense fees, was preferable. Mayo said it is committed to paying employees accurately and appropriately and reviews its compensation policies regularly. Neither the announcement nor the statement says how many workers are covered or how far back the unpaid time goes.
 
"Under Minnesota law, workers need to be compensated for all the time they work," Ellison said. State law requires employers to pay employees for all time spent on duties connected to their jobs, including time on the employer's premises. Ellison said Mayo cooperated with the investigation and changed its policies on its own to pay workers for the time. He said other employers should take note: "they're on the clock and need to be paid" if they are on site or doing work duties. Ellison encouraged any worker who believes they're being underpaid to contact his office, saying it may be able to help co-workers as well.
