items.title: Anthropic's Safety-Conscious Corporate Culture Still Envisions Superintelligent AI
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
The Washington Post looks at Anthropic's "unique" corporate culture, where CEO Dario Amodei "leads his workforce through essays, long memos posted in Slack and twice-monthly all-hands talks jokingly known as 'Dario Vision Quests'... 

"The CEO's output has established a constellation of beliefs treated as obvious, urgent and righteous inside the company: AI that supersedes humans is inevitable, the United States must limit China's AI development, and Claude might be conscious."

Inside this tight-knit culture, Anthropic staffers, who call themselves Ants, get to feel that they are working on the world's most urgent problems, with the smartest people, in a shared mission to safeguard humanity, according to interviews with more than a dozen people familiar with the company's ethos, including several current and former employees. At its core is a belief that Anthropic — and Amodei — know what's best for the world... "A pervasive thing at Anthropic is: We're going to put on our capes and we're going to be the responsible ones, and we're going to accrue great power, but ... because we're doing it responsibly, it's responsible to acquire more power," said a former employee who left the company this year and, like others, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid retaliation from the company.... 

Its message to investors fit with a vision of the future that Amodei often sketches out for his staff, people familiar with the company said, in which AI companies have the power of nation-states. After nearly six years of telling his workers that powerful AI will force society's leaders to makep difficult decisions, Amodei is now one of the powers who must decide how to act, in a major test of the corporate culture he has created.... [Amodei] set out to create a more safety-conscious culture when he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 with six people from his inner circle, most of them from OpenAI. In an internal memo the following year, Amodei laid out the stakes. "The current trajectory of AI development makes me think that there's a 20 to 30 percent chance that AGI will lead to the destruction or permanent stunting of humanity," he wrote, referring to the concept of artificial general intelligence, previously unreported court records show. He added that truly capable AI "seems more powerful/dangerous than nuclear weapons." 

Amodei was careful about those he hired to work on that existential challenge. Recruits were screened with a "culture interview," even for back office and policy roles, according to former employees and an archived copy of the company's careers page... It's "a bit of an 'are you ready for the cult' interview," an Anthropic hiring manager texted the unsuccessful candidate, according to a screenshot reviewed by The Post... 

Before ringing in Anthropic's record initial public offering at Times Square in New York on Thursday, Amodei delivered a short speech with some of his greatest hits. "To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control," Amodei said.

items.title: Alice Huang In Touch With Chinese Spy Agency During Affair With Nvidia CEO, NYT Says
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Reuters reports: Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the heart of Nvidia's recent scandal, kept in contact with an official from China's top spy agency for more than a year during her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang, the New York Times reported on Sunday. Alice Huang was in touch with an officer from China's Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the report said, citing people with knowledge of intelligence reports that describe the encounters... The scandal has also prompted a deeper look at Washington's approach to export controls on China, with lawmakers from both parties questioning whether the Trump administration has been too lax on enforcement and regulation of the prized semiconductors. Reuters points out that several U.S. officials "have cast doubt on initial suggestions that Alice Huang was a spy..." "A spokesperson for Jensen Huang declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang for comment..." But the New York Times also reported U.S. intelligence agencies have gathered evidence "that Ms. Huang's business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency." American author/journalist Greg Palast has his own unconfirmed theory, speculating that maybe Alice Huang wasn't a romantic interest but the Nvidia CEO's "business conduit to the Chinese military industrial complex... arranging the secret handoff of roughly one in five Nvidia chips." Why did the two Huang's make the affair so obvious? If she's a spy, why flaunt it before TV cameras and paparazzi? Because Huang and Huang wanted you to know... If Jensen and this guy's wife are conspiring to move hot chips to China, they can't exactly talk about it over the phone or in emails. So, they agree to meet-up in various hotel rooms during business conferences, doors locked...

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

And if that were to happen, Android forks would struggle to survive under that. Supporters are being asked for introductions to prosecutors and regulators, with assurances that the project has the necessary resources to carry on no matter what happens. items.title: America's Shipping Ports Now Face Thousands of Cyberattacks Each Day
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"A number of ports across the U.S. are reporting an onslaught of cyberattacks," reports The Hill, "amid a growing number of AI-enabled attacks targeting notable infrastructure." The Port of Corpus Christi, Texas, which functions as the U.S.'s largest passage of oil exports, said it was targeted with "hundreds if not thousands" of attacks per day, according to reporting from the Financial Times. The port's chief executive, Kent Britton, told the outlet that attacks surged from "known bad actor" countries and organizations that are searching for high-profile targets. ["Experts link countries like Iran, North Korea and China to hacking operations targeting shipping infrastructure," the Financial Times reports.] The attacks against Corpus Christi's port went after its computer systems by attempting to find weaknesses. Attackers also sent phishing messages, posing as senior executives, to trick staff into allowing them access, per the Financial Times... "They're poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities," Britton said. "With AI, it'll only get more complicated." He stated the port was seeking additional help from Washington but "if you're playing defence, you have to get it right every time ... if you're planning offence, you only have to get it right once." The Port of Los Angeles — the country's busiest port — similarly stated that in August it had stopped 120 million attempted attacks into its networks through network exploitation, credential harvesting and malware attacks, Bloomberg reported. Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, expressed that all potential attackers "have to do is to get it right one time" and that it was "front of mind every day." "The attacks have escalated sharply in recent months..." reports the Financial Times, "exposing vulnerabilities in the ageing networks that enable international commerce." The FBI last week warned that hackers are using an AI tool named Artex to automate cyber attacks... The threat is growing across the US. The US Coast Guard reported a 17% increase in cyber maritime incidents last year and investigated cyber attacks on two US-bound oil tankers in August with the FBI... The agencies said the joint offshore security boardings on August 21 and 24 were to "ensure integrity of the vessel's operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised"... Ports are taking action to defend their waterways. The Port of Virginia, a major hub for consumer goods, agriculture and coal, said the threat of attacks is now "more acute because of the rise of AI". It is heavily investing in its cyber security team, with employees undergoing monthly training and drills with the US Coast Guard.... The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey is also investing heavily in cyber defence. A spokesperson said it has "multiple independent layers of protection" and "recovery plans with terminal operators and partners, so that critical operations can continue and cargo can keep moving". Other ports are reluctant to discuss the threat they face — and their defences. The Port of Oakland said it would not publicly discuss its "cyber security defences or protective measures", citing national security concerns. The article notes it's not just affecting U.S. ports. "Cybersecurity company Shieldworkz said Russia's Noname057(16) threatened European operators this October...

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Have Investors Lost Their Faith in the AI Boom?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion," writes NPR, adding that "investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions." While the world embraced the AI boom ,"now many are having regrets," argues a Washington Post technology reporter: The AI boom's key ingredient has always been faith — that more money can be found to pay for it, that AI will keep rapidly improving, that the masses will come to love it, that business productivity and profits from AI are just around the corner. Faith is now in short supply... By mid-year, AI executives started to say that business customers were balking at the high prices charged by providers of cutting edge or "frontier" AI like Anthropic. Many businesses began to save money by hopscotching among a range of AI technologies, including low-priced options from Chinese companies... Investors began to rebel, too, against the trillions of dollars that AI companies are spending to construct data centers and provide them with computing equipment and electricity. Last month, Google's stock market value dropped by half a trillion dollars in a single day, when it seemed like even the rich technology leader would take longer than expected to see an AI financial payoff. Such stumbles by AI companies eroded faith in AI, said Howard Marks, an investor famous for predicting the dot-com bust. "It somewhat burst the bubble of infallibility," Marks told Bloomberg TV this month. Like many AI companies, Anthropic can't afford to cover its AI development costs. The company said it will keep coming back to investors for cash and needs a steady stream of customers to pay the $900 billion it owes in coming decades. Perhaps the biggest wild card for the AI boom is growing public resentment toward AI and data centers and widening fears of AI-enabled cyberattacks, human deaths and widespread job losses. In this month's midterm elections, Americans voted in a wave of elected officials who have been skeptical of the AI industry and construction of data centers. The results could slow the AI boom that's already hitting major bottlenecks, including difficulty lining up enough electricity to expand AI computer capacity... Diane Swonk, chief economist at the accounting firm KPMG, isn't surprised that the public is uneasy about AI. During the dot-com boom, she said that Americans' wages rose alongside corporate profits and U.S. inequality narrowed. By contrast the AI boom's economic and prosperity payoff has been uneven. "Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting," writes NPR, "just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000..."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Sellers are Closing Etsy Stores in Response to Its New AI Training Policy
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"I burned my Etsy shop to the ground this week," illustrator Aaron Millard posted on Instagram: 8 years, 11,200 sales, 3k+ reviews, hundreds in a customer base. Deleted. Etsy decided that selling on their platform now means letting them train AI on our artwork AND resell that data to third parties, with no way to opt out (in Canada, anyways)... Etsy's new Terms of Use — going into effect December 15 — include this language in their section about "Your Content": You also recognize our legitimate interest in using it... This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy. "My work took years to learn and create," illustrator Millard wrote on Instagram. "I won't let it be stolen. It's not free fuel for an AI slop business model." Following Etsy's announcement "artists are shutting down their shops in droves," writes Cartoon Brew, "and posting illustrated goodbye notes to tell customers where to find them next." Ironically, just weeks ago, Etsy announced tighter rules on misleading AI product photos and bot-generated listings. The marketplace still allows sellers to list work generated from their own prompts, as long as they disclose the use of AI to buyers. Etsy says it uses sellers' content to spot fraud and help shoppers find products, and that it doesn't train models designed to copy artists' work. That said, the vague terms leave open just how its partners and vendors might use that same content... The artists posting their goodbyes have decided it's worth walking away from that revenue source to keep their work from being used to train AI. "In the wake of that reaction, Etsy vice president of customer operations James Ossman posted a separate update," writes PC Gamer, "saying it's not really like that at all... [T]hat 'we do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity.'" "... we're enabling actions like translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work," Ossman wrote. "We also use your content to develop tools that make running your shop easier, like listing optimization tools or stats summaries that help you better understand your shop's performance. As always, your needs and feedback help guide how we build and improve these tools." As for providing third-party access to that content, Ossman said that too is for "services and tools that can help you run your business," and promised that "when we partner with third parties, we do so thoughtfully to help protect your content and data." That hasn't satisfied everyone. Ossman's commitment doesn't exist within the actual terms of service, which as seen above states only that Etsy and partners can "use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies." Ossman also noted in his update that the terms "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models," but that (as far as I can tell) applies to Etsy users and unauthorized third-parties, not Etsy itself or those it licenses... Others also complain that AI training should be opt-in rather than on by default — and worse, there's apparently no opt-out option available at all, so users who are opposed to having their work used for AI training for any reason are out of luck. Ironically, the blowup over Etsy's embrace of AI training comes just weeks after it earned plaudits for banning AI-generated recipes and patterns, a move Ossman said was necessary to establish "trust" in the platform.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: The New 'Riemann Hypothesis' Proof Has Been Confirmed in Mathlib/Lean Communities
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Experts say the claim checks out," reports the Guardian. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," reads Saturday's announcement on the Lean prover community blog: The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct... [Besides checking the code] The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean's official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean's logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit... We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof. "The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems," writes the Guardian, "even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems." "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line." Scientific American captured more mixed reactions Friday: As Massachusetts Institute of Technology mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems." "This is indeed an historic moment," Sutherland tells me today after he had independently compiled Alpöge's result in Lean. "The world has changed.... I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration." Sutherland says that it's worth celebrating the human work behind the development of Lean and LLMs — and, for that matter, the millennia of mathematical achievements upon which today's advance rests. But processing the earthshaking reality of what has occurred "is going to take some time." "There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof," he says. "And I can't wait to dig into them. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Funniest/Most Insightful Comments Of The Week At Techdirt
items.author: Leigh Beadon
items.content:
Let’s say the words, shall we? The shorthand abstracts it, it accepts the framing that it’s some kind of meaningless buzzword.

Diversity, equity, inclusion. Say the words and it becomes a lot clearer what kind of person you’d have to be to see anything wrong with them.

The power to censor anti-vaxxers is the same power of anti-vaxxers in the government to censor vaccines advocates. So no, it wouldn’t be nice. It’s literally what we have now and it’s awful. Why do you want to empower anti-vaxxers? Because that’s functionally what you are encouraging.

It doesn’t work to say, “no, I mean, only good people with takes I agree with should have that power…” The world doesn’t work that way. This retribution fantasy world where “your side” can’t lose will never exist because, like every other errant revolutionary, you can’t imagine that a counter-revolution would ever occur later or that you wouldn’t be able to permanently purge all bad people. You’re just Hitler with an ideological reskin and literally a caricature that a right wing fascist would use to paint leftists as “the real fascists.”

It’s bad enough when “what if the wrong person is in power” is a hypothetical. But it’s unbelievable to me that people can, during the current administration, seriously say that the government should be able to silence people who disagree with it.

Another way to prevent this type of ambulance chasing: Reasonable copyright term limitations.

Right now a musicians and their attorney can go after anything from nearly the past century and this will eventually expand into nearly two centuries due to copyright extensions.

Yeah thanks Captain Obvious.

His expert is named, Claude.

Wow, good thing the attack drones are incredibly expensive and time consuming to build, while our interceptors can be mass-produced cheaply and easily! Otherwise, this would be pretty embarrassing for the US!

That’s all for this week, folks!

items.title: Microsoft Admits Some Emails Bounced During Global Outlook Outage, Reveals New Failures
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
After millions lost access to Microsoft 365 services (including Outlook) on November 12, Microsoft "has published the final post-incident report," writes Neowin, "and it reveals that some emails were never delivered to their intended recipients." "The report also details previously undisclosed failures affecting Microsoft's email security features..." Microsoft confirmed that all queued enterprise emails were eventually delivered and that it found no enterprise messages that were permanently lost. However, it is not the same with Outlook consumer users. The company acknowledged that some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days expired, and senders received non-delivery reports. Microsoft did not reveal how many emails were affected or how many users received non-delivery reports. The final report also reveals that the outage disrupted several important email security capabilities in Microsoft Defender for Office. For example, the Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) feature, which automatically removes malicious emails after delivery, was delayed because updated threat intelligence was unavailable. This means affected messages may not have been removed as quickly as usual. Microsoft also confirmed that users experienced problems opening URLs protected by Safe Links. Depending on their organization's security policies, some users may have encountered a "Skip verification" option when Safe Links attempted to check a URL... Microsoft also acknowledged that its first customer notification arrived approximately 20 minutes after the widespread impact began. It plans to improve automated outage notifications by the end of 2026 to improve communication. "Microsoft eventually restored the services about 12 hours later..."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Climate Change Talks Fall Apart In Final Hours Over Fossil Fuels
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
NPR reports international climate talks "broke down in overtime hours, over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels." At Sunday's U.N. climate summit, "nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas." The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room... After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected — including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands. The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this." "Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions," the article notes, adding this is the first U.N. climate summit with a scientific consensus that the planet has already warmed past the threshhold countries agreed not to pass in 2015 of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit).

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: How Does GTA 6 Depict Electric Cars?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 as seen by the EV news site Electrek: GTA works as a mirror. In 2013, the EV was a punchline: a Tesla parody that overheated if you drove it too fast. In 2026, it's just another car in Vice City traffic, and the joke is on the guy in the pickup parked in the charging stall. That's a good sign of where EVs actually are. Satire goes after what's common, and Rockstar decided EVs are common enough to be part of everyday Leonida, more so in the city than in the Keys, just like real life. And that message is reaching a huge audience... Tens of millions of people are now driving EVs that charge as fast and as cheaply as gas cars, with no range anxiety. No automaker ad campaign gets close to that. They point out GTA 6 is "the first mainline GTA where energy matters." Gas cars burn fuel and need a pump, and EVs have a battery level and need a plug. Rockstar could have used that to make EVs a pain. It didn't. In my testing, the EVs have about the same range as the gas cars, charge just as fast as a fill-up, and cost the same or less to top up. Kotaku's range test backs that up. On the same highway loop, a Tesla Model 3 lookalike lasted 20 minutes and 23 seconds on a charge, longer than the Banshee sports car at 18 minutes and 31 seconds, and not far off an old pickup at 29 minutes and 8 seconds. Crossing the whole map by highway takes under 15 minutes, according to Kotaku. And finding a charger isn't a problem. Wccftech counted 120 EV chargers marked on the map, against just 57 gas stations... GTA has always been a parody of American life. With EVs, it's now slightly ahead of it. Florida is one of the strongest EV markets in the country, with a 9.4% share of new passenger vehicle sales in Q2 2026 versus 7.4% nationally, according to the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy.. But real Florida still has roughly three gas stations for every public charging location, based on the Alliance for Automotive Innovation's count of 3,267 charging locations and xMap's count of more than 10,500 gas stations. Leonida flips that ratio. GTA 6's Vice City has public fast chargers — branded "ReVolt America," which Electrek calls "an obvious copy of Electrify America's stations." And Electrek also spotted a giant charging hub at a power plant "with dozens of stalls and several EVs plugged in." There's even EV chargers being blocked by gas-powered cars, a phenomenon Electrek first covered in 2019

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Python Devs Document 'De-fanging Dangerous Triggers In GitHub Actions'
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"A handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets," warn two security developers at the Python Software Foundation. Have dangerous triggers caused real incidents? Yes, repeatedly... The maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one... When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. That's the safe one. pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets. GitHub built it for chores like labeling pull requests from forks, where the workflow never touches the contributor's code. The trouble starts when a workflow checks out the pull request and runs it anyway... Anyone with a GitHub account can open that pull request. Their code now runs with your credentials. This is called a "pwn request", and GitHub's docs describe it as the root cause of multiple supply-chain compromises. The issue_comment trigger carries the same risk. This trigger fires when anyone comments on an issue or pull request, and the workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets... Sometimes the workflow pastes the comment text into a templated shell command, and the comment turns out to inject different instructions into the workflow shell. Python's official security developer in residence Seth Larson joined PyPI safety/security engineer Mike Fiedler to remove these dangerous trigger, also applying the policies Python Software Foundation-stewarded GitHub organizations (psf, python, and pypi). "They also wrote up technical documentation on how to roll these policies out to your own projects and organizations. "On a GitHub Team or Enterprise plan, you can turn them off for every repository in your organization with one policy. On a Free plan, you can do it one repository at a time. Set the policy up, check what it would block, then enforce it."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Ask Slashdot: Should an Indie Game Developer Outsource Their Art?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Slashdot reader MillerMark has been working on his own small indie game "for about eight months now. And the art side is honestly killing me..." I can draw basic stuff, but nothing close to what I had in mind when I started this project. Is it even worth outsourcing 2D character and environment art at this stage, or should I just push through and do it myself? He's "looking for advice from people who've actually dealt with this" to share their stories in the comments. And Slashdot reader AlexKrav says "Outsourcing saved my project honestly... Quality held from first asset to last. If your vision is clear but the execution is not there yet, handing it off is the right call." Someone on a thread had suggested game art studios specializing in 3D and 2D game art, and he'd discovered there were lots of choices — 2D Game Art service, VSQUAD Studio. I've also successfully hired digital artists through freelancing platforms likes Upwork. Any Slashdot readers want to share their own experiences in hiring artists? Leave your stories and opinions in the comments. Should an indie game developer outsource their art?

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Aptera Completes Its First Solar Electric Vehicle for Customer Delivery
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Car-maker Aptera announced Thursday it "completed its first vehicle for sale to a customer, a milestone years in the making." Aptera's three-wheeled solar electric vehicle charges from solar panels integrated into its body, and it plugs in like any other electric vehicle. Its built-in solar panels are designed to add up to approximately 40 miles of driving a day from sunlight alone, under favorable conditions. "This is the moment our team has worked toward for years," said Chris Anthony, Co-CEO of Aptera. "To Accelerator #1, and to every reservation holder and shareholder who believed in this vehicle: thank you. We're working to complete more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible..." "What excites me about Aptera is how innovation can redefine the way we use energy in everyday mobility," said Martin Hartono, CEO of GDP Venture [and the proud recipient of Aptera solar car #1]. "By combining solar technology, battery power and an ultra-efficient vehicle design, Aptera offers a compelling solution for people who want to minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances. As an early believer in Aptera, I am proud to be part of this milestone and to see this vision become a reality." "Excuse me while I go find a hat to eat," jokes the blog InsideEVs... Nothing against Aptera specifically, but when a company hangs around for 20 years, while exchanging ownership hands several times without actually producing anything for customers, I start to get skeptical. However, Aptera Motors just did what so many doubters thought it'd never do: It delivered a road-legal production vehicle to one of its first early investors... [Aptera] does offer a interesting concept for customers who don't have long commutes and leave their car parked outside for most of the day while they work. In addition to plugging in to recharge, doesn't it sound nice to recoup your morning commute mileage with the sun while you're in the office? Whether this three-wheeled rolling solar panel ends up being a hit or not, and whether Aptera can stick around long enough to become a successful automaker, will take much longer to learn. But actually delivering a production car is a good place to start. Seven weeks ago Aptera said its first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, reports Electrek, with customer deliveries in early 2027 "subject to financing."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Quantum Computing's First Real-world Payoff May Come In Energy Solutions
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
While quantum computing's biggest breakthroughs "are still likely to be years, if not decades, away," CNBC reports the technology is already being tested in energy applications, "from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production." Quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture. Another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently... For [quantum software company] Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator, the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The company says its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing... [Phasecraft] is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones. Separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen. Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, [cofounder/CEO Ashley] Montanaro said the returns were there too. "When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he said.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: GTA 6: 32.5 Million copies, Cameos, and Easter Eggs - but No Physical Discs
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News, which is liveblogging all the videogame history happening after GTA 6's Thursday launch. Like how singer The Weeknd says he found his real-life mansion appearing in the game... How players found a glitch that apparently lets you override the game's third-person point of view to play in first-person. And apparently it's also possible to jack an old woman's mobility scooter. (Though it makes for a very slow getaway, it's reportedly the GTA 6 vehicle that's least likely to crash...) - The jet-skiing dog in 'GTA 6' appears to be based on a real Florida dog. Swim too far out to sea in GTA 6 and a dog in goggles and a life jacket will come to the rescue on a jet ski... Florida locals quickly recognized it. The dog appears to be a nod to Loosy, a golden retriever from Fort Lauderdale who went viral in May riding a jet ski down the New River while her owner, Eddie Inch, towed her along on a jet-powered hoverboard... — GTA 6 isn't approved for sale in mainland China, but that hasn't stopped gamers from getting their hands on it — or Rockstar Games from promoting it there [Reuters reports]. The developer has been pushing the blockbuster game on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, despite the country's strict rules on violent video games. Meanwhile, Business Insider reports that Chinese gamers are circumventing the restrictions by using imported consoles and overseas digital stores. Zac Ling, a project manager at Shanghai-based consultancy Daxue Consulting, said gamers in mainland China could buy 3 million to 5 million copies of the game in its first week. The game's graphic content has also prompted censorship in Japan, according to IGN. - Beloved '80s song parody writer and GTA fan "Weird" Al Yankovic said Thursday that he's the host of the non-stop '80s radio channel Vice City FM in GTA 6. In social media posts, Yankovic said he also wrote some of the in-game commercials and voices the Burger Shot ads. Grand Theft Auto 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it was even released, reports Yahoo News. Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels, according to the BBC. And "New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access." At its peak, nearly 8 million people were watching GTA 6 livestreams at the same time, Axios reported. PlayStation's network suffered a brief outage Wednesday afternoon as the game became available and players made the required update to their consoles. But since Wednesday evening, it's been smooth sailing. [Around 75% of Grand Theft Auto VI sales have been on PlayStation 5, with the rest on Xbox, the BBC reported, citing estimates from analytics firm Sensor Tower.] Yahoo news shares lots of crazy stories about GTA 6's world-building, like its cameos of real-world celebrities, its in-game hiking trails, and the way a GTA 6 house Rockstar first teased in 2021 hides a conspiracy-minded NPC who's convinced that he's in a video game. But they note that GTA 6 also brings questions on how videogames are sold and accessed: The game is being sold for $80 in boxes containing download codes instead of discs, meaning players can't trade in or resell their copies. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," [GameStop CEO Ryan] Cohen told Bloomberg. "Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it's also hurt GameStop." Cohen said the move away from physical games also reduces competition from the secondhand market.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Several Waymo Self-Driving Cars Stalled in Traffic as San Francisco's Streets Flooded
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
San Francisco's streets flooded this week after heavy rainfall — confusing several Waymo self-driving cars. The San Francisco blog Sfist describes what happened after the flooding in some places rose as high as three feet: Two lanes of Oak Street by the Golden Gate Park Panhandle were flooded Wednesday morning, with water spouting out of manhole covers, leading to a traffic backup that was made worse by a Waymo that couldn't figure its way out of the situation. The Waymo vehicle came to a stop in front of the spouting water, blocking one of the only passable lanes and worsening the traffic situation, as seen in the video below that is going viral... ["Other drivers had to veer into deeper water to weave around it," reports the San Francisco Chronicle.] Elsewhere in the city, Waymo rider Edward Frazer posted the video below to X, also around 10:20 am, saying that he had been in a Waymo for an hour and a half trying to get from North Beach to Mission Bay, with the vehicle pulling over around 10 times as it encountered flooded streets. The video shows the Waymo on what appears to be Townsend Street near Adobe's headquarters, stalled as water puddles in front of it. Waymo subsequently suspended all service for the rest of the day. But "frozen robotaxis were already clogging San Francisco streets by the time Waymo decided to rein in the fleet," reports the San Francisco Chronicle: Rider Amy Gutierrez said her Waymo suddenly stopped on Fell Street at the intersection of Masonic Avenue, where rain was coursing into rivers. She contacted company support and was transferred to three specialists who tried to move the jammed vehicle. It took a half-hour of false starts before they managed to remotely maneuver it to the right lane. "We were kind of just stuck there — cars were honking," she said, and other drivers were frustrated as traffic backed up. "One person drove by smacking their window, like 'Get out of the way.'" Or, as the New York Post puts it, "Waymos spark terror as they trap drivers in rapidly rising floodwater as monster storm hits California city." Waymos have sparked chaos in San Francisco as they trapped passengers in cars despite rapidly rising floods. Multiple self-driving vehicles were paralyzed across the streets and left those inside frantically calling the company to help get them to safety. One was trapped in the middle of a busy intersection when the car refused to go around an overflowing drain, leaving other drivers to go on the wrong side of the road to get around.... The San Francisco Chronicle also remembers that last year's power blackout caused 1,600 Waymo vehicles to stall "because they required a 'confirmation check' from a human operator before navigating stoplights after the power was cut. Hundreds of requests overwhelmed the system, leaving San Francisco streets full of paralyzed self-driving vehicles." Thanks to Slashdot reader AzWa Snowbird for sharing the news.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: US DOJ Charges Suspected Russian Agent for Stalking Palintir Employees in California
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
America's Justice Department is prosecuting a suspected foreign agent in "a state-sponsored operation" that targeted tech workers in Palo Alto, California. "We will not tolerate any efforts — by foreign governments or otherwise — to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian. The alleged Russian agent was arrested in October for "stalking and harassing employees of the software and AI firm Palantir, sources told ABC News, because of its assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia." The indictment says D'iu traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City last June and was connected with a person who helped him illegally cross the southern U.S. border. Once in the U.S., he was instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones and remote access software that his co-conspirators used to help him in his alleged targeting of the company's employees. At one point, prosecutors say D'iu was directed by his co-conspirators to visit a coffee shop where many of the company's employees would work and try to identify them and take pictures of their screens while they were working... In September, prosecutors say D'iu allegedly followed a female employee of the company in his vehicle for nearly 30 miles after she left the company's Palo Alto, California, office. Even as the employee attempted various maneuvers to evade him, D'iu aggressively sought to follow her until she ultimately phoned police and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department's Mission Station. The nonprofit news site Palo Alto Online notes the government's affidavit "identified at least two other instances in early September in which employees of the defense company reported being followed by a car matching the description of D'iu's silver Lexus SUV. The coffee shops and other locations where D'iu stationed his laptop — sometimes for hours at a time — are in close proximity to the Palantir office in downtown Palo Alto... FBI agents executed a search warrant on Oct. 8 at D'iu's residence in East Palo Alto. There they found the California state ID, passport and Social Security card that were present in the DHL packages, as well as two Russian passports, $18,000 in cash and a notebook with 10 Palo Alto area addresses. Five of them correlate to the home addresses of employees at the unnamed Silicon Valley defense company. The agents also recovered three employee "target package profiles" that included their names, names of relatives, education and employment history, leadership qualities and a list of strengths and weaknesses. After searching D'iu's phone, the FBI found messages from a Telegram contact with photos of four employees and their addresses. D'iu was instructed to act like a food delivery driver and knock on their doors to verify if the employees did live at those addresses, according to the affidavit... If convicted of all charges, D'iu could face a cumulative maximum sentence of 21 years in federal prison and $850,000 in fines.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

The nonprofit news site Palo Alto Online notes the government's affidavit "identified at least two other instances in early September in which employees of the defense company reported being followed by a car matching the description of D'iu's silver Lexus SUV. The coffee shops and other locations where D'iu stationed his laptop — sometimes for hours at a time — are in close proximity to the Palantir office in downtown Palo Alto... FBI agents executed a search warrant on Oct. 8 at D'iu's residence in East Palo Alto. There they found the California state ID, passport and Social Security card that were present in the DHL packages, as well as two Russian passports, $18,000 in cash and a notebook with 10 Palo Alto area addresses. Five of them correlate to the home addresses of employees at the unnamed Silicon Valley defense company. The agents also recovered three employee "target package profiles" that included their names, names of relatives, education and employment history, leadership qualities and a list of strengths and weaknesses. After searching D'iu's phone, the FBI found messages from a Telegram contact with photos of four employees and their addresses. D'iu was instructed to act like a food delivery driver and knock on their doors to verify if the employees did live at those addresses, according to the affidavit... If convicted of all charges, D'iu could face a cumulative maximum sentence of 21 years in federal prison and $850,000 in fines.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: 59 Years Later, 'The Prisoner' is Getting a Second Remake - from Amazon Studios
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
The Prisoner is getting a remake, reports ScreenRant. "Amazon Studios is currently developing a new and modern twist on the short-lived series..." ITV only aired 17 episodes of the original Prisoner back in 1967 and 1968, but it did receive a nomination for Best Dramatic Presentation at the Hugo Awards. Reviews were overwhelmingly positive... The Prisoner, considered one of the greatest sci-fi fantasy TV shows of all time, currently holds a perfect score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 93% with audiences. You can watch all 17 original episodes on YouTube. And apparently the production team for the remake "is apparently full of fans of the initial series," writes Inverse, citing an article from The Hollywood Reporter, "and ITV, the British TV network, is on board as well, which lends a little credence to it." More details on the remake from ScreenRant: Susan Montford, Don Murphy, Philippe Maigret, and Lucienne Papon have signed on as executive producers, but a showrunner has not been selected yet... Murphy has produced every single live-action Transformers movie, as well as the animated flick Transformers One. He also worked with Montford on Real Steel, Shoot 'Em Up, While She Was Out, and Vampire Academy... There have been attempts in the past to create a movie based on The Prisoner, with big names like Christopher Nolan, Ridley Scott, and Simon West all interested at various points, but nothing ever materialized... It took 41 years after the end of The Prisoner for any remake to finally make it to air. The six-episode 2009 miniseries had a solid cast that included Ian McKellen... McKellen and cinematographer Florian Hoffmeister even scored Emmy nominations. Unfortunately, reviews weren't kind to the show, which has a very low 17% critic score and 41% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the news.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents... Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor. CBS includes this quote from an official NACS, an advocacy group for the convenience/fuel retailing industry. "Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended. NBC News points out that the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector's versions of pennies in "limited quantities," reporting on what has and hasn't changed now: The penny can still be used as legal tender "for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues," according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence "for as long as possible...." And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint's currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel [according to the newly-signed law]. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc.

items.title: Will AI-Fueled Cyberattacks Lead to Better Funding for Critical Open Source Projects?
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Remember that famous XKCD comic joking that all modern digital infrastructure rests on "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." Politico Europe's cybersecurity reporter wonders if this recent spate of outages suggests that supporting block is coming loose? (Especially after Politico reported Thursday that internal services at EU institutions went offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack.) Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them... Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated. Since the web's early days, an unruly cast of idealist engineers and non-profit foundations have been essential for looking after decades-old critical code that's been used to build our digital world. This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can't keep up with the power and pace of AI. "We're running on fumes," said Robin Bender Ginn, executive director of the OpenJS Foundation, which looks after JavaScript, among the most widely used programming languages. "It keeps me up at night." Cybersecurity agencies around the world rang the alarm last month about major flaws detected in PHP, another critical coding language that underpins 70% of the web. This week, similar scares have spread over Java and NGINX, which also fuel large swathes of technology. Helmut Reisinger, the European chief executive of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, said in an interview that the company is seeing "more or less" ten times as many incidents compared to about four months ago. He predicts the constant drumbeat of attacks and scares in the last month is going to become the "new norm...." The rise of AI models and their capabilities of finding software flaws is putting more pressure on open-source software engineers, who are inundated with reports of vulnerabilities — some of which are false or exaggerated. Reports of flaws discovered by AI are "quite verbose," Ginn said. Juhan Lepassaar, the head of EU cyber agency ENISA, said in an interview that the agency has observed a similar pattern of false positives. While some hope the AI-fueled attacks "will put the needs of open source software on the map and prompt an intervention," according to the article, "many of those steeped in the ecosystem... have their doubts." "I'm a bit pessimistic," says Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member. "I worry that people will just not care enough to actually do anything about it."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

They had been down more than 6% before Reuters published its report... The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. Reuters says they "could not immediately determine" exactly what potential accounting issues America's SEC is examining." (And Reuters points out that "Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.") Their article adds some historical context — that U.S. authorities "have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week." And the Financial Times reported Tuesday that Nvidia removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown of revenue sources, Reuters points out, "even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue." Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers... Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks. On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.

items.title: Earth has a New Moon
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN: Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar... The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system.

items.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board. The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED. "We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Scientists Discover New and Horrible Eagle-Based Way Our Ancestors Died
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that dive-bombed our ancestors, brightened the sky, recalled an old tune, and got hosed by marine mucus.

First, scientists discover that eagles are hunting large baboons, hinting that early human relatives once sated ancient avian appetites. Then: star-on-star contact, a musical memory lane, and the secrets of cetacean snot. 

Eagle-eyeing you…for dinner!

Death came from the sky for early humans, according to a new study that suggests giant eagles preyed on our ancestors far more recently than was previously known. 

Birds of prey (raptors) have hunted primates for at least 20 million years, including early human relatives, known as hominins. For example, a hominin toddler known as the “Taung child” shows signs of being killed by a raptor roughly 2.5 million years ago. But scientists have assumed that hominins outgrew their status as bird bites since that time, and there are no reports of raptors preying on primates that weigh over 28 pounds on record—until now. 

In 2025, scientists discovered that Verreaux’s eagles—one of the largest eagle species in the world—at Ennedi Plateau in Chad are likely hunting adult olive baboons weighing up to 57 pounds. The team found baboon remains among the region’s sandstone cliffs that show signature marks of eagle predation, such as talon punctures on the skull and scrapes to the shoulder bones.

“We cannot definitively rule out scavenging activity, but the severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip,” said researchers led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St. Andrews. The team also observed the baboons rapidly retreat when eagles approached, suggesting that they feared aerial attacks.

Some researchers have argued against the “raptor-mediated predation” of the Taung child on the grounds that the hominin would have been too heavy for a bird. The study’s authors get extra points for including a quote from the comedy Monty Python and the Holy Grail on this point: “It is a simple question of weight ratios. A five-ounce bird could not carry a 1-pound coconut.” IYKYK.

However, the laughs stop there, as the team refutes this idea by recounting the grisly “low flight with sustained grip attack” that eagles perform on ungulates, such as antelopes or cattle, which reveal that raptors can kill animals that are many times their own weight with the right approach. 

“Briefly, an eagle will land on the back or neck of a moderately large ungulate, gripping it firmly with its talons. If the prey withstands knocking to the ground, the eagle will ride it with wings outstretched and flapping to maintain balance until the quarry collapses, either from exhaustion, shock, or internal injury. A similar tactic is described in the of a Harpy eagle ( attacking a 52-kg adult woman.”

Wow, new fear unlocked! Imagine being an early hominin, minding your own business banging rocks together or something, when suddenly a giant bird of prey either pushes you off a cliff or rides you to death. For everyone preparing to eat a huge bird for Thanksgiving next week, be grateful that it’s no longer the other way around.

Speaking of unwieldy meals, scientists have captured an unprecedented glimpse of a star eating another star, thereby forming a new mega-star. 

Over the past few years, scientists noticed that something weird has been unfolding in a binary star system called AT 2025abao—nicknamed “Bao” (yum!)—in the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, which is about 2.5 million light years away from the Milky Way. One of the stars, “Big Bao,” was expanding into its dying red giant phase, which pulled its companion, “Little Bao,” into a deadly spiral. Last year, the system rapidly brightened, signaling that Big Bao had swallowed Little Bao.

“In October 2025, the star underwent a dramatic eruption” and exhibited “a sudden increase in its photospheric temperature to about 8,000 K,” said researchers led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University. The system “shows the defining hallmarks of luminous red novae,a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection…during the merger of a star with its companion.”

“This inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly,” the team noted. 

Congratulations to the newly-fed couple! Long may Bao shine.

Girl, put your records on / but don’t think you own that song

We’ve all had that feeling of hearing a familiar song and being transported to a specific time and place in our lives. But as it turns out, the recollections stirred by those cherished songs are probably not all that special, according to a new study that surveyed 233 undergraduate students about these so-called “music-evoked autobiographical memories.”

The students (aged 18-23) listened to clips of grouped into two categories: “new” songs released from 2014 to 2019, during their adolescence, and “old” songs released from 1985 to 1995, before they were born. When asked to reminisce about the songs, students with similar backgrounds were remarkably aligned in their answers.

“Memories evoked by country songs were more strongly associated with very recent time periods (college) and themes relating to family, driving, summertime, romantic partners, and listening to music (particularly music selected by someone else),” said researchers led by Cara Turnbull of Texas Tech University. 

“Alternatively, memories evoked by hip-hop songs were most often associated with friends, acquaintances (such as classmates, coworkers, and teammates), dancing, and being at school, while those evoked by pop songs were most associated with middle school, listening at home or by oneself, and singing along,” the team added. 

As an elder millennial, it was humbling to realize what counts as an “oldie” these days. I also felt my generation’s soundtrack was done dirty by offerings like “Achy Breaky Heart” by Billy Ray Cyrus or “Whoomp! There it is” by Tag Team. No Stevie Nicks? Madonna? Wu Tang? All I ask of future generations is that you do not judge us solely by the croonings of C+C Music Factory and Bryan Adams, I beg you. 

Join hands, dear friends, for we are about to run directly through majestic fountains of whale snot. Scientists who flew drones through whale “blow”—the mucus-filled vapor exhaled by whales through their blowholes—have successfully sequenced whole genomes from the snotty samples, representing “a major step towards non-invasive cetacean sampling,” according to a new study.

“Preserving biodiversity requires the genetic monitoring of wild populations, which is traditionally done through invasive sampling techniques for DNA collection,” said researchers led by Éadin O’Mahony of the University of St. Andrews. “However, this approach can impact animal welfare or be impossible to implement due to behavioural responses to anthropogenic factors or national/international legislation.” 

Indeed, I think that we can all agree that humans have stressed whales out enough as it is. Instead of invasive biopsies of skin and flesh with darts or scrapers, O’Mahony and his colleagues equipped drones with petri dishes and flew them through a total of 58 blows from 26 Northeast Pacific humpback whales in the Gitga'at First Nation territory of northern British Columbia.  

The team “established that a whole humpback whale genome can be recovered from exhaled respiratory vapour (‘blow’), marking a significant methodological advancement in non-invasive cetacean genomics.”

While it’s not the kind of blow most people associate with breathing orifices, it just might be what we need to study whales without hassling them.

Thanks for reading! See you next week. 

Corrected: A previous version of this story erroneously used "miles" in place of "light years."

items.title: Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports: A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins. The Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away and a well-characterized astrophysical source of X-ray light. By observing it, the team can work out the performance characteristics of MIXS in space and compare these with calibration measurements made with the same instrument in the laboratory in 2015. These observations provide MIXS's first view of an astronomical X-ray source. The main observation sequence consisted of 55 spacecraft slews, with 39 hours of observations during Sept. 11-12. Measuring how much the Crab Nebula's image is spread across MIXS's detector helps the scientists measure MIXS's angular resolution, or how sharply it will be able to distinguish features on Mercury's surface. They found this to be slightly better than when it was last measured in the lab in 2015. "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out," said Professor Emma Bunch, Principal Investigator (PI) for the MIXS instrument and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester. "We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after eight years in space. We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine-tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Slashdot has been covering the Riemann Hypothesis for years. 2000: Prove The Riemann Hypothesis And Make.Money.Fast 2002: More on Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Claimed Proof of Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Prominent Mathematicians Rebuke Recent Riemann Hypothesis Proof Add a new headline to the list... 2026: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math's great mysteries joshuark shares a report from Scientific American: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has claimed to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model Claude, but the proof is not yet independently verified and remains under scrutiny. [An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion.] The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order. [...] Alpoge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI's mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. [...] Alpoge's statement is elegiac -- recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling -- but also optimistic. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light," he wrote, "but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." [...] The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn't have any immediate real-world applications -- it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems." "If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. "Something like a Rosetta Stone." "If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," added mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind. In a separate article from Scientific American, independent mathematicians say the AI-assisted proof is almost certainly valid. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland said the chance of anything being wrong was "approximately zero" after independently compiling and checking the code. However, researchers are still conducting final checks to ensure the proof accurately represents the original hypothesis and does not exploit any loopholes in Lean's verification system. But did a human beat the AI? The Washington Post reports: Just hours after Alpoge's claim circulated on social media, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society and a professor at Stanford University, said in a hurried statement that mathematician Alessandro Masullo had a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis without AI several months earlier. The draft, which runs some 940 pages, is in need of significant revisions, Masullo said in a statement, and was not ready for publication. Online observers quickly noted that it contained omissions and apparent errors. But in the introduction to the draft, he published a striking flag. "If any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this," he wrote. "We are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.
