items.title: White House Withdraws Latest Nominee To Head The FDA; HHS Chaos Engine Goes Brrrrrr
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
I have said repeatedly that whatever else we can call RFK Jr.’s department of Health and Human Services, it is undoubtedly also a chaos engine. Between nominees who can’t get confirmed, vacant director level positions, other positions being filled by acting directors, and all the rest, HHS is currently producing confusion and incompetence more than anything else. We’ve also seen this at the FDA more specifically, with one chief regulator calling it quits after only three weeks, even though he himself was replacing another regulator who only made it a few months. Further up the chain, you’ll recall that Marty Makary only made it about a year as FDA commissioner before he quit.

In Makary’s place, Kyle Diamantas was named Acting Commissioner in May of this year. He’s still in that role today. The Federal Vacancies Reform Act limits an Acting Commissioner’s ability to serve in that role to 210 days. Diamantas is currently just shy of 200 days in his role to date. And, wouldn’t you know it, the White House has just withdrawn its nominee for FDA Commissioner for reasons nobody seems to totally understand.

The White House withdrew the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) amid opposition from Senate Republicans, it confirmed to The Hill.

Overton was set to face a key vote Wednesday in the Senate health committee, where Republicans hold only a one-vote majority — meaning losing one member would be enough to sink the nomination if all Democrats oppose it.    

The White House said it was pulling the nomination because she didn’t have the votes needed to be confirmed. Strangely, the White House seems to be the only one that thinks that’s true. All that needed to happen was to placate a bunch of anti-abortion GOP senators, which seems like the lowest of hurdles over which the White House needed to leap. Here’s a guy who is routinely fooled by fake promises during confirmation hearings saying so out loud.

Cassidy said he was having “productive conversations” with committee members and believed Overton would have cleared his committee. The final hangup, he said, was anti-abortion senators seeking assurances from the administration about its commitment to “life issues.”

“My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk,” Cassidy wrote. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments. Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”

That… doesn’t make a whole lot of sense. The Trump administration has never been shy about bowing to the anti-abortion wing of its own party. For her part, Overton is anti-abortion. She celebrated when Roe v. Wade was overturned. She refused in confirmation hearings when questioned to admit that mifepristone is medically safe.

This is starting to look instead like the MAHA movement is responsible for this and that it has nothing to do with abortion.

Former Kennedy senior adviser Calley Means, a prominent figure in the MAHA movement, said this month that Overton wrote a policy relaxing standards for fruit-flavored vapes.  

He also alleged Overton helped the Justice Department “construct a legal argument” for why the Supreme Court should take up a case that involved shielding major chemical company Bayer from lawsuits connected to its pesticide products. 

RFK Jr. recently stated that he now has the freedom to go full MAHA with Stephen Miller being named Chief of Staff. This smells for all the world like him, or other MAHA administration creeps, flexing this perceived new muscle and getting the Overton nomination pulled. That is rank speculation, of course, but it makes a great deal more sense than any concerns about abortion from Republican senators.

But, as Cassidy rightly stated, confirming the next FDA Commissioner will fall instead to a Congress controlled by Democrats. There will likely be another Acting Commissioner appointed, since Diamantas’ time will have run out. There won’t be time for new confirmation hearings.

The FDA, like it’s parent agency HHS, is once again outputting chaos.

items.title: FCC Backs AT&T's Plan To Remove Copper Landlines In California
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. In May, the company urged the commission to declare that federal laws preempted California's regulations, thus clearing the way for AT&T to discontinue the service as it prioritizes high-speed fiber and expanded 5G cellular coverage. Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. "While we preempt those requirements that necessitate that AT&T obtain a variety of CPUC [California Public Utilities Commission] approvals before it can discontinue POTS [plain old telephone service] in accordance with federal authorization, we do not preempt the COLR and other obligations more generally," the 74-page document says. [...] Despite the FCC's order, it's not entirely clear if AT&T will pursue the copper landline phase-out in California. In May, the carrier sued to overturn the local regulations and block the CPUC from enforcing them against AT&T, which noted it spends $1 billion each year to maintain the copper network. That court case remains ongoing. [...] According to the regulator, AT&T has proposed discontinuing the legacy telephone service in the state on or after June 1, 2027.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Tech Companies Are Trying To Shift The Entire Concept Of Privacy (Again)
items.author: Thorin Klosowski
items.content:
Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did.

Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants, rings, and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long.

Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps, collaborative software, or your cloud backup solutions, have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game.

Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have. 

This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense.

Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses. 

How to Think About the Technical Promises Companies Make

Ask Apple about privacy concerns and they’ll point to a white paper that explains all the technical barriers between them as a company and the data generated by the watch. Ask Meta and they’ll talk about all the ways you can customize the privacy controls or how certain details, like faces, may be blurred out when you interact with Meta AI through the glasses (but not during standard recording). Google does this too. Amazon will also talk about how you’re always in control, and no audio is stored (though it’ll also let you enable Amazon store integration, so your conversations can directly result in ads for products). And so on across all the companies making these products.

Some of these solutions do a better job than others at cutting out potential law enforcement or company access to this data. There will be a time to dive into these details more deeply, but the technical privacy promises these companies focus on only cover the consumer and user of the device. They ignore every bystander you interact with and their inability to actually opt out. There is no technical protection for you as a non-user of these devices, the person who finds yourself captured by them. 

Still, we hope to look deeper into the technical differences between this category of devices soon.

There Must Be Some Laws to Consider, Right?

With something like Apple’s Audio Intelligence and Amazon’s Bee devices, it may be best to treat them similar to an always-recording microphone, even if companies try to claim there’s “technically” no audio recording. These tools still often use a microphone to capture raw audio from conversations and convert it into summaries or transcripts before discarding the audio. Google’s blog post notes that it has whole responsible use part of their Terms of Service where users have to agree not to record others without permission or in sensitive places. 

But it’s not just the question of the legality from the point of view of the user. Law enforcement will eventually try to compel access to the data that these products create (either real-time audio or the summaries and transcripts they create). And while some products, like Apple’s Audio Intelligence, are engineered to make that difficult, not every product will be. We know from history that when data exists, governments will do everything they can to access it. There’s no reason to think something would change today.

No Tech and Legal Solutions Will Reduce Social Issues

There is a problem humming along in the background that is impossible to address with technical or legal solutions. If secretly documenting conversations becomes the norm, it makes every private conversation less spontaneous and open. It breaks a longstanding social norm that you will not record and document every conversation with friends, family, colleagues, or strangers. 

The companies that make these sorts of products like to claim they’re no different from tools we already have. You can easily record everything right now with a phone or a camera. Heck, you can do so with a camcorder or cassette recorder if you want. And you can transcribe conversations with pen and paper, too. But those are actionable steps we take that both require effort from the user, and are clear to others around us. This new wave of passive surveillance tech is designed to encourage continuous monitoring and hide its use. 

Even taken at face value, none of these products can understand the complex social context we all navigate every day. We intrinsically know there are different social agreements we all make when we’re standing on a street corner, at a protest, in a bathroom, at a doctor’s office, at the gym, or in a restaurant. Taking notes in a meeting at work is completely normal. Getting a summary of a conversation with your best friend about their divorce is not. Always-on monitoring of our conversations is an unacceptable burden on our conversational privacy. 

Google seems to all but admit this problem in a conversation with CNN when it described the company’s experiments with a notification system that would alert people’s phones when someone was recording nearby: 

“And just alerting bystanders doesn’t do much to help, [Juston Payne, senior director of product management at Google] said. “It can actually be weirdly disempowering to you in that you’re like, ‘What am I meant to do now?’” he said.”

It’s easy to buy into the tech company line that these products are inevitable, but we’ve seen so many vaporware products over the years that we should take those claims of success with a grain of salt. We’ve seen entire product categories come and go within just a few years, and if the public doesn’t want this stuff, the tech companies will have to throw in the towel. 

Products from the likes of Meta, Google, Amazon, and others might be harder to push back on, but politely and clearly engaging with those who use them in ways that make you uncomfortable is a good place to start. And if you see abusive videos on social networks where these sorts of products are used, report them. If you find these products useful for yourself, make it clear to those around you when you’re using them, and only do so with consent and in social moments where it makes sense to do so.

items.title: Signal Restricts Screenshots to Block AI Agents From Reading Messages
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Signal is introducing default-on screenshot restrictions to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations, warning that increasingly powerful assistants integrated into operating systems pose an "existential threat" to its privacy guarantees. "Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that's making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," it said in a blog post. Reuters reports: Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly. [...] Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device. Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from CNBC: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy -- which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements. Trump said Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them." "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump said.

items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a "Zero Data Retention" label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Earlier this year, TP-Link announced plans to begin assembling routers in Mississippi as early as 2027, "but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task," reports Ars. "The government reviews of router makers' requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy."

items.title: Judge Says DHS’s Seizure Of An Immigration Lawyer’s Phone Likely Violated The First Amendment
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
It’s logical to assume what happened here was a deliberate violation of immigration lawyer Andrew Lattarulo’s rights. The problem is that even deliberate violations need to be litigated. The ruling here paves the way for Lattarulo to continue his lawsuit against immigration officers who violated his rights. Unfortunately, winning here just generates another on-ramp to roads littered with insurmountable jurisprudence roadblocks.

But let’s not dwell on the potential futility of this lawsuit and instead dig into a decision where a federal judge has bucked the Supreme Court’s desire to excuse and all federal officers from accountability. This ruling finds in favor of someone whose rights were violated, rather than automatically assuming precedent demanded immediate dismissal. (h/t Kyle Cheney)

Early on in the decision [PDF], you can clearly see why immigration officers decided to engage in punitive action against Lattarulo. It’s not just that Lattarulo regularly defended people ICE wanted to make disappear, but he also actively informed other migrants of their rights via viral-esque videos:

Andrew Lattarulo is an immigration lawyer and part owner of the law firm Georges Cote LLP, which represents “thousands of clients in active immigration proceedings.” Lattarulo also runs a popular Instagram account featuring videos of himself discussing “know-your-rights information about U.S. immigration matters,” [id. ¶ 59], which regularly “amasses hundreds of thousands of views…”

At some point, this lawyer and the law firm drew the attention of Trump’s anti-migrant forces. This led to normally unimaginable legal action by the Trump administration. The DHS’s Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit claimed the Cote law firm employed undocumented migrants. It demanded the firm turn over documentation on its employees — a demand the Cote law firm apparently complied with.

While HSI went through the motions of trying to find literally to shut down a law firm that provided zealous representation to detained migrants, Lattarulo and his employer decided to spend the weekend in Aruba. Cote returned from this trip and went through customs without incident.

Things went way worse for Lattarulo when he returned from the same weekend trip:

When his flight arrived at Logan Airport, three U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”) agents and one HSI officer stopped Lattarulo as he got off the plane. The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone. Eight days later, they returned the cell phone via overnight delivery.

What’s on the record suggests the government did this not because it was essential to its border-securing work but simply because , given that it happened in one of the nation’s many constitutional dead zones, which not cover any international airport but anything up to 100 miles inland from any physical border crossing.

Supposedly, the government has not yet performed a search of the seized phone. But it definitely intends to… or at least believes it can work its way backwards from an unconstitutional search via any of the handy Get-Out-of-Lawsuit-Free cards the courts have provided it over the years.

The seized cell phone data is currently in a format that is not readable or reviewable, but the government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits.

The data includes confidential information, including privileged attorney-client communications related to Lattarulo’s clients.

So, there’s more than Lattarulo’s First Amendment rights at stake here. But if the government wants to engage in deliberate violations of attorney-client privilege, it first needs to convince a court that the seizure of Lattarulo’s phone has nothing to do with his immigration law work or his popular Instagram account that discusses these same legal issues.

Thus far, it’s not working out for the government. As the court notes in its discussion of the case, there is “no dispute” that Lattarulo’s public statements via his Instagram account (which include criticism of government policies and practices) are protected by the First Amendment. What needs to be demonstrated is that the seizure of the lawyer’s phone would likely not have happened if he hadn’t engaged in this criticism of the government.

This sure looks like illegal retaliation against this lawyer, says the Court. Before even getting to the matter of the phone seizure itself, the court points out that HSI aggressively accelerated its “investigation” of the law firm — trimming the response time for the firm to turn over documents from the stated ten days to , apparently for the sole reason of giving it a justification for the seizure of the lawyer’s phone upon his return to the United States.

Furthermore, if the government was truly interested in securing information from the law firm, rather than just looking for an excuse to seize an immigration lawyer’s phone, it would had detained the head of the law firm (Georges Cote) and demanded access to devices upon his arrival in the US a full day before Lattarulo’s plane landed. That HSI showed no interest in Cote — despite him being the ostensible target of its illegal employment investigation — makes it abundantly clear this was all about the government finding some way to punish Lattarulo for his speech and, possibly, illicitly gain access to his communications with ICE detainees.

The government asked the court to not only reject this lawsuit but to apply a “bright line” ruling stating that anything the government pretends to be “reasonable suspicion” is sufficient to excuse any resulting rights violations. The court says lol no, that won’t be happening.

Defendants seek a bright-line rule that because they had reasonable suspicion to conduct the search, Lattarulo cannot show that retaliation was a but-for cause. [Opp’n at 14–15]. The Court disagrees.

[T]he limited record before the Court suggests that searches of cell phones are not regularly conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here and that Lattarulo’s own law firm partner was not subjected to the same seizure and search of property. The presence of reasonable suspicion therefore does not categorially bar a finding of causation under Nieves.

The court also addresses some of the Fourth Amendment concerns generated by HSI and ICE’s actions. While it’s not willing to rule on this issue (yet), mainly because these violations flow from the initial First Amendment violation, it doesn’t let them pass without comment.

The question this case raises is: reasonable suspicion of what? In other words, what types of suspected criminal activities can the government use a warrantless advanced border search to investigate? The First Circuit in Alasaad stated that the exception applies to searches for “contraband” or for “evidence of contraband or a border-related crime.”

The difficulty of this case lies in the fact that the suspected violation at issue—employment of unauthorized aliens in the United States in violation 8 U.S.C § 1324a—involves a law that is “enforced or administered by CBP or ICE” but arguably is not a “border-related crime.” Based on the information before the Court, there appears to be no connection between Lattarulo’s border crossing (or, more broadly, the government’s interest in policing the border) and the suspected crime that formed the basis for the government’s border search. Rather, it appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating.

At the end of the day, the court finds in favor of the Constitution. Since the phone has already been returned to Lattarulo, the court doesn’t need to do much else other than forbid HSI from looking through the content it downloaded from the lawyer’s phone until further notice. Given what’s stated here, “further notice” will likely take the form of a ruling ordering the government to destroy the data it copied from the lawyer’s phone. If we’re lucky, the government will appeal this and end up creating even more precedent that works against it.

Until then, the government is on notice that this sort of stuff won’t fly, even when it’s happening in “Constitution-free zones” where a majority of US citizens reside, or — at the very least — pass through on a daily basis.

items.title: California Issues Subpoena to Nvidia Over Chip Sales to China
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued subpoenas to Nvidia and former CEO Jensen Huang regarding reports that they misled investors about advanced AI chips potentially reaching China. "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a press release. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information -- and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law." The probe follows Huang's resignation amid allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy and comes as the SEC reportedly conducts a similar investigation. The Hill reports: Bonta's office said the information obtained through the subpoenas will help it to determine if Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., violated state law through its alleged actions. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta continued. items.title: Wired Says ‘Please Let The Internet Die.’ Some Of Us Are Busy Building A Better One.
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
It remains incredible — and disturbing — to me how many people now think of the entire internet as being made up of a few giant enshittifying companies. I understand that is. The big companies absolutely do dominate much of the internet, and it’s close to impossible to avoid them entirely. But that doesn’t mean that that’s the entirety of the internet. And when you act as if it is, you do real damage to the good parts of the internet that still exist outside of the blast radius of those giants.

Five years ago, I wrote an article listing out a bunch of “other” internet websites, in the form of a “test suite” for anyone proposing internet regulations. Since most attempts to regulate the internet focus on the alleged (often not clearly proven) “harms” of one of the internet giants, I wanted people to think through the harm that these rules will do to the actual parts of the internet worth saving. These included forums and smaller shopping sites and web hosting and chat groups and more. It also included Wikipedia, which later picked up on the idea (I was told by someone there that this was partly inspired by my original article) and offered up “The Wikipedia Test.“

And yet, it seems difficult for people to remember this. It’s just so to bitch and moan that the internet now is just Meta and Google and Amazon and TikTok and (these days) OpenAI or whatever. And it leads to silly articles like Wired’s recent article Please Let the Internet Die.

But if you read through it, the entire article is about enshittifying internet giants, with the assumption that because all suck, the rest of the internet should die as well.

It is ridiculous to conclude that because some giant parts of the internet are enshittifying, there’s little worth saving in the rest of it. But that’s exactly where this article lands.

To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn outbad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs haveto such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by

In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.

You can open up any of those links in the last two sentences and read about the excitement and the building, but I’ll just grab a bit from that last link:

The open web of the nineties didn’t win because the tools were better. It won because a critical mass of people decided that the alternative, a handful of AOL-style walled gardens choosing what everyone saw, was not the future they wanted. Then they built their way out of it. Slowly, unglamorously, in rooms that looked a lot like this one.

Whether atproto ends up being the thing, or a stepping stone to the thing, I don’t know. Nobody in the room claimed to know. But the work is real, the apps are shipping, and the people building them are taking it seriously without taking themselves seriously. That combination is rare, and historically, it’s the one that wins.

But if people just accept that “the internet needs to die,” we don’t get there. We get more stupid regulations that lock in those enshittifying giants and make it impossible to build a better internet.

The Wired piece is, in theory, a review of a new book called “The Internet Will Die,” which, at least as Wired presents it, frames the internet as fragile and doomed to cycles of decay, with big companies making things worse and deleting our digital histories along the way:

For one, West argues, people misperceive the “vastness” of the internet, which really amounts to “a vanishing fraction, a rounding error, of the human experience.” Moreover, it is remarkably fragile—West opens with the story of how a 2001 train derailment in a Baltimore tunnel took out a major bundle of fiber-optic cables, leading to internet slowdowns nationwide—and continually undergoes cycles of death and rebirth as a result of this natural instability.

If the internet is much smaller and less solid than imagined, West’s book suggests, then it’s crucial to recognize the forces that determine how those deaths unfold, or which pieces are preserved while others crumble. Because the market has falsely sold us the web as a comprehensive library of accumulated wisdom, each transient phase of this global network comes to define the present, for better and worse. Today we witness a dismal paralysis brought on by algorithmic incentives to churn out inflammatory garbage: Full-time influencers are in alosing arms race for attentionwith low-effort, high-volume channels that streamline production by delegating the creative process to bleeding-edge software.

But, again, that assumes an internet dominated by a handful of giants, the ones you hand all your data to, is the only internet possible.

But we already know that’s not true and it doesn’t need to be true in the future either. It sounds like West’s framing in his book is to encourage users to be more thoughtful about where they spend their time and energy online — and that’s great — but as Wired frames it, it’s all a wasteful endeavor since it’s always going to suck.

I certainly understand the fatalistic feeling that the internet sucks and will continue to suck. But that’s only true for people who lock themselves into the environments controlled by the internet giants you hate, rather than getting out and looking around at the cool things people are building which put the users in control of their own experience.

The piece ends with the author of the article, Miles Klee, admitting that the author of the book, John West, at least is open to the idea that a better internet can be created. But Klee, a self-described failed composter who’s “too lazy” for the gross work involved, doubts enough people will ever bother to do it.

“Look, the internet is rotting,” West says. “The question is, where are we going to put our energy?” A metaphor he often turns to in his book is compost. “Compost is just rot harnessed for a purpose,” he says. Can a decaying internet be fertilizer for something better? It’s a rosy notion, but speaking as a perennially failed composter—it’s just too gross, and I’m too lazy—I have my doubts about whether enough hardy, patient gardeners can be mobilized to make our digital landscape bloom once more.

And, again, I get the attitude, but I find this self-defeating nihilism to be pointless. The entire point of the internet, as Konstantinos Komaitis reminded us recently, is that it is . The internet is built on protocols that let anyone come in and build something better. Deciding we should just give up because some of the biggest players now suck is letting enshittification win.

The seeds of a better internet have already been planted. You can join Klee and Wired in doubting that enough gardeners will show up, but plenty of people are already out there digging. Come join us!

The Thursday ruling from the U.K.'s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret. The tribunal's ruling rejected the Home Office's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security. items.title: Tesla Starts ‘Selling’ Cybercabs You Can’t Buy With A $299/Month Automation Fee In Latest Ploy
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
Instead, Musk envisions pivoting Tesla so it focuses more on AI and automation — despite the fact that the company’s AI systems aren’t profitable or particularly popular amidst a sea of better options, and many of Musk’s robotics and automation efforts mostly consist of hype, vaporware, or stuff that will never really see a mass commercial launch (like the nonexistent Optimum robot).

Speaking of hype, Tesla recently took to Elon Musk’s right wing propaganda website to announce that the company would soon be “selling” Cybercabs to consumers. According to the announcement, the Cybercab is being sold for $29,990 (before taxes and insurance). Plus a mandatory $299-a-month “Autonomy Subscription” charge:

Of course with everything Musk, the actual details matter. It’s invite only, meaning you won’t get one. Indeed it’s pretty clear that most people won’t actually be able to buy one. The car is only allowed to drive in a few cities (mainly, Austin, Texas), so you probably wouldn’t be able to actually drive the vehicle if you were actually able to buy one (which you won’t). And even if you happen to live in one of the zones where it currently can drive, you can’t leave those zones.

And the fine print indicates that on the off chance you actually get one (again, you won’t), you won’t be able to put the car to work as an automated taxi, despite Musk and Tesla’s earlier promises on this front:

“One of the biggest selling points of Musk’s 2024 “We, Robot” pitch was that regular people could buy a Cybercab and add it to Tesla’s Robotaxi network to earn passive income while they sleep or work. But the order terms explicitly prohibit owners from using the vehicle for commercial purposes — meaning no Uber, no DoorDash, and no putting it on Tesla’s own Robotaxi network to offset the $299/month fee. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy has floated Q2 2027 as a possible target for letting customer cars join the network, so early buyers are paying full freight with zero way to monetize the car.”

That $299 per month fee adds an additional $17,940 to the vehicle sticker price over five years. And the fine print indicates that Tesla reserves the right to charge you even more for automation, provided they give you a 30 day advanced warning. So the rich layers of bullshit are all .

There’s also the fact that these vehicles likely aren’t going to be very safe as the company conducts a glorified alpha test on public streets. Musk’s legendary decision to overrule his engineers on radar/lidar and go camera only for self-driving has already resulted in no shortage of human deaths. Meanwhile America’s safety regulators have been too corrupt, captured, or feckless to do anything about.

While Tesla’s CFO insists the company wants to “literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation,” there’s very little indication that the company has the chops to fend off competitors and dominate the space. Most of what Musk now does is designed to prop up his fake supergenius engineer mythology, despite the ratio of bullshit to actual innovation becoming more and more lopsided.

So to prop up that mythology and goose comically inflated stock valuations, Musk is clearly keen on bundling and conflating Tesla’s increasingly stale vehicle lineup and “me too” automation and AI efforts with SpaceX’s actually innovative launch and Starlink technologies, and hoping the lion’s share of the press and public isn’t bright enough to notice the AI and automation stuff is .

You can expect a Tesla and SpaceX merger in 2027 specifically for this reason.

It continues to say nothing good about America (or our media) how easily Elon Musk convinced the press and public he was a supergenius engineer who could cobble together complicated rocket machinery wearing coveralls in his backyard shed.

Hindsight continues to illustrate how Elon Musk’s skill sets are opportunism, taking singular credit for the innovations of real engineers, the manipulation of a very broken media, and taking legal, regulatory, environmental, labor, and consumer protection “shortcuts” wherever possible.

items.title: Google Signs Deal With Blue Origin to Send Satellite Data Centers Into Orbit
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Google has partnered with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to launch satellite-based AI data centers into orbit as part of its experimental Project Suncatcher initiative. "Engadget reports: Each of these satellites will be equipped with "roughly the capacity of a data center rack" and will enter into a sun-synchronous orbit via heavy-lift New Glenn rockets. The rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers. The first launch isn't scheduled until early 2029, so we have a couple of years to see if this whole project even works. This is an experiment that Google calls a "long-term moonshot" to see if it's possible to put AI infrastructure in space by "tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit." The benefits of this would be massive. Data centers here on Earth are notorious hogs, with their snouts all over electricity grids, land and cooling systems. The hope is that the harsh vacuum of the cosmos will be a better fit for the technology.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Bill Cassidy, Who Got RFK Jr. Confirmed As Sec. Of HHS, Calls For Him To Be Fired
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
So there’s no misunderstanding, let’s start this post with the following: fuck Bill Cassidy.

This simpering, boot-licking, about-to-be-former-senator was the key vote in the confirmation hearings for RFK Jr.’s appointment as Secretary of HHS. Seen as a serious person with a background in the medical profession, his vote was essentially permission for enough other GOP votes to get Kennedy across the finish line. And if you don’t understand by now just how calamitous Kennedy’s tenure has been at HHS, then you’re so far lost that you’re unrecoverable. It’s been a .

Despite trying to lick Trump’s boots ever since he voted to convict during Trump’s second impeachment trial, Dear Leader never forgives and never forgets. As a result, Cassidy was rewarded for his trouble by getting primaried out of his reelection campaign thanks to Trump’s endorsement of his opponent. In the wake of his failure to get reelected, Cassidy suddenly found portions of his spine once more. He suddenly realized that RFK Jr. is bad and sucks at his job. He flipped his previous vote to a “no” in a failed Senate bill to end Trump’s military adventures in the Middle East.

After former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles was let go, Kennedy that the Senate “no longer has any leverage over me” as Stephen Miller is now in the role. 

CBS’s “Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan asked Cassidy on Sunday to respond to these remarks. 

“Well, first, he’s obviously trying to provide cover for failure as Secretary of Health and Human Services. He was supposed to be doing something positive on ultra-processed foods. That’s what MAHA moms wanted. There’s been minimal progress, and now we’ve lost our measles elimination status, and we have infants dying from measles,” said Cassidy. 

“There is no logic. This is about covering a series of failures,” he added. 

I could say the very same about this call to fire Kennedy, Senator. put him there! You are what allowed these failures to occur. You were the very first potential firewall against children getting sick and dying from measles, from cyclosporiasis ravaging the GI tracts of Americans, from the bullshit about Tylenol causing autism, the chemtrails, and so on. You failed in your role during the confirmation hearings. You failed to live up to the Hippocratic oath you took as a doctor. You failed to properly hold Kennedy accountable once he was in his role as Secretary.

While expressing dismay over Kennedy’s actions as recently as August, saying it was “pretty evident” that the secretary had about his plans to change the vaccine schedule, Cassidy avoided expressing any regret over his decision. 

A series of failures, attempted to be papered over by a call for Kennedy to be fired that came far, far too late to be of any use. It is time for you to go home and do whatever it is you’re going to do now that you’ll be out of elected office.

And, with any luck, the new Congress will fix the problem you created.

items.title: Amazon Fights the Delivery Protection Act With Homepage Banner, In-App Pop-Up
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill. When I log into Amazon today, I'm met with a vertical banner that reads: "ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order" with a button that says "Act now." The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn't specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I'm logged into Amazon. Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses. Clicking on "Act now" on Amazon's homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states: "Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees." The move marks an unusual expansion of Amazon's political advocacy, reports Ars, and raises concerns about the company's ability to influence shoppers and present a one-sided view of legislation. The bill, which also affects companies like FedEx and DoorDash, remains stalled in a City Council committee, with no vote scheduled.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Iowans Brace For Lead Dust Cloud As Army Plans to Detonate 5 Tons of Bomb-Making Chemicals
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The U.S. Army plans to detonate roughly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Friday. "The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," an advisory states. "Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure." PBS reports: Officials have released maps showing the potential drift north, and the Army will continue to update the maps based on weather. Some schools in the region have already canceled classes. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more could be affected. The vibrations from the two blasts will be quick but could break old windows in town. The resulting dust is expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said. While the Army recommends cleaning cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough. [...] Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered. "The safety of our people and our neighbors is non-negotiable," Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production. The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?
items.author: Jacob Hoffman-Andrews
items.content:
It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email, fly, spend money, use an Apple device*, or do signals intelligence. Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it?

Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12, any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless.

One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service.

While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI (or to malicious hackers), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse.

Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. That’s why so many update notes say things like “performance improvements and security fixes” the security fixes are patches to vulnerabilities.

Companies and governments that run infrastructure face a challenging tradeoff: deploy patches quickly or slowly and cautiously? Patching quickly is important to keep systems secure. But every software update runs a risk: any change to a deployed system can have unintended consequences that snowball into a disastrous outage.

This exacerbates a much deeper problem long discussed in the engineering culture of many, if not most organizations. Keeping networks, servers, and applications not just secure but resilient in the face of patches, reboots, and capacity changes requires an investment in staff, time, hardware, and processes for frequent maintenance, redundant systems, realistic staging environments, automated rollbacks, monitoring, and pre-deployment testing. These investments are rarely as attractive to decisionmakers as a new product or feature, or at times, sadly, as layoffs.

This should come as no surprise when we think of our apps, web sites, airlines and bank cards as supported by electronic infrastructure. As in the more visible physical world, maintenance can only be deferred for so long before the costs become immediate and dramatic. We accept the cost of an occasional short term bridge closure to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse, and highway departments schedule road work nearly every night of the year to repair and prevent the worst potholes.

When this kind of work is endlessly deferred in the world of software, we speak of debtissues we already know about that aren't causing a big enough problem right now to divert us from other work, but that, if left unaddressed, can easily multiply and interact to cause outages or other complications This can show up as routine steps that have to be done by hand instead of automatically on a schedule, a programmer's shortcut that works well in one specific situation but is more fragile in general, an operating system six months (or years) overdue for a reboot, or a piece of networking hardware no longer supported for patches by its manufacturer. On the other hand, when maintenance work is well-resourced and routine, it should be rare for even major security updates to cause significant issues.

What’s needed in the short term is a big investment in the people and training needed to roll out patches promptly and safely. What’s needed in the long term is a big investment in software security, eliminating entire classes of vulnerabilities, like memory safety, before they are ever written.

For organizations that have gotten used to patching slowly and cautiously, suddenly switching gears to patching quickly is a big challenge. And the flood of vulnerability disclosures enabled by AI means that everyone is being asked to switch gears like that at once.

Fortunately, it’s not a zero-sum game: patches can be rolled out quickly and cautiously, with investments in reducing technical debt and expanding maintenance budgets as described above. These measures are expensive and time-consuming, but necessary. For governments asking how to respond to AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, investing in the people and training necessary to stay on top of patches will pay big dividends in reliability and security.

For individuals, consider the trade-offs when relying on a single provider for many services you rely on. Consumer cloud and device offerings tie together many of the things we need to function on a daily basis like email, messaging, file storage, and even payments, but that convenience and simplicity comes with the risk of losing access to it all if that service goes offline (or suspends your account). Trying out interoperable alternatives is a great way to reduce your reliance on a single company.

Finally, for any critical data, learn the 3-2-1 rule for backups: Keep three different copies on two different types of storage with one copy in a different physical location. For many users, a laptop or other personal device, cloud storage, and a local backup disk exemplify this rule, as long as the laptop stores data on its own drives, not only in the cloud.

Among other things, the accelerated rollout of AI has made it all the more critical  to reinvest in people and systems to keep our software, networks, governments, and interconnected world stable.

items.title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
items.author: Joe Mullin
items.content:
The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies.

The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying.

Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system.

In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only 37 IPR petitions were filed in September 2026, compared to 129 petitions in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges.

This dramatic decline shouldn’t just concern patent lawyers. EFF has fought bad patents because so many software and internet patents make claims to the basic tools of free expression online, like sending email, using online ads, or publishing web pages. When bad patents go unchallenged, they affect everyone who cares about the freedom to write new code and make new technology.

That’s why EFF has defended IPR since it came on the scene more than a decade ago. It provides a faster and less expensive way to challenge patents that should never have been granted. Congress created IPRs because the Patent Office makes mistakes. District court litigation is an extraordinarily expensive way to correct them. Without a meaningful administrative review process, bad patents remain powerful weapons in the hands of patent trolls and others seeking to extract settlements from companies that often did nothing wrong.

Now, USPTO leadership is dismantling that safeguard.

Petitions and Institution Rates Are Falling

Since Congress created the IPR patent challenge process in 2012, the PTAB has always had some discretion in deciding which petitions deserve review. But institution rates today are much lower than their typical historical range.

Between fiscal years 2022 and 2024, the PTAB instituted between 66% and 68% of IPR petitions. In fiscal year 2026, which concluded in September 2026, the institution rate fell to 41%. And institution is only the first step of an IPR—it means the PTAB has agreed to hear the challenge, not that the challenger won, and the patent will be invalidated.

That decline helps explain why fewer petitions are being filed in the first place. Preparing an IPR petition takes substantial time and money. While cheaper than federal court, it’s still a complicated administrative process. Before filing, a challenger typically needs to search for prior art, hire experts, and develop detailed technical and legal arguments about why the patent never should have been granted.

Companies were willing to pay for IPRs because, historically, they could expect a predictable process. Petitions that met the statutory standard generally had a reasonable prospect of being heard and decided on the merits. But the USPTO has made it harder to get petitions heard and is throwing them out for reasons that have nothing to do with the merits of the challenges. Faced with these odds, many potential challengers aren’t filing at all.

Even After a Challenge Is Accepted, The USPTO Director Can Cancel It

When the PTAB decides to hear an IPR case, that means the petition has been “instituted”—but that has never meant that the petitioner will definitely win. It means the PTAB has determined the challenge warrants a full merits review, and the parties could expect the proceeding to continue toward a final written decision. But under the current USPTO leadership, that expectation has disappeared. The PTAB’s institution decisions are being repeatedly vacated by the Director.

USPTO Director John Squires has vacated at least 29 decisions granting institution of IPR proceedings, and subsequently denied the petitions, terminating those proceedings before a final written decision. These include cases that PTAB judges had already agreed to hear, as well as proceedings that Squires himself had previously allowed to proceed. This level of retroactive intervention is unprecedented.

In some cases, the parties had already invested substantial time and money litigating before the PTAB, only to have the proceeding terminated based on new reasoning by the Director’s office that arose after institution.

For example, in Revvo Technologies v. Cerebrum Sensor Technologies, the Director vacated an institution decision and remanded the case to the Board. The Board then instituted review again, but the Director reversed that decision. Using a new approach, the Director said that the petition had inconsistencies between claim construction positions taken before the PTAB and in district court. Since then, that decision has been cited as a basis for terminating several other instituted proceedings.

The result is another layer of uncertainty for people who want to challenge bad patents. Getting through the front door of an institution decision is much harder than it used to be—and now, even getting through that door doesn’t mean the PTAB will decide your challenge. Predictability is one of the things that made IPRs work.

Congress Created the PTAB To Avoid Costly Litigation

Congress created IPRs in part because challenging a questionable patent in federal court is enormously expensive and risky. Patent examiners work under serious time constraints, and some patents that shouldn’t have been granted will inevitably issue. Not every patent dispute requires years of expensive district court litigation. Congress recognized that, and created an administrative process, staffed with experts more capable of correcting those mistakes.

That system has benefited the public. Since 2012, it has helped invalidate thousands of patent claims that never should have been issued. The IPR process has protected startups, software developers, nonprofits, and small businesses that otherwise would have faced crushing litigation costs simply for building products or offering services that use everyday internet technology.

EFF supports a balanced IPR system because it should be easier to fight against bogus patents that should never have been issued. The cost of fighting a patent can be a weapon in itself, and weak patents don’t just burden large technology companies. Patent trolls routinely target small businesses and independent developers, and have gone after podcasters, retailers, and even coffee shops and nonprofits. These organizations have neither the resources nor the desire to spend years litigating over potentially invalid patents in federal court. IPR offers a chance to challenge those patents before litigation costs get out of control.

If we weaken the IPR system, bad patents become much harder and more expensive to challenge.

We Shouldn’t Accept This as the New Normal

Some defenders of the current approach argue that lower institution rates reflect more balance in the patent system. But institution rates at the PTAB have plummeted from 68% to 41% in just two years—a nearly 40% decline. IPR petition filings have reached historic lows. And even proceedings that have already been instituted can now be terminated months later, without a decision on the merits.

These developments send a troubling message to members of the public who might want to use the PTAB: don’t bother. The PTAB doesn’t need to institute every petition. But it does need to provide a process that is transparent, predictable, and fair. Right now, confidence in the system is disappearing.

If companies, individuals, and nonprofits conclude that IPRs aren’t worth pursuing, the consequences won’t stop at the PTAB. More weak patents that never should have been granted will survive, and patent trolls will use them. That means more defendants facing expensive district court litigation or paying settlements driven by the cost of litigation.

items.title: Nvidia Approaches Arm Boss Rene Haas In Search For New CEO
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Nvidia has reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as it searches for a replacement for co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned last week amid a personal scandal. According to Bloomberg, Haas is emerging as a leading contender for the job. The 64-year-old previously worked at Nvidia as general manager of its computing products business before joining Arm, giving him firsthand experience with the AI chip giant. The Guardian reports: Heidrick & Struggles, the recruiting firm hired by the company's board, has started contacting potential candidates, according to Bloomberg. It reported that Rene Haas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, is among those approached. [...] Haas, 64, is viewed as the leading contender for the top job at Nvidia, having previously worked at the $3.6tn company for seven years as the general manager of its computing products. Reports suggest that other potential candidates include: Ian Buck, an Nvidia vice-president; Lisa Su, AMD's chief executive; and Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer. Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Nvidia, Apple, Samsung and Qualcomm. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including more than 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech firm headquartered in Britain, now valued at $196bn. Haas told a tech conference in Austin on Wednesday that Huang was "a legend." "What he built at Nvidia is historic," he said. "You don't have many champions like that."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard Disclose Cyberattack On Third-Party Vendors
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard have disclosed cyberattacks involving third-party service providers that exposed customer marketing data, including names, email addresses and, in some cases, phone numbers and postal codes. All three companies said their core systems or payment networks were unaffected, while JPMorgan emphasized that the incident was unrelated to the banking disruptions earlier this week. Reuters reports: A cyber extortion group called "n0n" claimed on November 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses," according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch. The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data. The same hacking group on November 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data. [...] The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses. The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. "Customers don't distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here," said Carissa Robb at SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm. "There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinizing the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared," Robb said.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Court Tells Cops That The 4th Amendment Doesn’t Cover AI-Generated ‘Probable Cause’
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
I don’t know where this decision will take us, but its implications reach much further than the single case it covers. AI is pretty much everywhere, and if a court says an algorithm can’t make probable cause determinations, it affects/infects everything from facial recognition tech to predictive policing software to Axon adding AI shovelware to its omnipresent body cameras under the (correct) assumption cops don’t like writing reports.

In this case, Alain Osorio was arrested for allegedly passing a bad check at local bank. The only pictures of the suspect came from the bank’s CCTV footage. This was handed over to Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence (KY) Police Department.

The detective decided to run a screenshot of the suspect’s face (derived from the CCTV footage) through the PD’s facial recognition program. The decision [PDF] doesn’t specify which facial recognition program was used, but given that the match was made using photos found on Facebook, it suggests Clearview AI might have been involved, given its scraping of hundreds of billions of images from the open web since its inception.

Not that it did anything useful in terms of actual detective work. Nor did it do anything remotely constitutional, not when the operative word in “probable cause” is “probable.”

Relying solely on the AI identification, Detective Kilmer concluded that the match was accurate. [Id. at 4–5]. The Facebook profile belonged to an individual known as “Yony Smith Npoles Charon,” and for an unknown reason, Detective Kilmer concluded that “Yony” was actually Alain Vizcay Osorio—the man in the booking photo.

The court says “for an unknown reason.” I can make an educated guess, however. Passing a bad check is the sort of crime most cops won’t really dig into. Detective Kilmer was handed the case and did the bare minimum: he ran an AI-assisted search. He didn’t actually do anything that resembled detective work. But he still felt his 30 seconds of non-existent effort were enough to support a criminal complaint and the issuance of an arrest warrant.

Osorio — who lived in — was arrested and extradited to to face criminal charges. He was released on bond the day after his arrest (January 24, 2025). He was then indicted by a grand jury in March 2025 and arraigned roughly two months later. Again, Osorio pleaded not guilty. At that point, the state’s attorney’s office dismissed the charges after Osorio provided proof he had been working in Nebraska at the time the bad check was being passed by (the presumably still at-large) suspect captured by the bank’s security camera.

The only thing the AI used by the detective seemed to be capable of doing was reinforcing the investigator’s “all Black people look the same” prejudices. (To be clear, I don’t specifically know if this detective has these prejudices, but the chain of events in this case certainly support an assumption of this person’s assumptions, if you catch my drift.)

The individuals in the security footage and the Facebook profile image do not resemble the booking photo of Osorio. [Id. at 6–7]. Based on the booking photo, the only thing Osorio has in common with the suspect is that he is a black male with facial hair. [Dkt. 3-1 at 2–3]. Based on the photographs, it appears that Osorio has a different head shape, different haircut, different facial features, and different complexion.

Detective Kilmer told the court (via his affidavit) that he had used “investigative tools” to “match” Osario to the suspect. In reality, the court says, Kilmer only used a tool and rolled with its obviously faulty conclusions despite Florence PD policy stating facial recognition AI alone is not enough to “establish probable cause.”

Kilmer runs directly into this policy and the Fourth Amendment itself, which poses multiple problems for his desire to walk away fiscally intact from this lawsuit. The policy is undeniable, which means Kilmer deliberately ignored his “training” and any “expertise” it was supposed to impart.

But beyond that, there’s the Fourth Amendment itself, which can’t as easily be ignored as cop shop software clickwrap. That much is made perfectly clear in the court’s introductory paragraph:

The Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution does not allow a detective to delegate to AI the task of assessing probable cause. In other words, the Fourth Amendment does not permit an individual to be arrested based on nothing more than an uncorroborated conclusion by AI that the individual in question has committed a crime. And no reasonable detective in the Defendant’s position could conclude otherwise.

The first part of that suggests implications far beyond this case, given how often “detectives” are letting their fingers do the walking (so to speak) and pretending whatever the computer coughs up is arrest-worthy. That’s not just the facial recognition tech used in this case. This is also the AI that steers patrols and public interactions via so-called “predictive policing.” That’s also the AI that writes reports for police officers, allowing the computer to create the permanent, official record of stops, arrests, and uses of force.

But what’s also important is the last sentence of that paragraph. That’s the thing that’s going to make this stick. The detective isn’t shielded by qualified immunity, which means this is sure to be appealed. But if this officer does this (rather than “allow” the people who he’s supposed to be serving to buy him out of a lawsuit via a settlement), he’s going to make this an appellate case. And there’s definitely no reason to assume the higher court is just going to blow off the obvious concerns raised by this lawsuit and allow QI to cover up this compendium of wrongs.

For now, the decision stands as it is: AI isn’t probable cause. Never has been. Never should be. And if this court has anything to say about it, it never be. Detectives who prefer to let computers do their thinking for them might want to dial back their reliance on algorithms. Justice should never be subject to available processing power. And if you lack the desire (or intelligence!) to do detective work properly, well…
