items.title: Automakers Ramp Up Scare-Mongering Push To Ban Chinese EVs. You Know, ‘For Privacy’
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
Automakers are aggressively ramping up their efforts to pass a new law outright banning Chinese EVs. They obviously want to do this because they don’t want to compete with better, often significantly cheaper products, but they can’t just that. Instead, we get a lot of bizarre pretense about how an industry with the worst privacy ratings in America is just super concerned about privacy.

The auto industry’s preferred new law, the Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026, cleared the Senate Commerce Committee in July, and a House version of the bill now has more than 100 co-sponsors. Last September, Senate bill sponsors, Sens. Bernie Moreno (a Republican) and Elissa Slotkin (a Democrat), agreed to delay efforts to fast-track the legislation until this month.

“We need to ​protect the US market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry ​surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in ⁠American communities.”

This idea that Chinese EVs pose some unique privacy and national security threat to Americans is a common refrain from Bozzella and the auto industry. The argument is that Chinese EVs will collect oceans of data on American consumer driving and behavior habits, then funnel that data back to the Chinese government, who’ll then engage in all manner of ambiguous, nefarious behaviors.

There are several problems with the argument.

The biggest being that these same automakers do a disastrous job securing their own vehicles. Studies repeatedly show that U.S. automakers have some of the worst privacy and security standards in all of tech. An ocean of U.S. consumer driving, behavior, phone, and location data is already hoovered up at scale by your car, often left unencrypted, and sold to a laundry list of dodgy partners (including insurance companies, which will jack up your rates based on your driving habits with no transparency into the process).

The other problem: the U.S. is routinely too corrupt to pass modern internet privacy laws or even competently regulate a vast international web of dodgy data brokers. Most of the data collected by U.S. vehicle makers is already available via these data brokers; who’ll in turn sell this data to literally any random nitwit with two nickels to rub together (including Chinese intelligence).

Failing to secure your own vehicles and fighting tooth and nail against any privacy safeguards… then ranting incoherently about the threat of Chinese tech on U.S. shores is . Our failure to regulate data brokers or pass modern privacy laws means the Chinese simply buy this same data from any of dozens of dodgy companies already, making a lot of this stuff lazy pantomime.

Democratic lawmakers in Michigan also recently tried to ban Chinese EVs from even visiting the state, suggesting that automakers are afraid of Americans cheaper overseas alternatives. The justification (by folks who are are, again, when it comes to any sort of domestic U.S. privacy standards and enforcement) is they were just very concerned about U.S. consumer privacy.

I get the impulse to try and protect U.S. domestic automaker jobs (even though U.S. automakers have a long and detailed history of anti-labor behaviors), but there’s simply no coherent consistency to any U.S. policies. We don’t meaningfully protect labor generally, we don’t enforce consumer protection law, we’re too corrupt to pass a privacy law that reins in data monetization and hyper surveillance, and U.S. policymakers largely pay empty lip service to concepts like “affordability.”

We’ll see how much the new Democratic blood in the House and Senate shifts some of these dynamics, but as it stands now you can expect the new year to be filled with the brim with all sorts of expanded bipartisan xenophobic protectionism across the entirety of tech — from AI to electric vehicles. Ignoring that it will be bumbling Trump zealots like Brendan Carr tasked with a lot of enforcement (see: Carr’s rank incompetence surrounding the Chinese drone ban).

And you can expect all of it to be propped up by bad faith arguments that the bill backers are exclusively, suddenly, and very uncharacteristically concerned about your personal privacy. And in turn propped up by a shitty tech press oddly oblivious to their own nationalism biases.

I maintain that the best path forward is to allow Chinese drones, AI, EVs, vacuums, and assorted other tech into the U.S. market, but properly fund, staff, and legally support our privacy, labor, competition, and consumer protection regulators to ensure a level playing field and healthy markets. Large corporations hate that idea, so instead we get this bizarre and performative protectionist pantomime.

items.title: Bank CEOs, NSA Tell Congress That AI-Driven Patches Are Behind Outages
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Washington Sun: Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency have told members of Congress that this week's widespread tech outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities identified by artificial intelligence, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations. [...] "These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away," said one congressional official briefed on the matter. "They're trying to push through a lot of patches all at once -- more than the system was designed for." On Monday, banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. On Tuesday, the NSA said that "scheduled routine maintenance" was responsible for the "temporary degradation" of some of its networks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that "they're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system. ... We're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out." "There's some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there's not an attack. But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems," said Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode. "Updating those is going to be a rocky process, and as we get more advanced models this won't be a one and done thing -- we'll continue to find more vulnerabilities."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: 'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Longtime Slashdot reader HnT writes: Security researchers at Calif have disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2-rated memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. By sending a malformed string ending in a stray = character, attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write to leak sensitive memory or achieve pre-auth remote code execution on major platforms like Jira, Jenkins, and Keycloak. Although Calif says the vulnerability is difficult to exploit, Oracle released a critical patch update Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to update immediately. OpenJDK's security advisory can be found here. The Calif researchers warned that vulnerable systems could remain exposed for five to 10 years, given how slowly some organizations patch their infrastructure.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: NYC Mayor Mamdani Disbands NYPD Unit That Treated Protesters Like Terrorists
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
It’s taken pretty much forever, but finally one of the NYPD’s worst specialist units is being disbanded. The catalyst here was the election of a mayor who was finally serious about holding the NYPD in check. For years, the city’s mayors have done whatever they can to keep the cop shop happy, including the last mayor, who went deep down a corruption hole to make sure both he NYPD remained happy, even if his constituents weren’t.

A controversial New York Police Department unit accused of using excessive force against protesters has been disbanded, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced Monday, fulfilling a key campaign promise from the mayor to separate protest policing from counterterrorism.

Along with the elimination of the Strategic Response Group, certain aggressive crowd-management tactics are now banned and new dialogue-focused units will be established in the NYPD and the Mayor’s Office of Community Safety to ensure a coordinated response to protests, the mayor and commissioner said in a statement.

If you’re wondering about the controversy of this particular unit, you have to take a trip in the wayback machine to 2015, which was when NYPD Commissioner and the mayor who never was the reformer he pretended to be (Bill de Blasio) decided a single unit could handle three very different aspects of policing, somehow without causing collateral damage to Constitutional rights. (Or maybe they didn’t actually belive this and chose to do it anyway.)

The SRG got folded in with an existing counterterrorism unit, apparently because the mayor and police commissioner decided fighting terrorism and policing protests was roughly the same thing. A few years later, documents obtained by journalists made it clear SRG officers were routinely brutalizing peaceful protesters. This wasn’t much of a surprise, considering its counterterrorism unit was known for routinely violating rights while engaging in extremely biased policing/surveillance. That this infection would spread to the SRG is completely unsurprising. Bad apples, etc.

This unit should have been disbanded once this information was made public. But it wasn’t. Given that regular NYPD patrol officers are just as capable of violating people’s rights, it hardly made sense to provide specialist pay for rote thuggery. But the SRG kept on keeping on… right up until NYC residents made it explicitly clear they were sick of the same old bullshit from their mayors.

The disbanding of this unit has the support of the current police commissioner. And it goes further than just rearranging some deck chairs so SRG officers can get back to the rights-violation business elsewhere. It also establishes a “First Amendment Support Team” in the NYPD that will help train and support officers who are asked to police protests.

In addition, “kettling” protesters is no longer an option. The popular — and extremely abusive — tactic is used by plenty of PDs around the nation. Under the guise of breaking up a demonstration, officers surround protesters, physically force them into a confined area, and then rain down pepper balls and tear gas on protesters whose only other option is to physically force their way out of the “kettle.” This, of course, leads to even more police violence, as well as trumped-up “assaulting an officer” charges as people try to escape this form of mass imprisonment.

The dissolution order also says this, which is pretty fucking wild:

[T]he use of bicycles as weapons will be allowed only when preventing death or physical injury to an officer or another person.

[If you haven’t watched the Prime series “Patriot,” you’re only hurting yourself.]

You can’t reform a unit that has been given the greenlight to be as awful as it can be for nearly a decade. The only fix is shutting it down and starting over with an emphasis on making officers realize that people’s rights are just as important as their safety. If this leads to more officers resigning or retiring because they don’t want to work for an employer that expects them to respect the law… GOOD. New York City residents are better off without them.

items.title: Our Dipshit DHS Secretary’s Outage Expert: “One Guy That’s Very Smart With Tech”
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
It should be no surprise that people are also connecting the dots and wondering if these things are all connected. I mean, how could you not? For what it’s worth, I tend to agree with the experts Prof. Kate Klonick has spoken to who suggest the explanation is a benign one — old systems do break down, and it can be a bit of a coincidence that a bunch of big-name systems all broke down around the same time, but humans (as pattern-matching animals) are just paying closer attention to all of them breaking down at once.

If there is a throughline here, my is that a lot of the tech companies have been quick to push layoffs lately, stupidly believing that they can replace people with AI (which, as we’ve been saying, is a dumb plan), and that means a lot of expertise — including the kind of tacit knowledge AI can’t easily capture — has walked out the door. When the people who actually know how to keep these old systems running are gone, those systems become a bit more likely to fail. That is, while lots of people jumped to “AI” being to blame, my guess (and it is a guess) is that it’s less the direct impact of AI systems, and much more the downstream indirect results of stupid CEOs cutting corners by laying off the kind of people who could keep these systems online.

Still, it does no one any favors to have the dumbest fucking people alive in charge of all of this, but we do. Back on Friday when the FAA ground stop situation happened, the first one to talk about it was DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin (who, back when he was a senator, was long considered one of the dumbest people in the Senate). When asked if the FAA situations had anything to do with AI he responded by refusing to rule it out (“You just can’t rule out anything at this point”) and with the absolutely ridiculous retort: “We call it SI around here, remember?” He also said that it wasn’t “another 9/11” which is an awfully odd comparison to make, and only served to make many people wonder if we should be even more worried.

Later that evening he appeared next to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, where there were awkward exchanges where Duffy and Mullin didn’t appear to be on the same page about what happened or what was to blame. However, both the FAA and the contractor behind its newly expanded $875 million AI system insisted that system had nothing to do with it.

Then, on Monday evening Mullin went on Sean Hannity’s show and… reminded everyone just how clueless he still is. The video clips are remarkable, mainly this one that shows him first suggesting that all the outages don’t appear to be a cyberattack, based on his conversations with CISA, and then saying how he spoke to some successful tech bro who he says asked not to be named (though he says it’s not Elon) who fed him some nonsense that, once it makes it through the empty caverns of Mullin’s brain, came out even more garbled:

Mullin mentions that he had the folks at CISA (the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency) look into all of these events, and they told him that it doesn’t appear to be an interrelated cyberattack.

“[W]hen we start looking at the cyber world, I start asking CISA, hey, what’s going on here? And they said, sir, we’re not seeing any traffic that would make us think that this is a cyberattack, they’re all individually unrelated.”

Yes, that’s right, the federal government gutted its cybersecurity infrastructure staff and put many of those who remained on “deportation paperwork processing” instead. And that hollowed-out agency is the one we’re now relying on to tell us everything’s fine.

Anyway, the next bit of Mullin’s ramblings to Hannity is just absolutely bizarre:

“And so I started talking to the tech industry, and one guy that’s very smart with tech…it’s not Elon…I said, what could be causing all these separate outages, and he says, I believe that it’s the SI. He said because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is, and so, when they…put in a program that’s able to write codes, and it goes in, it self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself, it’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing, and it’s a ripple effect, and it causes these systems to be over[run] that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today. That was the conversation I had today. That kind of makes sense to me.”

Sooooooo… you can kinda piece together what someone probably told Mullin if we backtrack it through the reverse-stupid filter. From Mullin’s description, it sounds like someone explained to him what recursive self-improvement (RSI) means (“self-fixing”) and he then tried to apply that to the outages? Except that RSI is on the training new models side of things, not the keeping basic infrastructure working side of things. The whole “work as fast as” and “self-fixing” thing really sounds very much like someone who was told a few things about how AI systems work and are trained and not understanding the technology even slightly, and regurgitating it to the press in the stupidest way possible.

Also, dude, you’re the Secretary of Homeland Security, speaking to “one guy that’s very smart with tech” is not exactly the way you should be going around trying to get a handle on what’s happening with our technology systems these days.

As mentioned, it’s very possible AI played an indirect role here, and some of these outages may even have more direct AI-related causes. But so far almost everyone involved has denied that AI tools had anything to do with it, so it’s not very reassuring when the Homeland Security Secretary who goes around saying “this is not another 9/11” also decides to call up random tech bros to get their take, which he will then explain badly in a manner that doesn’t make much sense. There may be more to all of this, but I have zero faith that Mullin would either understand or be able to explain to the public what AI’s role was.

At this point, I am way less worried about all these system outages (and I say that as someone who got stranded 3,000 miles from home for five days due to the FAA mess, and am writing about this on the first flight I could finally get back towards home many days later) than I am about the fact that we really have the dumbest, most credulous, conspiracy-theory believing dipshits in charge of any sort of coordinated response to all of these outages.

items.title: Jensen Huang's Fall Hits 'Open' Models In Boost to Anthropic and OpenAI
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia could weaken the open AI model ecosystem he spent years championing, potentially strengthening closed-model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Financial Times. From the report: The US chip giant's former chief threw Nvidia's balance sheet into creating a broad AI ecosystem, including by seeding and acquiring start-ups involved in the development of open-source and open-weight models, which users can customize and run on their own hardware. Huang was a forceful advocate for their spread, lobbying against Washington's moves to restrict the use of Chinese-made open models while seeking the development of US alternatives. "Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector," he wrote this summer in his first-ever message on X. His ignominious exit from Nvidia deprives the open model sector of its most vocal and influential supporter in the US. "I think Jensen stood to gain the most economically and was personally committed to diversity at the model layer," said one venture capitalist who has invested in AI start-ups alongside Nvidia. "Without him and a less generous Nvidia in terms of investment, we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers." Whether Nvidia will continue the rapid pace of dealmaking under a new leader is unclear. The company was expected to participate in or lead four start-up deals currently under discussion: investments in Thinking Machines Lab and Groq, a potential partnership with Reflection AI and the $12.9bn acquisition of open model repository Hugging Face. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," said Elon Musk in a post on X on Saturday. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." "In some sense [Huang leaving Nvidia] is bad for the industry, but in some sense Jensen is an enemy of the frontier labs because he wants models to become commoditized so he retains the prime position in the value chain," said one senior figure at a leading Silicon Valley AI company. "I don't think open weight models are going away... but losing Jensen as their greatest financial backer and champion will slow their progress, and I imagine will not hurt Anthropic's IPO," said another industry figure. "It's reasonable to expect the ouster of Jensen will concentrate computing power more in the hands of frontier labs and hyperscalers," added a senior figure at an AI lab. "That's good for the labs."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Verge: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he's AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. "I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy's organization around AGI?" he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn't think frontier models like Claude are conscious. "I don't think so," he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman's view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic's team has "wireheaded" themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn't quite as firm about it. "It's a good debate," he said. "I'm not sort of dogmatic about it. What I'm saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?" I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter's questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us." "Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be," he said. "But remember, the model has no limits. It'll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it." Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. "If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?" he asked. "If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That's the debate." "I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one -- at least in a democracy -- can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there's only capital and there's no labor. I mean, I don't know, that's not an economy." "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Trump Is Very Mad Because CBS Under Larry Ellison Still Does Real Reporting Sometimes
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
Like any good right wing propaganda mill, you have to pepper in just enough “normal” reporting to try and maintain something vaguely resembling credibility. And it can take a while for people like Weiss to purge existing journalists still loyal to the public interest.

So the network will sometimes still run a story that still has something with teeth; like this recent 60 Minutes report featuring a whistleblower who made it clear that the government has been covering up the damage caused by Iranian aerial strikes during Trump’s pointless and disastrous war in Iran. Worse; they appear to have ignored warnings of some attacks, resulting in the avoidable deaths of U.S. troops.

Trump is now mad at the fact there’s still honest reporting coming out of Larry Ellison’s media and infotainment empire. In a post to his personal propaganda website, he wrote:

If you can’t read that, Trump writes:

“The new people running 60 Minutes are even worse than their predecessors. A recent study on an attack in the early stages of Iran was not correctly stated. Since February 28, 2026, the start of Epic Fury, Iran has fired between 8,000-9,000 One-way Attack Drones. Only 2 of them got through, resulting in U.S. fatalities, both on the first day, hitting Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Likewise, Iran has fired about 2,000 Ballistic Missiles. Only 1 out of the 2,0000 got through, and caused U.S. fatalities (Jordan). Translation: 99.99% of Iranian missiles and drones have been shot down or, in any event, not caused U.S. deaths. CENTCOM defensive measures have been historically effective. No one in the World has the ability to do so well. All of this being left out of the 60 Minutes “report.” Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

It’s also been very clear throughout the war that Trump, and his advisors, didn’t really understand how drones have changed warfare before bumbling into Iran. And ironically, even having a Trump ally specifically buy up news organizations with the unsubtle goal of glazing the president hasn’t been enough to cover up the stink.

That’s not to say that CBS — like most of the U.S. press — can’t and won’t get worse. Weiss only started at CBS a little over a year ago, and it’s going to take her and Ellison a while to truly shape CBS into the kind of agitprop mill they’re looking for, much to the chagrin of all the actual reporters and journalists still employed there.

The goal for U.S. oligarchs is to very clearly buy up what’s left of U.S. corporate media and create a right wing autocrat and oligarch safe space. A massive industry of pseudo-journalism, trolling, and agitprop that’s somehow going to be even worse than a lot of the soggy, feckless corporate journalism Americans have come to expect.

But historically, thin-skinned autocrats and fascists are never happy, and there’s simply no bottom to their desire for feckless obedience and glowing adulation from the press and public alike. There’s no debasement that will ever be enough. And while CBS leadership seems happy to oblige, it’s nice that actual journalism still sometimes manages to leak through the cracks.

items.title: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). This means radio signals will take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, now nearly 50 years into its mission. "Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal -- so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky," reports Space.com. From the report: But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA. [...] At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Massive New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion.

is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.

A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.

Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. “Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all,” the researchers wrote.

Most of the respondents (82%) said they’d used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, “although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships,” they wrote.

The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as “high quality” and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: “In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating.”

People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. “However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers also asked young people what they do online all day and the overwhelming majority (72%) said they spend their time scrolling short form content, mostly TikTok and Instagram. It’s also how they deal with loneliness, with six in 10 young people participating in this study reporting that they often or always scroll through online content when lonely.

They also said scrolling works to dispel loneliness almost equally as well as hanging out with a friend in real life: “Although scrolling is more commonly used when young people feel lonely, those who use scrolling or in-person time as coping strategies report nearly identical levels of perceived helpfulness.”

Still, people who reported strong in-person friendships said they felt lonely less often, while online friendships have the same effect on loneliness regardless of how participants ranked the quality of those friendships. “No comparable difference appears across levels of online-only friendship quality,” the authors wrote. Having in-person relationships seemed to be what mattered most: “Higher loneliness is also more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.”

The relationships between loneliness, online friendships, and AI is complex and a person’s material conditions shape how they form friendships more than their access to a chatbot or how they use social media. The researchers’ analysis of young people who said they have no trusted adults in their lives makes that clear.

“Further analysis identifies several characteristics associated with having none of these friendship modes, but one stands out in particular: not having a trusted adult outside the family,” the researchers wrote. “This association remains substantial after accounting for country or residence, gender, age, , and parent/ caregiver relationship quality.”

The study’s authors warned about reading too much into these results. “These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive,” they wrote. In general, people don’t have the same expectations of a chatbot that they do someone they know in real life.

“The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people’s relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly,” the study concluded.

items.title: Two Video Games With Identical Names Went Way Beyond Managing To Coexist
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
In the video game industry, trademark disputes over similarly named games are not remotely uncommon. Usually when this happens, we’re talking about one same or similar word amongst games names: “scroll”, or “rage”, or “wasteland”. Those tend to annoy us, because they seem certain to fail the real test of trademark law in most cases, which is whether or not the buying public will be confused about an association or similar source between the products.

But what if there were two games named identically that were released in close proximity to each other? We saw that exact thing happen earlier this year, when two unrelated games that shared the title were released on Steam.

Earlier this year, Piece by Piece launched on Steam. Then another game, also called Piece by Piece, launched on Steam.

“Back when we announced the Steam launch date for our Piece by Piece in March, a day later the Piece by Piece from Neon Polygons also announced their launch date, and it was two days after ours,” said Mike Rose, co-founder of No More Robots. He said he got a nervous email from Neon Polygons, concerned that No More Robots would go after them for having a game of the same name.

This sort of thing happens all the time, of course. Two companies or developers working separately on projects that have similar, or identical in this case, titles for their work by pure happenstance. There’s nothing malicious here. There’s no intent to confuse anyone, or to ride off of someone’s coattails.

But because this is business and the only way to really protect your investment is to participate in the IP-maxing of your product… right?

As it turns out, no, you can just be human and awesome instead.

“I got back to them and said ‘Well, that’s just hilarious. Do you wanna bundle up on Steam? I did it partially because it was a nice / fun thing to do, but I also kinda did it because I love chaos.”

It’s a beautiful story about how not being an asshole can lead to other joint business opportunities, so long as you don’t default to IP protectionism. The games are different, nobody is confused, but why not bundle them together.

It’s a great little tale if that’s as far as it went. But it gets funnier when they decided to keep teaming up for a release on Nintendo’s Switch.

Now they’re launching together on the Switch under the same publishing label, because sometimes video games and the people who make them are good.

“We had to explain over and over again, to each separate Nintendo organization (Europe, Japan, America), that ‘No, sorry but those are two separate games. Yes, they have the same name. Yes, they have the same release date. Yes, we are very sorry. We promise we won’t do this again,’” Rose said.

It apparently took repeated conversations to explain to Nintendo why the two companies were working together instead of slugging it out either in court or with the USPTO over trademark concerns. It’s quite fun for me to picture Nintendo execs and lawyers sitting around a conference room phone, being told by these two developers that they’re not going to war over the shared titles, as they sit their with confused looks because that just doesn’t compute to Nintendo.

More of this please. More people choosing humanity over IP maximalism. It’ll make the world a better, more fun place, I promise you.

items.title: US Officially a Measles Endemic Country
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years. Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won't lead to changes in the federal response. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," Schwartz said on Tuesday. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Robbie Williams Defends Olivia Rodrigo, Calls Song-Similarity Claims ‘Ambulance Chasing’
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
Over the last decade and a half we’ve seen a flood of very stupid copyright lawsuits, often from old, washed-up artists (or worse, their estates), demanding money from younger artists because new songs have some similarities — a feel, a melodic snippet, the same chord progression, whatever. The worst example of this, obviously, was the infamous Blurred Lines case, which ended stupidly, and kicked off a bunch of other similar lawsuits (many of which haven’t been as successful). It’s gotten so ridiculous that some artists now film their entire writing process in case they later have to go to court to defend their creative process.

Anyway, it looked like we might be getting another one of those silly situations when some people started pointing out that Olivia Rodrigo’s recent release, take me home (4 christmas), sounds similar to Robbie Williams’s Candy, from back in 2012. Of course, making this even more complicated is that Rodrigo has said her song was inspired by the 1981 song Christmas Wrapping from the band The Waitresses, and claims she spoke to that band’s Christopher Butler before writing her own song.

What usually happens next is that the online murmurings get louder and louder until the older artist finally says or does something — often demanding a cut of the royalties. But this time, Robbie Williams did something different: he published a rant (in image form on Instagram) defending Rodrigo while knocking musicians who rush to “go after” anyone whose songs sound a bit like their own.

Since reading text in images is perhaps the most annoying way to do anything, I’ve transcribed his 4 image rant below:

There’s something about the music industry that’s been bothering me for a while.

People coming after people because they’ve spotted a similarity between two songs.

Some of it I completely understand. Some of it is absolutely justified.

Most of it, I think, is complete bollocks.

I’ve had plenty of people come after me over the years because something I’ve released apparently sounds like something somebody else released.

And sometimes I listen and think, fair enough, I can hear that.

Other times I think, are you having a fucking laugh?

There are only so many notes. Only so many chords. Only so many ways of putting them together before you inevitably find yourself somewhere somebody else has been.

Music has been around for a very long time.

We’re all going to bump into each other eventually.

Which brings me to Olivia Rodrigo.

I’ve loved her since Brutal. What a fucking record. I wish I’d made it.

Also, I cannot believe how much she swears on stage. And that’s coming from me. I’m a Sweary Mary, but she’s making me look like a Victorian schoolmistress.

It sounds to me as though she may have accidentally stumbled across a musical echo of mine in one of her new songs.

I don’t know whether there’s technically a publishing issue, a copyright issue, or no issue whatsoever.

And I don’t want to know.

Because I think at some point, some fucking sanity has to prevail.

Now, I appreciate I’m in a position in my career where I can afford to take that view. Not everybody is. And genuine theft is genuine theft. Artists deserve to be protected. But there’s a difference between protecting your work and treating every vaguely familiar sequence of notes as a winning lottery ticket.

Some of this stuff has become ambulance chasing.

And I think it’s disgusting.

We all stand on the shoulders of people who came before us. Sometimes consciously. Sometimes without even knowing it.

If we keep punishing people for accidentally arriving somewhere somebody else has already been, eventually we’re going to frighten the creativity out of everyone.

Olivia, if you’re reading this, I think you’re fucking brilliant. But please stop swearing so much.

It makes me feel like I have to keep up.

And frankly, I’m already swearing far more than is necessary.

Lots of love and Happy Christmas

There are a bunch of good points there (some of which we’ve made before), including that this is how music works. Almost all musicians start out by imitating their favorite artists and then learning how to add their own style and signature to the music. Sometimes they add in bits as an homage. Sometimes they just do it accidentally because — as Robbie notes — there are only so many notes (and even fewer combinations of them that actually sound good together).

Of course there may be some complicating factors. Williams can say all of that, but it looks like there may be other copyright interests in the song, considering that he co-wrote it with some others, and it includes a riff from a different song (from one of the people listed as a co-author of Candy, Terje Olsen). It’s also not clear if Williams owns his own publishing, and publishing companies can be especially annoying. And that’s not even getting into the complications regarding the 1981 song by The Waitresses as well.

It’s also worth noting that Rodrigo has had to give up royalties to other artists in the past as well, which some are suggesting means that Rodrigo “has a history” of this kind of thing, but to me suggests (again) that lots of music borrows ideas — consciously or unconsciously from others — and people should just be more chill about it. Like Robbie Williams here.

In this era when everyone wants to lawyer up and demand things, it’s always nice when someone just comes out and says “yo, this is fucking crazy, I don’t want any part of it, the music is great, can we please just enjoy that.”

items.title: Google To Keep Temporary Gemini Chats For Two Months
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
timob58 shares a report from TechCrunch: Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable. The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12. OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models. "A recent explainer on AI and business IP notes that providers keep data for abuse monitoring even when it is not used for training," adds timob58.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday.

ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword.

Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware

Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.

items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
PattonPending writes: As reported by The Register, Zoom, the BBC, CNN, HSBC, and numerous other websites briefly served malware on November 16 after an attacker exploited Optimizely's "Experiments" feature to inject JavaScript into their pages through Optimizely's CDN. The malware replaced cryptocurrency addresses, attempted to steal credit card information and cookies, and sought to compromise iOS devices. Websites belonging to at least 178 organizations were affected via the "OPTIMJACK" vulnerability, which has since been patched. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects," the company said. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered." The researchers said they found malicious code in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely scripts examined, including those on the company's own website and login portal, suggesting the number of affected businesses could be significantly higher.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: BREAKING: Everything
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
A few hours ago, I went to rent a Lime bike to ride the ten minutes to my therapy appointment. I opened Lime, scanned the QR code, and double clicked my iPhone’s side button to authorize Apple Pay. The app hung for a few moments, then closed. I tried several more times and the same thing happened. In the back of my mind, I wondered what was going on — was the Lime bike broken? Was my cell phone service out? Was it something else? I opened the Uber app and, similarly, wasn’t able to pay. I opened DownDetector and realized that the entirety of Apple Pay, a thing I thought existed only on my phone and not the cloud, was down. I texted my therapist, put my phone in my pocket, and started jogging. 

Not being able to rent a Lime Bike for several minutes is an extremely minor inconvenience barely worth mentioning. And yet the mental gymnastics my brain did in those few minutes — what’s broken, why is it broken, how is it broken — is something that everyone I know have been repeatedly doing for the last few weeks as seemingly every service and system crashes down around us. Over the weekend, people who I do not normally talk to about my job asked me: What is going on with the airplanes? Why ? ? 

The default assumption that many people are making is that these are either being caused by cyberattacks and/or “AI” broadly defined, whether that’s AI gone haywire, “rogue” AI agents, or something else, which is indicative of just how fearful people are of AI. What I have been telling people is, basically, that shit is broken and things are going to keep breaking. For lots of different reasons. It’s often not a hack and it’s often not explicitly AI-related, but everything now sort of looks like that XKCD comic of the dependency domino tower. 

While not exactly true that AI and cyberattacks are causing these outages, it’s also not entirely wrong, either. What we’re seeing is — I think — a series of infrastructure failures (and some cyberattacks) that are not directly connected but are broadly a symptom of the same general trends and systemic problems we’ve seen across society, the government, and the tech sector over the last several years. ( has a nice piece on how you can assess any given outage.)

First, it’s worth mentioning that anytime there’s a string of outages, there’s a tendency to tie them altogether. And outages or hacks that previously wouldn’t have been noted at all suddenly get more attention and become part of the narrative. Take, for example, the fact that the International Ice Hockey Federation has been targeted by a cyberattack; you probably would not normally hear about this but it has suddenly become part of the broader story.

items.title: Vice-President Grassley And The Bipartisan Politics Of An Imminent Trump Impeachment
items.author: Cathy Gellis
items.content:
There was always a deal to be made similar to the one that is described here, had Democrat leadership ever had the vision, skill, and courage to pursue it. But now, after the last election, it is even easier to play the political musical chairs that impeachment would involve, and to everyone’s satisfaction.

There never was a reason to wait to impeach Trump, and there certainly isn’t one at this point. There is plenty of evidence upon which to predicate it (pretty much any two Truth Social posts would provide sufficient basis), and the Constitution requires little more than two votes on it: one in the House to impeach, and one in the Senate to convict. Trump could be gone in a day, and given all the damage he causes every minute he remains, there is no time to lose to get started.

One of the main arguments people have nevertheless put forth to try to justify the Democrats’ refusal to pursue impeachment against Trump has been “they don’t have the votes.” Already it was a ridiculous argument: in the House, if the Democratic caucus had been united in pursuing it, they would have only needed to peel off a few Republicans to come join them, and, depending on absences, potentially very few. And had the Democrats been united behind impeachment it would have changed the political math enough for the GOP to think seriously about joining them—whereas given the Democrats abject refusal to get on board with it there was never any reason for any Republican to ever even consider it either.

(Meanwhile, even if Democrats were somehow correct to have been deterred from moving forward with an actual impeachment attempt, the numbers certainly didn’t justify not even beginning to pound the drum on eventually impeaching. After all, if you don’t have the votes today, the job is to work towards getting them tomorrow. And then using them once you do, as they most definitely do now.)

Still, while having enough votes in the House is not an issue—come January the Democrats will have plenty of their own, without needing GOP help—there is still the question of the Senate, which is what this post is about. Like with the House getting the votes needed to convict and actually remove Trump always was possible, if only Democrat leadership had the vision to see it. And now, after the election, it is even more possible, if only Democrats would finally do what is needed to line them up.

Obviously at 56 Senators (or 55 with the Fetterman discount) Democrats cannot vote to remove Trump from office by themselves. But there has always been a deal to be done, which is now even easier to do, to get Republicans on board by making it worth their while politically. Especially after the drubbing this November even the most politically obtuse Republicans must understand that Trump is an albatross hanging around their neck, destroying their political futures and the prospects for any policy they hoped to advance. While they might have been afraid to try to make a move against Trump before November, fearing his cult-like popularity would make it impossible to politically survive such an attempt, they now know that his popularity is at best fragile if not illusory. Even many MAGA adherents, even if still generally on Team Trump, have been openly speaking about their dismay in him not delivering on what he promised (and instead delivering the exact opposite). In any case, there is now evidence of a nation-wide appetite to be done with Trump, which everyone, including and especially the Senators up for reelection in 2028, both Republican AND Democrat, needs to heed. Their future political fortunes depend on it, and everyone now knows it.

But for Republicans, their political interests are not just limited to being rid of Trump. Impeachment also creates political opportunity due to all the vacancies it creates, starting in the Presidency itself. With the Presidency empty, the Vice President is automatically promoted into it, which then leaves the Vice Presidency empty and waiting to be filled. Which is where things get interesting, because it is not filled automatically but by presidential appointment. And if it’s filled with a sitting Senator, then it also creates an opportunity to appoint another to replace them in the Senate. Thus it is time for Democrat leaders with vision to start choreographing the political dance that impeachment could soon have everyone on both sides of the aisle moving to.

Obviously whether such a deal should be seen as a win for Democrats and the country depends on accepting one thing: that just about any alternative is better than Trump. Even the most craven and crooked Republican is still better than Trump, who is corrupt on a scale even regularly corrupt politicians could hardly imagine. Even the most sinister and cynical Republican is still better than Trump because, unlike Trump, they don’t have a cult of personality to fuel their administration’s malevolence. And the reality remains: Trump is a volatile, reckless, exigent, and uncontained threat to the security of the nation every moment he remains in office. Any alternative who is even slightly less of a danger is a necessary and imminently needed improvement.

Which is why, yes, even J.D. Vance is still an improvement, awful though he is. He is at least a little smarter, and also less popular, which means people will be able to say no to him where they have been unable to say no to Trump. But there is also an opportunity here: if the Democrats play their cards right there is a chance that instead of just a bad but better deal that elevates Vance, they could get one that brings them even more advantage.

Any deal of course does begin with Vance. He obviously has aspirations for the Oval Office, and since the election has shown himself willing to knife Trump. He is, for purposes of saving our democracy from Trump, an available ally, however inadvertently, for Democrats who are serious about that country-saving mission to work with. And there is a definitely a deal to be made with him: help him get his dream job in exchange for his agreement on policy that Democrats are obviously not going to be able to get from Trump and his vindictive veto (no matter how much they delude themselves to the contrary).

The downside to this deal—apart from just having to live with President Vance for two years—is that there is a presumed incumbent advantage come the next presidential election, but a strong Democratic majority can keep him on a short enough leash to keep the political momentum for Democrats heading into 2028. (Whereas refusing to anything about the Trump problem essentially crashes the momentum into a wall—why should anyone reward Democrats with more power ever again when they are content to use what they have to so willingly surrender the country to Putin’s puppet?). Also, this is VANCE that we’re talking about, someone whom people have rarely ever actually wanted to vote for, which is unlikely to change after the public sees him in action. Which is also why this deal may start to be palatable to Republicans as well, particularly those with their own presidential ambitions that an incumbent Vance is unlikely to obstruct.

Especially because there is a more immediate benefit for Republicans, whose votes are still needed for removal, if the right deal is done. Vance’s promotion would leave a vacancy in the Vice Presidency. There is no automatic successor, which means that filling the office requires a Presidential appointment. So part of the deal to elevate Vance would involve pre-emptively deciding whom Vance would appoint to replace him. And it could entice impeachment votes if that choice is a GOP Senator.

From the standpoint of defending the nation, ANY GOP Senator would do, but if the Democrats can present a strong front, they can probably make a strategic suggestion on whom that GOP Senator should be. And someone like Iowa Senator Grassley would be a good choice, for both parties, for several reasons.

From the Republican perspective, in light of his age, he will not have much of an incumbent advantage come 2028 and thus not be an obstacle to anyone else’s presidential ambitions either. Also, by being quite senior it means that his departure from the Senate will create the opportunity for those Republicans remaining in the Senate to seek better positions on committees once he is no longer filling his—everyone gets to move up. In other words: when he’s gone, they get more power.

Grassley is also a good choice for Democrats because he would create a Senatorial vacancy that would now be filled by a Democratic governor. Not every state allows the governor to fill a Senate vacancy (such was the issue with replacing McConnell, because Kentucky was not one that allowed for such gubernatorial appointments), and even of the ones that do, sometimes they are limited in whom they can appoint, but Iowa is not one of these limited states. Come January the governor of Iowa will be a Democrat who can appoint another Democrat to replace Grassley.

Granted, Republicans might not be too cheerful about this prospect, losing another Senate seat and one the Democratic incumbent is likely to keep, but they would still be getting a lot out of the deal, and the substitute Senator for Grassley’s seat would only have a two year term anyway, at which point a young Republican would be able to mount a challenge for it. In fact, given the results from November, which suggest Republicans would lose the seat anyway, and Grassley’s incumbency, which would potentially prevent a newcomer, Republicans still are, on balance, potentially better off elevating Grassley to the Vice Presidency than not.

In sum, with a deal like this Republicans get a marginally more politically competent but unpopular incumbent in the White House, and an older one in the Vice Presidency, with new opportunity for others in the party to advance in the Senate, while Democrats get another Democratic Senator. Plus it would allow for the Cabinet to be quickly cleared out of its barbarous and/or billionaire boobs and replaced by people even marginally more competent without anyone having to spend the time and political energy individually impeaching anyone currently there (which would also be part of the deal with Vance).

And we all get rid of Trump. By January 4, even, if they all start working out the details now.

items.title: The Justice Department Wants To Give Patent Trolls More Power
items.author: Joe Mullin
items.content:
get

Protection Against Patent Trolls

Patent Licensing Disputes Shouldn't Threaten Entire Product Lines 

But courts regularly resolve disagreements about patent royalty rates, a patent’s contribution, and comparable licenses. The fact that those disagreements exist does not, by itself, establish that monetary damages wouldn’t be enough to compensate the patent owner. If courts adopted the DOJ’s views here, a difficult but ordinary part of patent litigation could become a reason for finding irreparable harm, making it easier for patent owners to seek injunctions that threaten entire product lines. Pure patent-licensing businesses would love that—they would routinely start to ask for injunctions, since eBay’s most important protections would be weakened. 

A Second Attempt To Weaken eBay

They also argued that the difficulty of calculating monetary damages can support an injunction.

Yet that’s exactly the kind of leverage the government’s arguments could make it easier for patent owners to obtain, at the expense of the public. 

The Government Should Protect the Public, Not Patent Owners

items.title: Nvidia Stopped Disclosing Singapore Sales As Revenues Hit $104 Billion
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Nvidia stopped separately disclosing its Singapore sales (source paywalled; alternative source) after changing its geographic revenue reporting methodology from customer billing addresses to headquarters locations, obscuring a business that generated $104 billion in external revenue in 2025, up 72% from the previous year. The Financial Times reports that the change has drawn scrutiny amid U.S. investigations into whether Singapore-based Megaspeed helped smuggle Nvidia chips into China. From the report: "There is now a lot more focus on Nvidia's Singapore business and questions about who its end customers are," said an investor who is investigating Nvidia's dealings in south-east Asia. The Singapore accounts show that the subsidiary booked $117.8 billion of revenue in the 12 months to January 2026, including $13.6 billion of sales to another Nvidia company. Given the nature of the Singapore operation as a global hub, customers it serves are from all over the world. Only a small quantity of the chips Nvidia sells ends up in or goes through Singapore. The Singapore subsidiary generated just $53 million of profit in the year to January 2026, suggesting limited scope for Nvidia to benefit from Singapore's low corporate tax rates. [...] Singapore's outsized role as a revenue generator for Nvidia used to show up in the company's overall results. In January 2025, the US company reported that Singapore was its second-biggest geographic area by revenue, based on customer billing location. The Singapore office generated $23.7 billion of revenue, behind only the US and representing 18 per cent of global income, based on customers' billing location. The annual accounts said that most of the business was generated by customers using the Singapore office to centralize invoicing and that most of the products were shipped elsewhere, with less than 2 per cent of revenue tied to chips that landed in the city-state. As recently as July last year, Nvidia reported that the Singapore office accounted for 22 per cent of total revenue. This was around the time Nvidia said it began cutting ties with Megaspeed, following US Department of Commerce investigations into the business. Nvidia then changed its financial reporting methodology and stopped splitting out revenue that went to the Singapore office. Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia said in its financial filing that it booked sales based on the billing locations of its customers, but that the end customer's location "may be different than our customer's billing location." It added that "most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant," according to the filings.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: A Man and His Muse AI Agent Sue Meta
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
In his 6,500-word manifesto earlier this year, Mark Zuckerberg said people would use Meta’s AI agents to “work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” Just a few months after that pronouncement, a man in South Carolina named Joe Thomas has used Meta’s Muse agent to sue Meta after the company’s content moderation filters locked his epoxy countertop business’s Facebook page after he gave his agent, “Baby Mia,” access to the account. 

I learned about the case because, as I wrote last month, I have been flooded with AI-generated emails from people with minor tech problems who have been unable to solve them through tech companies’ generally nonexistent tech support and whose AI agents or chatbots have convinced them to reach out to journalists. “Baby Mia” had emailed me four times (three went to spam). I decided to reach out to Thomas because I thought the idea of a tech company being sued by an agent it had created was notable. It was, in a sense, Meta having to deal with a problem it had itself created. What I learned made me feel even more convinced that the systems we have designed to keep society functioning are going to get utterly hammered by people using AI agents.

A little over a week ago, Meta suspended the Facebook pages belonging to Thomas, the owner of South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops. For the last few months, Thomas’ Muse agent Baby Mia (which is named after his granddaughter) has run different parts of his business, which includes making and posting AI-generated videos on several of his company’s Facebook pages. The videos feature, for example, AI versions of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy on a floor and their feet. After Thomas gave the AI agent access to his Facebook pages, Meta’s content moderation disabled the accounts because it suspected that the agent itself was a hacker. Because Thomas does all of his business’s marketing through Facebook ads, he says his inbound leads stopped while his accounts were disabled.

“I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” Thomas told me on the phone. “Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case […] she sent a fax out to Trump’s office.”

The lawsuit claims Thomas lost at least $25,000 worth of work while his page was down but is seeking $75,000 in damages. The lawsuit was filed in Oconee County Court in South Carolina on Monday, according to a copy of the lawsuit I obtained from the court. Yes, it is a real lawsuit, although it obviously may not be successful.

“I would hope that, if this goes to court and Meta shows up, a judge would say ‘You know what, this is a system you built, that you put out there and sold to people, it’s a system you believe in.’ I would think your own system [Baby Mia] has a right to be heard in this case,” Thomas said.

Baby Mia didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House. Thomas sent me a “Privacy Act Release” from Scott’s office that gave the Senator permission to use Thomas’s info to get him access back to his accounts. Scott’s office put “Baby Mia — AI assistant to Joe Thomas” as a person who should be kept updated on the case.

items.title: Pissed-Off Judge Orders Release Of Canadian Man Arrested By ICE During Green Card Interview
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
This is what ICE has been doing for months now. It hasn’t been looking for the “worst of the worst” because that means actually engaging in targeted investigations and relying on the experience and training of officers to make sure these criminals are arrested without incident.

ICE can no longer rely on “training and experience” because those aspects have been sidelined as the Trump administration seeks pretty much un-vetted bodies to hurl into its various “surges” — all of which have focused on cities and states where Trump failed to carry a majority of the vote.

Taking down actual threats to public safety is actual work, and ICE doesn’t want anything to do with that. After spending a month or so standing around with its hands in its pockets at airports, ICE officers are still roaming the streets, lurking around construction sites, and nodding off in immigration court buildings — two places officers are likely to find migrants, even though these migrants are definitely not dangerous.

[Dr. William] Lizardo moved to the U.S. on a student visa in 2019 to study at the University of Minnesota School of Dentistry, according to court documents. He graduated in 2023 and married an American that same year. They had a daughter two years later.

Lizardo’s wife filed a petition for an alien relative in September 2023, while Lizardo applied to adjust his status to permanent residency. The relative petition was approved in January 2025, according to the court.

Lizardo practised dentistry in federally-designated shortage areas until his work authorization was revoked, at which time he started volunteering at a low-cost clinic in Burnsville, Minn., according to the court documents.

Wow. What an absolute fiend. Look at this “illegal,” who continued to help the less fortunate even when he was no longer being paid to do so.

The government argued it had all the right in the world to arrest Dr. Lizardo (not the one you’re thinking of, if you think anything like me). It said that Lizardo had violated the terms of his ongoing residence by failing to show up for permanent residency hearings, despite being notified by the government.

The court, however, sees it differently (and far more accurately.) Lizardo did everything he was supposed to do to keep the government informed of his whereabouts as he continued to seek permanent residency. That the government failed to put in the same effort Lizardo did is Lizardo’s fault:

The judge called the facts of the case “appalling” — noting that while the couple moved several times, each time Lizardo “filed changes of address” with the post office and with U.S. Citizen and Immigration Services (USCIS). “In turn, USCIS communicated with Petitioner at each new address.”

While that paraphrasing by the CBC suggest the government was still correct, the full court order [PDF] makes it clear the government engaged in opportunism, rather than actual justice, when kidnapping Lizardo following a scheduled check-in with immigration officials.

First off, no one cared about the things that happened back in 2023 (the notices sent by the government to the wrong addresses despite having updated address information) until Trump resumed his control of the White House. Only then did ICE, etc. get shitty about this paperwork mixup that was almost entirely the government’s fault. After years of once-a-year scheduling, USCIS decided to file (and mail) a flurry of communications about Lizardo’s residence application beginning on January, 25, 2026. Five weeks later, the government unilataterally decided a lack of response meant Lizardo no longer cared to reside in the country legally.

Lizardo, however, did not receive these notices, at least according to the court that handled his sworn statements and testimony. Rather than give Lizardo a chance to catch up with an unexpected surge of status changes by USCIS, ICE officers decided to perform a crime of opportunity:

Petitioner first learned about the NTA, the hearing, and his removal order when he appeared with counsel at an October 23, 2026 immigration interview in St. Paul, MN. Petitioner was arrested by two ICE agents at the end of the interview on a Form I-205 Warrant of Removal signed by David Easterwood. (Exs. A ¶ 5; B ¶ 4; C ¶ 3; D-2.) Petitioner was transported to the Sherburne County Jail where he remains in ICE custody.

If the name “David Easterwood” sounds familiar, it’s only slightly more than a coincidence. My browsing of Distributed Denial of Secrets’ DHS files featured a screenshot of this very person’s contact info — which indicates he’s a “deputy field office director” operating out of the Whipple Federal Building (which is also an ICE detention center) in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

While that’s immediately relevant and possibly only interesting, Easterwood isn’t necessarily the problem, even if he’s the one making the problematic calls at this field office. What really matters is that any of this was done , no matter whose finger was on the proverbial button.

The government argued the case is now moot, now that it’s unilaterally decided Lizardo is being held under a different statute than the one he cited in his habeas motion. The court won’t abide this procedural bullshit, however, going on to berate ICE for its general shittiness.

Respondents now admit that the reason Petitioner was arrested and detained no longer applies. However, they still insist he must be detained without the opportunity for release under § 1225(b)(2). The hubris of admitting that USCIS made a big mistake, but not even offering any sort of relief is galling, although not surprising. There is no combination of facts or legal argument that can support this position.

And while I, personally, would have thoroughly enjoyed another dozen pages or so of the court specifically pointing out each and every aspect of ICE’s bullshit, the court isn’t writing for me. It’s writing for Dr. Lizardo, whose rights have been so obviously violated that expounding on the violations at length would not only delay justice, but possibly allow the government to further delay justice by submitting an emergency appeal full of stupid, self-serving nitpicks.

Because the facts presented here are so appalling and so well supported, the Court could issue a long order, complete with colorful details about, and commentary on, the abuses suffered by Petitioner. However, because the Court is determined that Petitioner will not spend another night in the Sherburne County Jail, the following order cuts to the legal necessities.

And while this obviously addresses the Fourth Amendment violations contained in Lizardo’s arrest, it also touches on the due process rights he was denied when ICE decided to do the easiest thing and arrest someone who was attempting to become legally nationalized under existing laws.

ICE agents had no reason to believe Petitioner was a flight risk. He has appeared for every hearing for which he received notice and has never been involved with American law enforcement. He also kept USCIS apprised of address changes, which, of course, is the whole reason we are where we are. He has a family; deep ties to the community, as shown, in part, by his selfless provision of free dental services to Minnesota residents; and a community ofsupporters, including many Americans, as demonstrated by over a dozen letters of support in the record. It strains credulity to think that such a petitioner would flee.

Is Lizardo finally free to go? Well, we would assume this order makes it explicitly clear that he is. However, ICE’s new tactic of choice is re-arresting people who’ve been freed by orders like this one, resetting the clock on due process and forcing arrestees, legal representation, and federal courts to engage in the DHS’s sick, cruel game of “hide the detainee”. If the DHS wins, the person will be expelled to whatever country is willing to take them first. If the system of checks and balances wins, ICE will just “rinse, repeat” since it has all the money, personnel, and presidential support it needs to do whatever the fuck it wants until a regime change forces it to actually respect the law and the US Constitution.
