items.title: Alex Karp Took The Mask Off For Fascism. Now He’s Pretending It Never Came Off.
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
Early in the Trump II administration, after pointing out that the biggest issue in tech policy was no longer tech policy, but democracy, I wrote a piece called “Fascism for First Time Founders,” as a warning shot for tech founders and CEOs who were quick to embrace Trumpism as a permanent new world order. Many did so primarily in the belief that having friends in the White House might wipe away some annoying red tape that the Democrats were insisting on regarding little things like the environment and consumer protection. Given that most of Silicon Valley isn’t actually down with fascism, it seemed like the crew of Thiel-pilled founders who felt otherwise might want to think beyond the immediate environment, regarding how it would look in the long term.

But, then again, the nature of being Thiel-pilled is that you don’t think about long-term strategy; you just keep seeking short-term opportunities to gain an advantage and take it at any cost, assuming you can keep grabbing those advantages over and over and over again.

Anyway, one of those Thiel-pilled CEOs is Palantir’s Alex Karp, who spent years in the past cosplaying as a half-hearted anti-war progressive, which was always suspect for the founder/CEO of a company whose entire mission was about empowering the state to surveil everyone. Karp, who tends to show up at conferences and on TV news shows as an erratic, confused person who is quite sure he’s the smartest person in the world, spent 2025 and 2026 making sure no one would ever again associate him with the progressive values he never really held.

He went full on MAGA, realizing that it would be a huge boon to his own bottom line.

And, as he’s known to do, Karp went at it with gusto. He embraced the grifting scam that was DOGE, announced Palantir was “completely anti-woke” while supporting the indiscriminate extrajudicial murder of people in boats, and supported Trump’s illegal war in Iran (while claiming to be against such wars). He also seemed pretty pleased that his technology was being used to kill people. Very “progressive.” Oh, and who can forget that time, just months ago, when he dunked on “female voters, who mostly vote Democrat,” claiming that in the new manly age of AI, “male, working class voters” would have way more power. And also the bit where he called Democrats beholden to a “woke pagan ideology.” This is not someone who believes in actual democracy.

Indeed, it became clear that Karp really, really enjoyed being on the side of fascism. He seemed to revel in it. Earlier this year, Palantir released a manifesto summarizing Karp’s book, The Technological Republic, and it reads like the work of a true believer in a MAGA-techno-futurist fascist future. We called it out as such at the time — and warned it was unlikely to end well, given the public backlash and clear hatred for Trumpian fascistic incompetence.

It talks about using Silicon Valley smarts “in the defense of the nation.” It mocks weak petty tech like smartphone apps and free email in favor of “A.I. weapons” and “hard power… built on software.” For no clear reason it attacks US post-WWII foreign policy, explicitly saying “the postwar neutering of Germany and Japan must be undone.” It also embraces surveillance tech and whines about the exposure of “the private lives of public figures” (hmm…)

And it closes on a truly fascistic note:

Some cultures have produced vital advances; others remain dysfunctional and regressive. All cultures are now equal. Criticism and value judgments are forbidden. Yet this new dogma glosses over the fact that certain cultures and indeed subcultures . . . have produced wonders. Others have proven middling, and worse, regressive and harmful.

We must resist the shallow temptation of a vacant and hollow pluralism. We, in America and more broadly the West, have for the past half century resisted defining national cultures in the name of inclusivity. But inclusion into what?

It is the silly rantings of a foolish person with little understanding of history, culture, or anything one learns in a basic liberal arts education.

But, after the recent midterms, Karp is suddenly trying to pretend that he’s always been “progressive” and is pulling a Steve Buscemi “how do you do, my fellow libs” act as he makes the media rounds.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir — all of our products are essentially progressive,” Karp said….

“My giving is equal Democrat, Republican,” Karp said. “I can tell you, without going into things I’m not gonna disclose, I’m very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I’ll tell you what, I’m also not the village idiot.”

My “I’m not the village idiot” t-shirt has people asking a lot of questions already answered by my t-shirt. For example, does Alex Karp not know that political giving is public? As Catherine Rampell showed using public FEC records, in the last two years Karp has given nearly $2 million to Republicans and less than $100k to Democrats:

That doesn’t seem that equal. Now, perhaps he’s quietly funneling millions to Democrats through 501(c)(4) dark money groups that don’t have to disclose donors. Or maybe he’s talking about pre-2024 (he did donate to Biden and Harris back in 2023). But at least from the public info available, there’s little to support the larger claim, and plenty to support the idea that he went all in for MAGA. Without any evidence other than “I say so” it’s tough to take his claims of equal support seriously.

Now, you can argue that Karp has no actual principles beyond what is best for his bottom line, and that he’ll switch positions overnight like a weather-vane, based on which way the wind is blowing. And, perhaps there’s some truth to that (and it’s also why he just hired former Democratic Senator Jon Tester as a lobbyist). But we should never forget that he bought into the idea of a 1000-year Nerd Reich, and publicly embraced MAGA fascism and cruelty, while helping power the tools and systems still being used today to disappear your neighbors — and Karp bragged about it, saying he didn’t understand why anyone found it controversial that Palantir “powers” ICE.

In my Fascism for First Time Founders piece, I pointed out that those who embrace fascist ideologues for expediency in their quest for commercial success usually find out it doesn’t end well. I also pointed out that it almost always burns trust with, and support from, other parts of the infrastructure stack that turn out to matter quite a bit. Karp’s sudden rediscovery of his supposed lifelong progressivism is a weak and cynical attempt to pretend he never embraced fascism, and to avoid taking responsibility for both his actions and his statements.

We shouldn’t let him get away with it. If he wants to admit that he was mistaken, he should say that and detail the actions he’s taken in support of dangerous authoritarianism, along with an explanation of how he’s going to fix all the damage he’s done. But don’t let him sit there and pretend he was never one of the leading captains in the MAGA-tech-industrial complex.

items.title: US Closes Loophole That Allowed China To Remotely Access Nvidia Chips
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Forbes: In a statement published on Monday, the Commerce Department said a new interim rule will address "rapid advancements in cloud computing" that have made it easier for countries like China to access advanced AI chips under export controls, including by accessing them remotely in data centers located in countries not under U.S. export controls. The new rule will require an additional license to export, reexport or transfer chips to companies in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Brazil, or any other country the U.S. deems a "higher-than-normal risk of diversion." Last week, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to having an affair, which was linked to a relationship with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese intelligence asset and a former executive at Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer that was previously under suspicion for allowing China access to the company's advanced AI chips. The news comes days after Axios reported Lutnick held back from cracking down on companies suspected of diverting chips to China -- despite clashing with other Cabinet members including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Speaking to Fox Business's "Sunday Morning Futures" over the weekend, Bessent said he did not think the U.S. needed new legislation for regulating AI chip sales, saying "we have all the rules we need, we just need them enforced" and insisting "many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen." The new restrictions come the same morning President Donald Trump leaves for an extended trip to Asia, which will include a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Microsoft Blames Monster Email Outage On Software Defect Introduced In July Fix
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Microsoft says last week's massive Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a software defect introduced in a July update that remained dormant until a Teams failover and a simultaneous 14% reduction in gateway capacity triggered a cascading failure. More than 80% of the affected gateway servers became unresponsive at the outage's worst point, and because the months-old change could not simply be rolled back, engineers spent roughly 15 hours developing and deploying a patch that restored the previous code path. The Register reports: According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted." "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued. It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and... you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive." So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help -- they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: How an AI Content Mill Put a Real Musician Through Copyright Hell
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.

“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.

Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to , where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video. Unbeknownst to Shokin, her version of “Bre Petruinko” had become popular among DJs and electronic artists and had been sampled in dozens of songs. Someone in the comments pointed her towards one of the more popular tracks. “ and it’s something that has millions of hits [...] and 30 seconds into this track I hear my own voice and I was utterly shocked. I didn’t know how to react,” she said (the video has more than 4 million views).

“The first thing that comes to mind is, ‘Oh my god, someone stole my voice and didn’t credit me,’” she said. Shokin said she talked to a lot of DJs and figured out how they’d gotten her voice. They’d purchased a pack of samples from a company called Loopmasters that was selling her version of “Bre Petruinko” as part of its .

“I got in touch with the distributor and they were deeply apologetic. They were unaware that this had happened and they immediately tried to make right of the situation and granted me royalties on the sample pack,” Shokin said. “At that point, countless DJs and music producers had been using my voice for their own tracks, unbeknownst to me. At least I’m aware and at least I was making something off of it and I was satisfied with that. I didn’t love the way that it came about, but whatever, they tried to make right of the situation.”

But Shokin’s “Bre Petruinko” saga wasn’t over. Last month, she opened YouTube and noticed her original recording was gone. A company called Media Nov Records had issued a copyright strike against her song, and YouTube had taken it down.She thought it would be easy to get this reversed. It’s a public domain folk song and she had the original recordings and a history with a distributor. “If I just explain it to YouTube, they’ll understand,” she thought.

Media Nov Records advertises itself as a “distribution company” that that partners with artists to release their music on digital platforms. But a focuses on rights management and copyright protection. “At Media Nov, we go above and beyond to safeguard your musical creations. Our comprehensive rights management system leverages cutting-edge technology and legal expertise to ensure you receive the royalties you deserve,” it said on its website.

YouTube uses automated systems to work through copyright claims. When someone files a claim against a video, the company tends to automatically approve it. The original uploader can file a “counterclaim,” where they argue that the video should stay up, or that it should not be demonetized.

Shokin filed two counterclaims, but neither worked. “It's unclear to us whether you have a valid reason for filing a counter notification, so we won't be able to honor your request,” YouTube said in its last denial. It told her to contact the copyright holder; in this case, it was a public domain song and so there was no actual “copyright holder,” just Media Nov, which was claiming to hold it.

“I tried emailing them,” she said. “I tried calling them. There doesn’t appear to be a working phone line. I got in touch with [Loopmaster, which was selling her recording]. They tried getting in touch. I’m being ignored by everybody, by YouTube, by this media company that, like, the website seems to be entirely AI-generated, and all I want is to talk to a human about this.”

Media Nov’s site boasted about its use of automated DMCA takedowns, YouTube content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition. “Our advanced AI identifies your music across platforms ensuring accurate tracking and protection,” it said. The company says it has been in existence since 1996, but ’s Wayback Machine doesn’t show much of a web presence until last year. Its website is basic and barebones. 

The company has two addresses on its website. One is an apartment building in Los Angeles on Marina Del Rey. The other is the Black Church in Dublin, Ireland — a cathedral that’s been converted into an office space. The site listed a Los Angeles phone number that was busy every time 404 Media tried to call it. 

According to corporate paperwork filed in Ireland and reviewed by 404 Media, Media Nov Records was founded a little more than a year ago. Its listed address is the Black Church in Ireland but both of its shareholders gave addresses in Turkey.

404 Media found four different YouTube pages managed by Media Nov Records. Each contained hundreds of videos — many with AI-generated art assets and music. The songs are sometimes cross posted between the different channels and are mostly looping electronic beats. Think low effort “lofi beats” knock offs. The art assets are footage of sports cars, anime girls, and AI-generated pictures of women. The songs are cross posted on multiple channels and often generate fewer than 100 views. Each also has few YouTube shorts that revolve around “random acts of kindness.” A Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok) watermark is present in some of these videos.

Media Nov Records told 404 Media that it operates 500 of these channels and “works with various artists, content creators, and music partners.” The company did not initially return emails or phone calls from Shokin or Loopmaster, but responded to an email from 404 Media.

It said it would look into its copyright claim of Shokin’s track. “We remain willing to review the relevant ownership documentation, original audio files, and supporting evidence to investigate the copyright claim thoroughly. If an error is identified, we are committed to taking appropriate corrective action promptly,” it said.

After 404 Media requested comment, Media Nov Records responded to Shokin and asked her to provide “relevant documentation supporting her ownership of the recording, including original audio files, recording evidence, original publication dates, and any other supporting materials,” which is a wild request considering that it has nothing to do with her recording and does not own the copyright.

The company told 404 Media that Shokin and Loopmaster’s emails had gone to its spam folder. “Regarding ‘Bre Petrunko,’ we would like to clarify that the musical composition and arrangement rights associated with Philip Koutev’s work must be distinguished from the rights in any individual sound recording. Media Nov Records also holds certain rights relating to the relevant musical content,” the company told Shokin in an email reviewed by 404 Media.

“Recording your own cover or performance does not automatically establish ownership of the underlying composition or arrangement. Likewise, rights in the underlying musical work do not automatically establish ownership of your particular recording,” Media Nov  said. 

“It’s ironic that they’re in the copyright business,” Shokin said. “It’s not the arrangement that’s in question. It’s the voice and performance [...] they clearly have no clue what they’re talking about.”

It's unclear why Media Nov Records brought Koutev into the conversation. 404 Media asked which song or work in its catalog triggered the copyright notice against Shokin but Media Nov Records did not respond. 

“That makes it really ridiculous,” Alfred Steiner, an artist and copyright lawyer, . “If it’s her voice and her playing instruments, what could she possibly be infringing if it’s a folk song from the 19th century?”

The situation between Shokin and Media Nov Records sounded odd to Steiner. “I've seen lots of providers where you say ‘I have the rights’ and basically say nothing more than that, and they put it back because they’re taking a risk now. They’re harming her. If they just put it back, they’re at no risk,” he said. 

“It sounds, to me, like a small company — despite the fact that they represent or run 500 YouTube channels — that are understaffed and is using a lot of different tools, probably a lot of AI, to identify tracks that are ostensibly owned by its clients and then automatically filing takedown requests,” he said. “They’re probably taking down far more than they have the right to take down.”

Minutes after it sent Shokin an email asking for proof she’d recorded the song, Media Nov Records followed up in an email addressed to both 404 Media and Shokin. “Following our review, Media Nov Records has decided to retract the copyright removal request for Samantha Shokin’s video. We are taking this step because the video has not generated revenue or received views, and we do not consider maintaining the removal request necessary at this stage,” it said. “However, this decision does not constitute a waiver of any rights we may hold. We intend to initiate appropriate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute.”

Around 24 hours later, Shokin’s original video was back up. A spokesperson for YouTube confirmed that it reinstated the video after the claimant withdrew their complaint. 

“It sounds like they got scared and feel like this is not a battle worth fighting,” Shokin said after seeing the email from Media Nov Records.

“Submitting a takedown request for rights that you don’t have can subject you to liability which includes actual damages and costs and attorney’s fees,” Steiner told 404 Media. “Doing this on a slipshod, shotgun approach is inadvisable from my perspective. Of course, if all of the people you end up offending are small parties and don’t have the resources to respond through the court system, and you are a fly-by-night entity that is hard to pin down and nobody knows who you are [...] it can be difficult to get a remedy.”

Shokin said she felt vindicated but was unhappy that it took a journalist emailing Media Nov Records to get them to listen to her. “They got my emails and they got Loopmaster’s email and they were just ignoring it because they only decided to respond because they got scared that it’ll be bad press,” she said. “It’s just not great all around. The whole system is broken. It feels like a broken system.”

items.title: Reporters Without Borders Calls For Brendan Carr’s Impeachment
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
His endless illegal actions may not not rise to the level of indiscriminate boater murders and the illegal mass murder of children, but Brendan Carr’s impeachment should very much be a priority. That’s the position of Reporters Without Borders (RWB), which last week called for Democrats — in the wake of their landslide midterm victories — to impeach FCC boss Brendan Carr in the new year.

It’s their first ever such call in the history of the organization:

“Carr’s tenure as FCC Chair has been defined by his campaign to intimidate and punish media organizations disfavored by the president. He has launched baseless investigations into news organizations, seized on vaguely written regulations to punish news outlets for speech deemed anti-Trump, threatened the broadcast licenses of TV and radio networks based on their editorial lines, gutted rules against media ownership consolidation, put his thumb on the scales of massive media mergers to benefit Trump allies, and improperly supported midterm campaigns. His consistent abuse of his office demands urgent action from Congress.”

Carr’s effort to roll back America’s already shaky media consolidation limits is a very clear, illegal act that undermines the will of Congress. As is stuff like Carr’s illegal efforts to dismantle the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides affordable internet access to rural schools, libraries, and communities.

And who can forget Carr’s illegal, unconstitutional assault on ABC for the “crime” of platforming journalism and comedians that dared make fun of the increasingly unpopular president. In that instance, ABC and Disney have provided evidence that Carr covertly worked with Trump-friendly TV broadcasters to pretend ABC broke the law — simply because the network aired an interview with Texas Senator elect James Talarico (particularly fertile ground for oversight subpoenas in the new year).

There are also numerous instances where Carr very clearly violated the Hatch Act, most recently when he he illegally leveraged his authority during a political rally for Alaska Republican Senate candidate Dan Sullivan. From the RWB statement:

“The American people have decisively rejected the Trump administration’s trampling of the Constitution. Few individuals have been more instrumental to the White House’s campaign to weaken the First Amendment than Brendan Carr. The incoming Congress now faces a defining test of its commitment to the Constitution and the freedoms it guarantees. Press freedom cannot be defended through words alone. RSF does not take the question of impeachment lightly. In fact, our organization has never before called for the removal of a US official. But the severity and persistence of Carr’s misconduct demand an extraordinary response. Congress has a constitutional responsibility to hold him accountable. Restoring the FCC’s independence must be central to that effort.“

There’s endless other stuff that tends to be obscured in the media by Carr’s ham-fisted attacks on free speech, whether it’s the way he’s made life easier on robocallers (while pretending to be tough on robocallers) and shitty prison telecom monopolies, stripped away every last shred of (already flimsy) U.S. oversight of our lumbering, unpopular broadband monopolies, rubber stamped endlessly harmful mergers, or turned a blind eye to the foreign-influence concerns of the recent Paramount/Warner Bros deal.

On one hand, Carr’s “policies” on telecom and media are utterly indistinguishable from industry. He’s never seen an AT&T or Comcast policy he hasn’t adopted as his own. But Carr’s unique in that he’s also an unapologetic fascist and bigot, and has spent a lot of time during his tenure demanding that telecom and media giants be more racist and sexist if they want their terrible, pointless mergers approved.

Trump’s first term FCC boss, Ajit Pai, was a textbook example of obvious regulatory capture, building an FCC dedicated exclusively to the interests of the biggest media and telecom giants. Carr’s similarly compromised, but his tenure has also been infused not just with dangerous and illegal authoritarian zealotry, but the sort of lame, edgelord meme-slinging you’d expect of a dim highschooler.

There’s simply no shortage of ammunition for investigations and impeachment in the new year. Without it, things will not only get decidedly worse for free speech and consumer protection, but the closest Carr will get to “accountability” is some post-FCC high six-figure gig at a telecom or media industry think tank, where he’ll spend the rest of his days using what’s left of his credibility to further ratfuck competition, consumers, and free speech.

If there’s ever somebody desperately in need of “making an example of” by a reconstituted Congress, it’s Carr.

items.title: Purism Announces 'Librem 5 v2' Linux Phone with RISC-V SoC
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
From the Linux-news blog OMG Ubuntu: Purism is crowdfunding a new version of its Librem 5 Linux smartphone, this one powered by RISC-V rather than Arm. Librem 5 v2 will use an octa-core SpacemiT K1 RISC-V SoC, replacing the quad-core Arm64 NXP CPU. This processor shift will provide better performance and longer battery life than the original Librem 5 and not run as hot in use. Memory is bumped to 8 GB RAM, up from 3 GB, and storage leaps to 128 GB from 32 GB. Librem 5 v2 will run PureOS, Purism's Debian-based operating system using Phosh as its UI. SD card read speeds are faster, which is handy since the device can boot a second OS from a memory card. On-board hardware encoding means the Librem 5 will be able to take 13 megapixel photos and shoot high-definition video for the first time.... "RISC-V is the future, and Librem 5 v2 is the perfect product to bring it to a mainstream audience", Jonathon Hall, CTO at Purism, says of the launch. "Freeing us from the control of Big Tech starts with the foundation, and RISC-V's foundation frees us from the oligarchy. The Librem 5 v2 puts you in control of your data, combining that with the ease of use we expect in the modern era". Its specifications include a 5.7-inch 720 x 1440 display, hardware kill switches, and a removable 4500mAh battery, writes Slashdot reader BrianFagioli: The asking price is $1,599, with production delivery targeted for roughly May 2028.. Purism acknowledges remaining work on graphics, peripheral drivers, ARM64 app emulation, and power management. NERDS.xyz argues that the concept is appealing, but the price and wait are difficult to justify for an everyday phone. Android already uses the Linux kernel, so the appeal here is an alternative built around PureOS and the broader desktop Linux ecosystem. Is this a reasonable cost to help fund that alternative, or too much money for hardware and software that buyers cannot yet evaluate as a finished product? Purism says they've already received 53 of their goal of 2,500 orders (2%) with 91 days still remaining. (The campaign runs through February 15 of 2027)

items.title: ULA Vulcan Rocket Failure Destroys 40 Amazon Leo Satellites
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
United Launch Alliance's new heavy-lift Vulcan rocket "malfunctioned while climbing into space yesterday," writes Engadget, "destroying its payload of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites..." Launch failures are always a risk, but amazingly, United Launch Alliance had never experienced one previously. Since the company formed in 2006 as a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, its Atlas V rocket has been famously dependable. Now, the company's more powerful, more complex Vulcan will be under review by engineers and is facing a possible grounding... As well as being a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the failed launch will be a blow to Amazon's Leo internet satellite system, intended to rival SpaceXSI's Starlink network. Leo has 38 Vulcan flights booked to launch its satellites, following eight successful Atlas V missions. Many of those are now likely to be delayed. Amazon's other launch provider, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin, suffered its own setback in May when its New Glenn rocket exploded on the launchpad. The Federal Communications Commission required Amazon Leo to have 1,600 satellites in orbit by July 31, 2026, but so far it only has around 390 in service... "No operator could have predicted that all three core heavy-lift launch programs... would experience repeated, concurrent scheduling slips severe enough to exhaust the buffers Amazon Leo had built in," the company said back in July. "Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something," the company said in a post on X, promising a transparent and thorough investigation. "We will provide further updates when new information becomes available. Thanks to long-time Slashdot reader schwit1 for sharing the news.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: AI-Generated Books Confront Publishing Industry With Big Questions
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Romance novelist Coral Hart publishes her own romance novels for the Kindle, and found a kind of superpowere when she realized "the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month," reports The Guardian: Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself "high six figures". Like any Kindle Unlimited author, she is only paid per pages read: it would make no business sense for her to churn out books that readers quickly abandon... "So, it's not taking the human out of the equation. It's taking the friction and the time and the business blocks out of the way." One study (awaiting peer review), led by Tuhin Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University, estimates that around one fifth of recently self-published books contain at least 25% AI-generated text. Hart now teaches courses on how to use AI to produce books. Unless disclosing the use of AI becomes a legal requirement, she advises other authors not to do so because of the public response. "The minute someone discloses [AI use] they get death threats, they get called names, they're ousted," she says.... In the literary world, many people fear the tech will undercut and replace them. "I think people are very afraid of AI, and people in publishing are delusional in thinking that it's not going to overtake our industry, that their screaming on social media is going to stop it." But the anger comes from another place, too. If large language models can spit out books that people want to read, or produce a convincing pastiche of your favourite writer, that's almost certainly because they were trained on established writers' stolen work.... Many writers oppose AI for both moral and aesthetic reasons. One group of 70 prominent authors wrote an open letter calling on the big five publishers — Penguin Random House, Hachette, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Macmillan — to promise that they will "never release books that were created by a machine". The publishers did not promise. [Tess Callero, a literary agent with Europa Content, says] "...you have to wonder the reason they aren't. Is it because they see a future in which potentially these books could be monetised?"] So where do we go from here? Will big name writers win the argument for keeping AI out of literature, or will our bookshelves and e-readers soon be crammed full of AI-generated stories? And if a reader can't distinguish human from machine writing, does it still matter? The Guardian's author notes this new technology brings new challenges to the book publishing world: Publishers have concerns about US copyright law, "which specifies that a book must be 'human authored' and considers AI-generated text public domain. " The article notes high-profile books being canceled after accusations their writers used AI. But even in those cases, "Another unresolved question is if and when publishers should withdraw books," since if publishers liked it enough to make the deal, shouldn't they stand behind that judgment? And should there be a way for authors who want to experiment with AI to work with top book publishers? (One theory is publishing houses are afraid of alienating a handful of top writers who almost universally oppose AI.) "Right now, to write without the aid of a machine is to swim against a strong cultural tide," concludes the article's author, noting a recurring reaction from friends who "have looked at me with something close to pity when I tell them I would never use AI to write."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Should Jensen Huang Return as Nvidia's CEO? Supporters and Critics Disagree
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia's chief executive," reports Reuters, "and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter." One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House... The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang. The Guardian adds that Friday two major Nvidia shareholders "urged the board to keep 'all options' open." In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look "outside" the company for its next chief. "They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said on Fox News. Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang's affair with the alleged spy for Beijing... Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang's behaviour within the next 10 days. The Guardian also notes Elon Musk "and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company... " The letter demands that the company's board members "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts"... Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang's return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco's most renowned business incubator. Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had "erred, yes — to err is to be human — but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company". More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company's workforce. But it's difficult to verify the authenticity of signatories, notes The Verge: Business Insider reports that signatures include "Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor" and "Xi Jingping," likely a misspelling of Chinese president Xi Jinping. Not all believe Jensen Huang should be allowed to return to his seat. According to the Financial Times, one ally acknowledged that, "Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense." 23andMe founder Anne Wojcicki told Bloomberg that "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible ... We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Wojcicki endured a messy public divorce from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, after it was revealed he was having an affair with an employee.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: FAA Router In Middle-of-nowhere Arkansas Identified as Cause of Nationwide Flight Chaos
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Though the nationwide flight-grounding ended Friday, "Nearly 2,300 flights in the U.S. have been cancelled Sunday in the aftermath..." reports ABC News. "Additionally, some 18,689 flights were delayed, per FlightAware." But "a single malfunctioning FAA router in rural Arkansas appears to have caused the air travel chaos," reports the New York Post: The problem originated at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a newly installed router flooded the network with excessive data traffic, disrupting communications between pilots and air traffic controllers, the Wall Street Journal reported. "We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds," Rebecca Guy, the FAA's technology chief, said on Saturday. .. [U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean] Duffy said the failure occurred during routine maintenance to replace aging copper telecommunications with fiber-optic cables — part of a broader effort to modernize the FAA's outdated infrastructure. The router began flooding other devices across the air traffic control network with connection attempts, disrupting both communications with aircraft and radar feeds. A radar station in Amarillo, in the Texas panhandle, is also being eyed as contributing to the outage. And new flight cancellations reported for Monday already stood at 144 as of Sunday afternoon, with 641 delayed, reports ABC News (citing data from Flight Aware): A spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, the company that manufactured the routers believed to be central to the ground stop, said in a statement to ABC News that the devices were working properly Friday, when the ground stop occurred. "Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer. It did not fail or act improperly," the statement said... L3 Harris is a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and that worked with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper to install the routers. "We have that router in the L3 Harris lab down in Florida," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told co-anchor Martha Raddatz on ABC's "This Week" Sunday, referring to the specific router in Arkansas that officials believe caused instability in the air traffic communication system Friday afternoon. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Pranksters Redirect Bitly's Links in X Posts for Trump, McDonald's and Burger King
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"A massive link-hijacking scheme has turned corporate social media archives into bizarre and offensive redirects," reports the New York Post: Posts from high-profile accounts — including fast-food giants McDonald's and Burger King, as well as President Donald Trump — are getting hacked, with over decades-old links suddenly redirecting users to unrelated website links including links about 9/11 and the Holocaust. An unknown party appears to be taking control of expired Bitly link shorteners — a widely used URL-shortening and link-management service — and altering their destinations.... Another Burger King tweet from July 13, 2011 — reading, "Now it's even easier to eat right at BURGER KING® restaurants with @WeRRestaurants. All you need is a zip code!" — was warped to link straight to Adolf Hitler's Wikipedia page... Two posts on Donald Trump's X account were also altered: a 2013 post redirected to a "Baby Fortnite" page, while a 2012 post linked to a video of Mario and Luigi from Super Mario Bros. The article notes that about 20 of Trump's old X posts had "switched" links, including some now pointing to videos of the Transformers. And it adds that "outraged web users are also slamming Bitly over its flaw that allows links to 'die' and be recycled by pranksters and bad actors." "Links dating as far back as 2009 from URL-shortening service Bitly were affected," reports CNN, "and only corporate and political X accounts appear to have been targeted, with President Donald Trump's personal account seemingly hit the hardest." "Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and former Vice President Mike Pence... were also hit to varying degrees." Bitly said Sunday afternoon in a post on X that it had "identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts." The company said it suspended the accounts that altered links and were working to disable the affected URLs... It's unclear whether hackers made custom Bitly links, which effectively allow them to copy the original URL and redirect to any website. That may have been possible if the original Bitly link to the website no longer exists or has expired.... Another 2013 post from Trump tagged former Republican nominee for president Mitt Romney, and links to the popular game "Geometry Dash".... A post in 2011 by Trudeau contains a Bitly link that redirects to a vulgar YouTube audio clip... Government accounts have also been ironically affected. A 2012 post from the FBI about computers infected by "Ghost Clicks" now directs to a page with a photo of a seal, while the Department of Defense account had a separately redirected post.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Siri Glitches Ruin Reviewer's Test of Apple's New 'HomeView' Smart Speaker
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Apple has started selling its new HomeView smart speaker, a 7-inch square-with-rounded-corners screen equipped with a built-in camera. It pairs with your iPhone or iPad to offer personalized content from your email or text messages, using facial recognition to identify each family member. But in a video report, one Wall Street Journal reviewer discovered an issue while testing its smart home feature: WSJ REVIEWER: I've spent the last few years turning my home into a smart home that I can boss around with Siri. A smart lock, a special garage door opener, motorized shades, even a Raspberry Pi in my basement hooked up to my router that lets non-HomeKit devices from Ring and Nest work with Siri. It was all going well, the smart home controller of my dreams even. But then... Reviewer: Open the garage door. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Please use the Home app. Reviewer: Siri, you have the Home app, and you're called the HomeView. Open the garage. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Reviewer: Open the smart wifi garage. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Please use the Home app... WSJ REVIEWER: Apple explained that for security reasons, Siri won't unlock your doors or open the garage through the HomeView using voice commands. You can only tap the screen to unlock them. The concern is that someone could shout a command from outside and gain access to your house. This security concern doesn't make much sense to me. This thing can recognize my face, confirm it's me, and pull up all sorts of information from my phone. But it can't recognize me enough to open my garage? Finally I got Siri itself to explain this top-security measure. Siri: For security reasons, I can't unlock your door or open your garage from this device. Because anyone nearby can speak to a shared speaker. Reviewer: But I'm looking at you! You see my face, and you hear my voice! Siri: I understand. But I don't have a camera to see you. And voice recognition alone isn't secure enough for unlocking your home. Reviewer: You don't have a camera? Siri: That's right. This device doesn't have a camera, so I can't see you. I can only hear your voice, which is why I need you to use your iPhone or Apple Watch to unlock the door. Reviewer: I see, Siri. You're gaslighting me. An Apple spokesperson said they'd send out a software update next month that would let HomeView unlock garage doors and other door locks by voice once it's recognized a user. (And Apple said the update would also fix Siri's hallucination that it didn't already have a built-in camera.) In the end, the speakers sounded good, and the reviewer appreciated how Apple's HomeView didn't have ads on its screeh like the Amazon Echo Show. But the device's built-in Siri voice assistant was "about as reliable as a Magic 8 Ball... And the frustration is so real. Sometimes Siri just doesn't get the voice recognition right... Oftentimes, other devices in the room think I'm talking to their Siri... And sometimes Siris just talk to each." iPhone: Siri is built into your device, so you don't need to download... HomeView: Downloading support for Siri. iPhone: To download the Apple Support app, open the App Store on your device, search for Apple Support, and tap get or the download icon. I've installed support. Reviewer (muttering): I honestly could cry. This might be a first — crying. iphone: I'm software, so I don't have feelings. But it sounds like you're going through a difficult moment. It can really help to talk to someone you trust, like a friend, family member, or a professional who can support you". They complained that sometimes Siri "is just slow, or it gets stuck thinking and thinking and thinking." (It took three minutes to answer their young son's question "What's 10 times 40?") They concluded HomeView's facial recognition feature works well, and so does its smart home functionality (especially when they fix its door-unlocking next month). But its built-in Siri AI is "not great." It's gotten better this year, and the reviewer found it "genuinely useful for some things on their iPhone. "But Apple still has a Siri problem. And on a device that's supposed to be the intelligent center of your home, that's a big problem." It reminded the reviewer of another new first-generation Apple product, the iPhone Duo: "good hardware waiting for the software to catch up."

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Funniest/Most Insightful Comments Of The Week At Techdirt
items.author: Leigh Beadon
items.content:
This week, our first place winner on the insightful side is Nimrod with a comment about the tool built by election deniers that claimed perfectly alive voters were dead:

Trump’s insistence that anything that goes against him HAS to involve cheating actually makes perfect sense if you look at the situation from the perspective of a serial liar who also habitually cheats at golf. Since HIS wins are predicated upon his own illegal manipulations, certainly those of others MUST be, as well.

In second place, it’s Stephen T. Stone with a comment about the somewhat surprising fact that Trump hasn’t made the expected attempts to interfere with the midterm results:

Quoting Norm Eisen here: “The reason ‘Trump didn’t steal the elections’ is because we & the pro-voter coalition stopped him EIGHT times over the past 21 months[.]” As I said in a comment on a different article, this is a lot like the Y2K situation: The problem coming and going without any real issues makes us feel like the problem was overblown…and makes us forget that a whole hell of a lot of people put in a hell of a lot of work so that the problem would come and go without any real issues.

You were right to worry. I’ve no doubt that, had Trump and his fascist goons been far more competent, they would’ve found an effective way to fuck with the midterms. The fact that they didn’t speaks to the strength of the institutional guardrails around our elections (including the Supreme Court, for once) and to the work put in by pro-democracy groups to keep those guardrails up. The American people did their part by electing Democrats in such large numbers, with large enough margins and large enough swings, that there isn’t any way for someone to explain those results with “the elections were rigged” without someone else wondering why Republicans would rig elections against themselves in states where they controlled the state-level government.

For editor’s choice on the insightful side, we start out with two more comments on that subject and the fact that the DOJ dropped its illegal voters lawsuit against California. First, it’s That One Guy reminding us that things aren’t over yet:

Never underestimate someone THAT spiteful and deranged

While it’s nice that they to have accepted the results for the moment this is the same person/group that has claimed for six years now that they actually won the 2020 election and instigated an insurrection to try to overturn it in their favor, so personally I’ll be waiting until the new congress is sworn in and at their seats before I believe that Trump and his goons have actually accepted this loss and aren’t trying to find a way to overturn it.

Next, it’s BernardoVerda with a comment about what the withdrawal of the lawsuit means:

Wasn’t the withdrawal of this “illegal voters” lawsuit essentially an admission that the charge was pure fabrication all along – just an exercise in generating smoke and confusion, to help steal seats if they lost?

Over on the funny side, our first place winner is Bob with another comment about supposed illegal voters:

homeopathic election rigging?

The DoJ only found 28 illegal voters in California, out of 23 million, because the election rigging is homeopathic! The multiple dilutions make the rigging ever more powerful.

In second place, it’s an anonymous comment about Starlink:

Starlink is great for improving internet access in remote, rural areas that lack adequate infrastructure.

You know, like downtown Washington, DC.

Things were a little slow on the funny side this week, so we’ll keep it to just one editor’s choice. It’s a reply from Pixelation to Bob, who accidentally double-posted versions of his winning comment above:

Sure. Clearly you are a Democrat voter, posting twice!

That’s all for this week, folks!

items.title: GTA 6's Upcoming Launch Celebrated by Wendy's, YouTube, the City of Miami, and 20% of America's Workforce
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Fast food restaurant Wendy's drew an image of their redheaded mascot in the style of GTA, posting it on social media with the message "Our ride-or-dies are gonna love what we have in the works," and the date 11/19/26. That's how widespread the hype has become for Thursday's release of Grand Theft Auto VI. The BBC reports that fictional brands from the game are now actually appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game's "Vice City" setting. And GamingBible.com reports Rockstar Games has announced Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival, "a real-life music festival to be held in Miami, Florida... on November 21, 2026. Featuring two stages, the festival will be headlined by some incredible artists that, to state the obvious, feature on the game's soundtrack...." YouTube said pre-launch videos about the game have already racked up a whopping 40 billion views (with 900 billion views for videos about all GTA games). And now YouTube is partnering with Rockstar Games to offer several special features on launch day: Fans can drop themselves directly into Vice City using the GTAVI: Visit Vice City Shorts Effect. The feature includes multiple iconic backgrounds, making it easy for creators and fans to build their own launch-week videos... Listeners can find the official GTAVI soundtrack (featuring Morgan Wallen's "Last Thing You Need") and the complete GTA series anthology playlist directly on the YouTube Music homepage throughout launch week... Starting November 19 at 12 AM ET, fans worldwide can tune in to youtube.com/youtube for a 24 hour stream packed with live gameplay, creator podcasts, and original content featuring top creators... [On launch day] fans can jump straight into the global broadcast by clicking the custom GTAVI-themed YouTube logo (Yoodle) on the YouTube homepage At one one study suggests nearly one in a five U.S. workers plan to skip work on Thursday, writes the New York Post: Roughly 18% of workers plan to take Thursday off to park themselves on the couch and wreak havoc across the revamped Vice City, according to data from BambooHR, which analyzed information from 3.4 million US-based employees... Half of the joystick jockeys planning to take off will simply call in sick instead of requesting time off, BambooHR reported. The hordes of workers playing hooky could cost the US economy $1 billion in lost productivity, International Business News reported. Forbes reports the game has $1.18 billion in pre-orders from 12 million buyers, according to market research firm Sensor Tower, puting it ahead of Grand Theft Auto V, which had 7 million pre-orders. The BBC points out that "Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history. This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it. But that's a problem for other games, reports GamingBible.com: With most current-gen consoles having somewhere between 512 GB and 1 TB of free storage before expansion upgrades, it means if you're a gamer with lots of games installed, you're going to have to make some sacrifices and delete any older games you're not currently playing. As reported by Push Square, it seems that Electronic Arts is also getting the message, as it allegedly is showing messages inside games asking players not to uninstall in anticipation of the GTA VI launch. GamingBible.com notes one final concern for hardcore gamers. "Rockstar Games recently confirmed the game targets 30fps, even on high-end consoles like the PlayStation Pro. While it probably won't affect the game's total sales, many gamers are appalled."

items.title: Huawei Set To Challenge Tesla Powerwall with New, 20 kW Home Battery
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery," reports Electrek: This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla's latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark... The Chinese tech firm is calling it an "all-in-one residential energy system" that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that's available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW. The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei's proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It's so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes. Huawei's basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with "just" 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That's enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you'll want to keep going if you're preparing for more than a day or two without power. If that sounds like you, Luterra's got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can keep scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel. Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini).

items.title: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills, Reports ProPublica
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Environmental activist Bill Gates has "quietly accumulated a $29 billion stake in America's No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services," reports ProPublica, in a new 5,000-word investigation. But inspectors from America's Environmental Protection Agency "have repeatedly found methane — a highly potent greenhouse gas — escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. Republic has lobbied against regulations that could make the waste industry cleaner, including by keeping organic garbage out of landfills in the first place." While Gates has invested at least $2 billion in green companies, he's "put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry," their article argues. And Gates has increased his stake in Republic "to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion." While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They're responsible for as much as a fifth of the country's emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.... [Gates] has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor... "It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic's behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits," said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder... Gates didn't respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn't find any public comments he's made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic's shares — "It's 'Garbage In' for Gates," the New York Post headline read — the company's stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows... A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune [in 1999]... To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he'd given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets... After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates' stake in Republic over the years that followed. [On behalf of the Gates Foundation] Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic's main competitor, Waste Management. Methane emissions weren't a major focus of climate activism until years later The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it's responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"In November's edition of the TIOBE Index, Rust has dropped out of Top 10," writes I-Programmer, noting that Rust ceded the #10 position to Go. "At the same time, another Google-originated language, Dart, has entered the top 20 ousting Julia after only one month." TIOBE explains Dart's popularity is mainly being driven by Flutter, Google's framework for building cross-platform mobile applications. In fact, Flutter has become one of the major technologies for cross-platform mobile app development. The Dart language itself is not particularly unique, although it incorporates many modern programming language features. Its success is largely driven by the strength of the Flutter ecosystem and the convenience of developing applications for multiple platforms using a single codebase... [In November's ranking] Visual Basic has also lost two places, making room for R and SQL in the Top 10. Further down the ranking, Assembly has re-entered the Top 20. So TIOBE ranks the top 10 languages in November as Python, C, Java, C++, C#, JavaScript, R, SQL, Visual Basic, and Go. But I-Programmer points out that "At the top of the table, Java is back in the top 3, after over three years in 4th position," pushing C++ down to #4. Are some changes more significant than others? If you think of the ratings as shares of a pie divided into 100 pieces, there is one huge slice — Python, accounting for a over a fifth of the pie, then comes C with a slice slightly less than half of Python's. Java and C++ then have smaller slices... and C#'s share is around half of their average size. Over half the pie has now been shared between just five languages... — Next 5 (#6-10): 10.17% (JavaScript, R, SQL, Visual Basic, Go) — Next 10 (#11-20): 11.12% (Rust, PHP, Fortran, Scratch, Perl, MATLAB, Assembly, Swift, Delphi, Dart) — Next 30 (#21-50): 12.81% — Final 50 (#51-100): 12.93% [So in this month's chart...] Java has overtaken C++, but as you can see from this month's Top 10 chart they are in lock step and the difference between them is insignificant. More obvious is that Python is way ahead of all the competition and that C has an edge over Java and C++. For more discussion of this see TIOBE — Two To Rule Them All in which Mike James argued that this: confirms the standard model of programming - code is written in Python and C and everything else is just noise. Back in July we reported Rust Enters TIOBE Top 10. After four months in #10 Rust is now back at #11, which is still three places above its position, 14, a year ago. Given the way these rankings operate it only takes a very small month-on-month change for a language to lose its position and even, as has happened here it can gain in terms of its percentage ranking while still moving down. So Rust with 1.63% in November is now in #11 when it had been in #10 with 1.44%.

Read more of this story at Slashdot.
